title: `# nolint next expr` (and `# nolint next line`?)
description:
One downside of `# nolint next` is it can sometimes be awkward to position it just right; and to maintain this positioning as the codebase evolves.

`air` skips formatting with `# fmt: skip`, which anchors to the subsequent _expression_. I think we should support something similar, provisionally `# nolint next expr` (`# nolint next_expr`?).

As a companion / for clarity, we could consider introducing the analogous explicit naming `# nolint next line` equivalent to the current `# nolint next`.

We could also consider whether `# nolint next line` behavior is actually needed once `# nolint next expr` is supported.

title: New linters for numerical correctness and stability
description:
I have implemented three new linters to detect some common problems with floating-point arithmetic in R. I think they could be useful additions to {lintr}.

### `float_comparison_linter()`

This linter marks exact comparisons involving numeric literals, including `==`, `%in%`, and `match()`:

```r
x == 0.1
x %in% c(0.1, 0.2)
match(x, c(0.1, 0.2))
```

These comparisons can give unexpected results due to floating-point rounding. By default, plain numeric literals such as `3` are also included, but `lint_implicit_integer = FALSE` restricts the checks to explicit decimal or exponent notation.

### `decimal_fraction_linter()`

This linter detects decimal constants used in expressions such as:

```r
as.integer(x * 365.25)
floor(x / 0.1)
```

It suggests using reduced fractions instead of decimal constants to avoid potential floating-point rounding problems. It also supports `ceiling()` and `trunc()`. Decimal values that are exactly representable in binary are ignored by default, but this can be changed with `lint_exact_binary = TRUE`.

### `numerical_stability_linter()`

This linter detects expressions for which R provides more numerically stable functions. For example:

```r
log(1 + x)                  # log1p(x)
exp(x) - 1                  # expm1(x)
1 / (1 + exp(-x))           # stats::plogis(x)
log(1 - pnorm(x))           # stats::pnorm(x, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE)
```

It also covers other distribution functions, logarithmic special functions, and complementary probabilities and quantiles. The code is only analyzed statically and is never evaluated.

All three linters are already implemented and have documentation and tests. Would there be interest in adding them to {lintr}?

I am also not sure whether it would be better to keep them as three separate linters or combine them into a single linter for numerical correctness and stability. What would you prefer?

title: Extend ifelse_censor_linter() to ignore parens in ifelse(x < (y), x, y)
description:
Doesn't come up much with just a symbol `y`, but this is not uncommon for a more complicated expression like

```r
ifelse(x < (k - 1), x, k - 1)
```

Stripping away parens is a much more general issue, which is hard to solve without recursion. I think we are OK to just focus on adding relevant logic in linters where it's more empirically likely, `ifelse_censor_linter()` is just such a case.

title: Extend boolean_arithmetic_linter to detect all()-like cases too
description:
Follow-up to #1579

Extend `boolean_arithmetic_linter()` to include `all()`-alike expressions like `sum(x == y) == length(x)` --> `all(x == y)`.

The issues are

 1. we can't just test for `length()` on the RHS (e.g. `sum(x == y) == length(z)` could be totally different)
 2. looking for `sum(x == y) == length(x == y)` (i.e., exact expression matching, which we do in some other places) will only find a particularly silly manifestation of the issue
 3. there is a bit of a combinatorial explosion if we have to look for _any_ symbol found inside the logical expression on the RHS (e.g. `sum(x == y) == [length(x) _or_ length(y)]`).

A first pass would be to check how many hits there are for the naive version (i.e., condition 1), to see how worth investing in this complicated logic is to begin with.

title: namespace_linter() is OS-dependent
description:
Consider in {knitr}:

https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/646ba86a2f2220454265b4ff1038fecfc5381923/R/plot.R#L70

```r
win.metafile = grDevices::win.metafile
```

{grDevices} _does_ export `win.metafile`, but _only_ when compiled on Windows:

https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/blob/bb087814dacb62ed5f44a3c449c31268e137b710/src/library/grDevices/NAMESPACE#L76-L86

```r
lint("R/plot.R", namespace_linter())
# R/plot.R:70:31: warning: [namespace_linter] 'win.metafile' is not exported from {grDevices}.
#     win.metafile = grDevices::win.metafile,

```

title: undesirable_function_linter could be namespace-aware
description:
Currently we ignore namespaces as all our defaults are `base` exports, but downstreams could be dealing with more ambiguous situations where namespace-qualified lints are better, e.g. `run_model()` is exported by `foo` and `bar`, but only `bar::run_model()` is undesirable:

```r
undesirable_function_linter(c(`bar::run_model` = NA))
```

Should "just work" and we add a `SYMBOL_PACKAGE` requirement on the XPath for `bar::model` and any other elements matching `::`.

description:
Now we would need to provide the backticked version:

```r

e = get_source_expressions(tmp)

length(e$expressions[[1L]]$xml_find_function_calls("%%"))
# [1] 0
length(e$expressions[[1L]]$xml_find_function_calls("`%%`"))

```

Should the former usage "just work" to save the user having to think through whether `` ` `` is needed?

title: undesirable_function_linter fails to match non-syntactic names
description:
```r
lintr::lint("`%%`(x, y)\n", lintr::undesirable_function_linter(c("%%" = NA)))
lintr::lint("`%%`(x, y)\n", lintr::undesirable_function_linter(c("`%%`" = NA)))
# <text>:1:1: style: [undesirable_function_linter] Function "`%%`" is undesirable. Disable this with a comment: `# nolint` (one line) or `# lintr: disable` (multiple lines). See go/tidy-style#linting for more.
# `%%`(x, y)
# ^~~~
```

It seems should either match in the first case, or perhaps throw a warning/error that non-syntactic names must be wrapped in backticks.

But the latter also seems off -- we apparently can't match a call in quoted form:

```r
lintr::lint("`%%`(x, y)\n", lintr::undesirable_function_linter(c('"%%"' = NA)))
lintr::lint('"%%"(x, y)\n', lintr::undesirable_function_linter(c('"%%"' = NA)))
```

(no lints from either call)

title: `unnecessary_nesting_linter()` incorrectly recommends to get rid of braces in ggplot2 chains
description:

``` r

x <- TRUE
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  {

  } +
  geom_smooth()" -> code

library(lintr)
```

title: Edge case on special `array` for `lengths_linter()`
description:
Found this edge case quite deep in a package and it's hard to come up with a less convoluted example. 

`lintr` suggests using `lengths()`:

``` r
lintr::lint(
  text = '
test <- array(
  list(NULL, c("max1", "min1")),
  dim = 2L
) |>
  structure(dimnames = list(c(NA, "data1")))

map_int(test, length)',
  linters = lintr::lengths_linter()
)
#> <text>:8:1: warning: [lengths_linter] Use lengths() to find the length of each element in a list.
#> map_int(test, length)
#> ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

But it would give an object with different attributes:

``` r
test <- array(
  list(NULL, c("max1", "min1")),
  dim = 2L
) |>
  structure(dimnames = list(c(NA, "data1")))

waldo::compare(
  purrr::map_int(test, length),
  lengths(test)
)
#> `names(old)` is a character vector (NA, 'data1')
#> `names(new)` is absent
#> 
#> `dim(old)` is absent
#> `dim(new)` is an integer vector (2)
#> 
#> `dimnames(old)` is absent
#> `dimnames(new)` is a list
```

## Description

When `lint('', text = ...)` is called with an empty string as `filename`, `object_length_linter` and `object_name_linter` crash on Windows with:

```
Linter `linter()` failed in '':
Caused by error in `normalizePath()`:
! path[1]="": The system cannot find the path specified
```

This happens because both linters call `find_package(source_expression$filename)`, which calls `normalize_path('', mustWork = TRUE)`, which fails on Windows when the filename is empty.

This is triggered in practice when the R language server (`languageserver`) calls `lintr::lint(path, text = content)` and the path is empty (e.g., for `untitled:` or `vscode-userdata:` URI schemes where `path_from_uri()` returns `""`).

## Minimal Reprex

```r
library(lintr)
txt <- c("x <- 1", "camelCase <- 2")

# Works fine:
lint(text = txt)

# Crashes (object_length_linter calls find_package -> normalizePath(""))
lint("", text = txt)
```

**Expected:** No crash; linters should handle empty filename gracefully when `text=` is provided.

**Actual:** Error in `normalizePath(path[1])` from `find_package()`.

## Root Cause

In `R/get_source_expressions.R`, `find_package()` calls `normalize_path(filename, ...)` without checking if `filename` is empty or `nzchar()`.

Both `object_length_linter` and `object_name_linter` pass `source_expression$filename` to `find_package()` unconditionally. When `lint()` receives `filename = ""` and `text = ...`, it sets `inline_data = TRUE` so `normalize_path("", mustWork = FALSE)` succeeds in `lint()`, but `find_package()` still calls `normalize_path("", mustWork = TRUE)`.

## Suggested Fix

Guard `find_package()` against empty filename at the top of the function:

```r
find_package <- function(filename, ...) {
  if (!nzchar(filename)) return(NULL)
  # ... rest of function
}
```

This is also related to #2847; the `inline_data` / `parse_settings` interaction means that `lint("", text=...)` defaults to `parse_settings = FALSE`, so even if `.lintr` disables these linters, the config is not read.

## Session Info

- lintr 3.3.0.1
- R 4.5.0 on Windows 10
- languageserver 0.3.16

``` r
library(lintr)
packageVersion("lintr")
#> [1] '3.4.0.9000'

lint(text = 'quote(italic(F) == "2.35")', linters = T_and_F_symbol_linter())

#> quote(italic(F) == "2.35")
#>              ~^
lint(text = "plot(1, main = expression(italic(T)))", linters = T_and_F_symbol_linter())
#> <text>:1:35: style: [T_and_F_symbol_linter] Use TRUE instead of the symbol T.
#> plot(1, main = expression(italic(T)))
#>                                  ~^
```

title: object_usage_linter should respect NAMESPACE file
description:
# Description

`object_usage_linter() ` reports no visible global function definition warnings for functions that are imported via the package `NAMESPACE` (e.g. `importFrom()` / `import()`). Those functions are actually available at runtime, so these warnings are false positives for package code.

# Reproducible example

In NAMESPACE

```
importFrom(dplyr,mutate)
```

In R/file.R

```
mutate(data, x = x + 1)
```

leads to: 

```
file.R:1:1: warning: no visible global function definition for 'mutate'
```

No warning should be emitted because `mutate()` is imported via `NAMESPACE` and therefore available to the package code.

# Proposed Solution

When running the `object_usage_linter` in a package project, it should parse the `NAMESPACE` file for imports and collect all imports from importFrom. This avoids noisy false positives for properly authored packages and makes `lintr` behave consistently with `R CMD check`.

# Notes:

I am not sure how to handle general package `import()` in `NAMESPACE` as the whole package needs to be checked which functions are exported.

title: object_usage_linter() should skip objects transitively attached by Depends
description:

```r
library(bit64) # NB: as of now, bit64 Depends on bit, but that will likely change in the future

  bit()
}
```

Linting this will lint on `bit`:

```
warning: [object_usage_linter] no visible global function definition for 'bit'

  ^~~
```

But because `library(bit64)` necessarily attaches {bit}, I think it shouldn't.

``` r
#> if (a <- 1 && b <- 2) { print(a) }
#>     ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

lintr::lint(
  text = "if (a <- 1 && b <- 2) { print(b) }

  linters = lintr::implicit_assignment_linter(allow_scoped = TRUE)
)
```

title: undesirable_function_linter could handle setter functions better
description:
This might be considered a false positive:

```r
linter <- lintr::undesirable_function_linter(c("time" = NA))

time(x) <- time(y)
", linter)
```

This mattered for me because `time()` is `stats::time()`, but `time<-` is ``zoo::`time<-` ``, not ``stats::`time<-` ``.

title: Rtex code extraction problematic

title: Error in first line of .R script files when missing function parenthesis
description:
When I open a .R file in VS Code (or Codium) some files are linted with an error at 1st line:
```code
Failed to run diagnostics: ! in callr subprocess.
Caused by error in `call[[1L]]`:
! object of type 'symbol' is not subsettable
```

I reported this in REditorSupport/languageserver: https://github.com/REditorSupport/languageserver/issues/723

They made a commit that make this error disappear in some files, but it remains in some. I found that it still happens in files where functions are called at the end without any argument, an called without parenthesis:
```R
data |>
  filter(id > 3) |>
  summary
```

@randy3k reproduced the issue:
```R
> lintr::lint(text = "data |> filter(id > 3) |> summary")
Error in call[[1L]] : object of type 'symbol' is not subsettable
> packageVersion("lintr")
[1] '3.3.0.1'
```

Although this code is correctly interpreted by R (and is accepted in RStudio or Positron), I believe it is bad practice and one should be warned by lintr. Yet if you want to adhere as closely as possible to the syntax variations of R, lintr should not break like this.

title: namespace_imports logic is wrong for import(foo, except=c(bar, baz))
description:
We currently assume that elements of `$imports` returned by `parseNamespaceFile()` that are length>1 are `importFrom` directives; actually, they might be `import(., except=)` directives.

For example, here's dplyr ([permalink](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/blob/55dfc1c5b49eae3f1b144ebe7d9fa2c3d79b1835/NAMESPACE#L473-L474)):

```r
parseNamespaceFile("dplyr", "..")$imports[2:3]
# [[1]]
# [[1]][[1]]
# [1] "vctrs"
# [[1]]$except
# [1] "data_frame"
# [[2]]
# [[2]][[1]]
# [1] "R6"
# [[2]][[2]]
# [1] "R6Class"
```

 And indeed:

```r
lintr:::namespace_imports("dplyr")[435,]
#       pkg        fun
# 435 vctrs data_frame
```

title: line_length_linter could optionally ignore `test_that()` long names
line_length_linter could optionally ignore wide tribble() declarations
description:
```r
tibble::tribble(
  ~a, ~b, ~c,
  "very_very_long_in_column_1", "short", "short",
  "short", "very_very_long_in_column_1", "short",
  "short", "short", "very_very_long_in_column_1"
)
```

`air` formats this by aligning on the commas:

```
tibble::tribble(
                            ~a,                           ~b,                           ~c,
  "very_very_long_in_column_1",                      "short",                      "short",
                       "short", "very_very_long_in_column_1",                      "short",
                       "short",                      "short", "very_very_long_in_column_1"
)
```

This can easily spill over a given line width (here, it increases the total width from 49 to 90). We can ignore expressions inside `tribble()` and `rowwiseDT()` in `line_length_linter`.

Closely related to #3130 + #3053

title: New branch_exit_companions= (?) for unnecessary_nesting_linter()
[bioc] Add a linter to enforce NO spaces around certain infix operators.
description:
Soft requirement for #3027.

[Bioconductor's style guide requires](https://contributions.bioconductor.org/r-code.html#use-of-space):

> No space around “=” when using named arguments to functions.

There's currently no linter that supports this; the maximum possible is to exclude `EQ_*` from `infix_spaces_linter()`. It would be easier to add a new linter so as not to modify the existing linter's interface.

title: Allow lints on expect* cases using info=
description:
E.g.

https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/b65cee563faf892bba83cd918e24987abbc94957/R/expect_comparison_linter.R#L55

Originally, we excluded those because there's not always a clean equivalent where the recommended replacement lacks an `info=` argument. This was raised upstream to {testthat} at the time:

https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/issues/1594

After some time, we've reached an understanding that, in such cases as benefit from `info=`, the better alternative is to use `expect()` directly to provide `info=`.

So we can throw lints in those cases, which should probably get custom metadata based on whether `info=` was provided.

title: Support `type = "bioconductor"`
description:
`lintr` currently supports `type = "tidyverse"` and `type = "full"`.

It would be useful (and likely fairly low effort) to add a `type = "bioconductor"` for use with Bioc packages, since Bioc has some style suggestions that differ from tidyverse style (e.g., https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/issues/1132#issuecomment-4055685902)

The bioc style guide has a link to [style and formatting resources](https://contributions.bioconductor.org/r-code.html#additonal-style-and-formatting-references). If this package supported bioc style, we could add it there.

happy to help work on this, just filing a bug so I don't forget.

Full bioc style: https://contributions.bioconductor.org/r-code.html

When I have time later I can add some comments to document the differences vs. tidyverse style.

title: regex '^' or '$' (i.e., trivial boundary check) should lint
description:
Based on some investigation here: https://github.com/gagolews/stringi/issues/529, it is almost certainly a mistake to write `grepl("^", x)` -- almost certainly, `grepl("^", x, fixed=TRUE)` was intended. I found 3 such clear bugs as a result of the above cursory search:

 - https://github.com/InsightRX/PKPDsim/pull/145
 - https://github.com/IgDAWG/BIGDAWG/pull/10
 - https://github.com/cran/redcas/blob/775d2d749c5e9aee701dca085f26f95f08556e5d/R/redcasltx.R#L267-L274

I am only unsure which linter should be responsible for surfacing this.

title: Requesting less indent of what should be in list long assignment
description:
Hi, this is weird, ```lintr``` is requesting less indent that should be:

```R
library(wrapr)

list(
  "segment" =
    c(
      1,
      2
    ) %.>%
      sum(.)     
)
```

At least in my experience, and evaluations of other codes, I'm using the right way the indent, actually use the same format out of a list does not trigger any message, is only there.

Error:

```R
/tmp/c.R:7:6: style: [indentation_linter] Indentation should be 4 spaces but is 6 spaces.
      sum(.)
```

Note: ```wrapr``` is smilar to ```magrittr``` we just write explicitly where goes the previous value.

Thx!

title: Multiline logical comparison indentation error
description:
When I use multiline logical conditions such as the following, lintr throws an error but this is the format that is automatically indented by RStudio (Ctrl + I) or by air.

```R
is.null(a) ||
  length(a) == 1 &&
  is.na(a)
```

A full reprex is here:

```R
code_lines <- "is.null(a) ||
  length(a) == 1 &&
  is.na(a)
"

writeLines(code_lines)
#> is.null(a) ||
#>   length(a) == 1 &&
#>   is.na(a)

lintr::lint(
  text = code_lines,
  linters = lintr::indentation_linter()
)
#> '<text>:3:2': style: [indentation_linter] Indentation should be 4 spaces but is 2 spaces.
#>   is.na(a)
#>  ^~~
```

I would expect this to pass as I "feel" it is indented correctly.

```R
packageVersion("lintr")
#> [1] ‘3.2.0’
```

title: Non-R code blocks are parsed as R in Rmd/qmd files
description:
While trying to set up lintr in the `rextendr` package, I noticed that lintr parses the Rust code in the `{extendr}` code blocks as R code and raise errors.
https://github.com/extendr/rextendr/blob/870a03a67b50168c4df8d84d8fcdebdb9f5c33a7/vignettes/rmarkdown.Rmd

This seems to be the same for Quarto markdown files, and the `{ojs}` code block is also parsed as an R code block.

````qmd

---

```{ojs}
data = FileAttachment("seattle-weather.csv")
  .csv({typed: true})
```
````

title: is_numeric_linter also applies in cases like `is.numeric(x) || is.integer(x) || is.factor(x)`
description:
Follow-up to #1635 -- currently the logic can't handle the operator precedence mixing here, but this usage could be replaced by `is.numeric(x) || is.factor(x)`.

Here is a test that was commented out:

```r
# hopefully, by passing this test we get cases like
#   is.numeric(x) || is.logical(x) || is.integer(x) free as well.
#   probably just need to crib some logic from vector_logic_linter().
expect_lint(
  "is.logical(x) || is.integer(x) || is.numeric(x)",
  lint_msg,
  is_numeric_linter
)
```

title: implicit_assignment_linter(allow_paren_print=TRUE) is wrong for multiple lints
description:
Discovered incidentally by the AI reviewer of #3114:

```r
lint("
  (a <- 1L)
  mean(b <- 2L)
", implicit_assignment_linter(allow_paren_print=TRUE))
# <text>:3:8: warning: [implicit_assignment_linter] Call print() explicitly instead of relying on implicit printing behavior via '('.
#   mean(b <- 2L)
#        ^~~~~~~
# <text>:3:8: warning: [implicit_assignment_linter] Avoid implicit assignments in function calls. For example, instead of `if (x <- 1L) { ... }`, write `x <- 1L; if (x) { ... }`.
#   mean(b <- 2L)
#        ^~~~~~~
```

It gives a lint for the first expression with the wrong metadata (there should be no lint at all)

title: Improve string_boundary_linter message by customizing
description:
First, we can customize the message -- the reason for inefficiency is different for the regex approach vs. the `substr()` approach (the former is similar to the `fixed=TRUE` reasoning, the latter is because `substr()` performs a subset, then allocation, then comparison).

Once #1175 is finished we can also provide a fixed-string equivalent for the regex versions.

I guess we should also consider recommending `stringr::str_starts()` instead of `startsWith()` when `str_detect()` causes the lint (ditto `endsWith`:➡️ `str_ends`), WDYT? Might want to check the performance of `str_starts(x, fixed(pattern))` to `startsWith(x, pattern)`...

title: Linting Google Style variable and function naming
description:
I have just started looking into R linting and am unsure, whether I am configuring the plugins correctly.
I am coding based on the [Google R Style guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/Rguide.xml), which recommends using lowerCamelCase or dot.naming for variables and UpperCamelCase for function names. As far as I have read in the documentation it seems to be possible to enforce either lowerCamelCase or snake_case, but I could not find settings to allow UpperCamelCase for functions.

Is it possible to configure it for this usecase? I would like to keep name linting to spot mistakes in my naming easier.

That means 90% of these packages are creating some 'noise' for the {lintr} development process.

For packages that include an `expect_lint_free()` in their tests/ unit tests, I would advocate for them to move this to a GHA instead -- I don't think they want to be booted from CRAN if some small change in {lintr} rules finds an issue with their coding style.

As to the ones that don't use {lintr} in `R CMD check` at all, the first thing is to decide what to do. I think the right way forward is for packages that use {lintr} on themselves and want to annotate this in DESCRIPTION to use a designated key there. I can think of two options:

 - `Config/lintr: <path to .lintr>`. I think then we'd also want to incorporate that into {lintr}'s code for finding settings. This approach has some aesthetic appeal and makes straightforward sense and is self-contained, but comes with some maintenance burden.
 - `Config/needs/dev` or `Config/wants/dev`: This declares {lintr} as a `dev` dependency in a way that could be re-used by {styler}, {covr}, ... The downside is we'd probably want to coordinate on an agreed-upon way so that we don't create any back-and-forth later. I prefer this approach but am more hesitant to strike out a path here as a first mover.

@Bisaloo @maelle have you come across this issue elsewhere in the past? I know Lorenz has pursued something similar in the past with {styler}: https://github.com/r-lib/styler/issues/1121

title: seq_linter gives wrong message
description:
```
writeLines('mtcars[1:min(8, nrow(mtcars)), ]', tmp <- tempfile())
lintr::lint(tmp, seq_linter)
# /tmp/RtmpWXD4Q3/file4c4595f9321d2:1:8: warning: Avoid 1:min expressions, use seq_len. Disable this with a comment: `# nolint` (one line) or `# lintr: disable` (multiple lines). See go/tidy-style#linting for more.
# mtcars[1:min(8, nrow(mtcars)), ]
#        ^
```

I think this is incorrect because `! min %in% bad_funcs`, i.e. it's not the `1:min` that's triggering the lint, it's the use of `nrow` in `1:`.

title: Differentiate PERL-specific regex features in is_not_regex()
description:
We could in principle build in logic to detect whether `perl=TRUE` and interpret "regex or not" accordingly. One place this comes up in practice is for `'\<'`, which is a special character in default regex but not in PCRE. Empirically relevant for HTML-related regex e.g. `\\<li\\>`.

I'm not sure I've come across a thorough comparison of the two engines, so it will have to be pretty heuristic.

title: Combine rules related to regular expressions: regex_linter
description:
I think it makes sense to combine all of the rules related to regular expressions under one heading. They are a bit spread out and the number could grow (e.g. #2012 and #2868)

- Linters to merge:
   + `fixed_regex_linter`
   + `regex_subset_linter`
   + `string_boundary_linter`
   + `which_grepl_linter`

There are two parameters we'd need to design a merged version of:
  - `fixed_regex_linter(allow_unescaped=)` which weakens the linter to ignore strings like `"ABC"` that are technically fixed but don't use any regex metacharacters, so adding `fixed = TRUE` _might_ constitute visual noise vs. any possible performance benefit
  - `string_boundary_linter(allow_grepl=)` which exists due to small differences in NA handling of `grepl()` string boundary checks.

title: Recommend expect_shape()
description:
{testthat} now has `expect_shape()` which should be preferred over e.g. `expect_identical(nrow(x), 4)` --> `expect_shape(x, nrow = 4)`.

https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/commit/6bb8053b871ad0728cbaaf9127323d4155e8d86b

Earmarking this for when `expect_shape()` has been on CRAN for sufficiently long.

title: unreachable_code_linter() triggers on code after a switch with an error
description:
```r
lint(linters = unreachable_code_linter(), text = '
foo <- function(x) {
  y = switch(x, a = 1, b = 2, stop("bad x"))
  return(x + y)
}
')
# <text>:3:44: warning: [unreachable_code_linter] Remove code and comments coming after stop().
#   y = switch(x, a = 1, b = 2, stop("bad x"))
#                                            ^
```

title: 'break' in switch() case flags later cases as "unreachable"
description:
Related: currently this is flagged as a lint:

```r
repeat {
  switch(x,
    a = break,
    b = "d"
  )
}
```

```
<text>:4:14: warning: [unreachable_code_linter] Remove code and comments coming after `break`.
    a = break,
             ^
```

title: Release lintr 3.4.0
description:
{lintr} is failing on r-devel, so we might as well package up a release.

Prepare for release:

Do all of this in a new `rc-x.y.z` branch for the target CRAN version.

If running from the minimal devcontainer, be sure to check details for the additional system requirements you'll need to install.

* [x] [`3.4.0` milestone](https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/milestone/9)

* [x] Update version number in DESCRIPTION and at top of NEWS
* [x] Re-read and refine the entire NEWS for the release
* [x] Ensure `backport_linter()` covers all released R versions
* [x] Check URLs: `urlchecker::url_check()` or `tools:::check_url_db(tools:::url_db_from_package_sources("."))`
* [x] Run `testthat::test_dir("tests", shuffle = TRUE)` to ensure more hermetic tests

Then submit to CRAN

title: vector_logic_linter() misses filter(x, A && B) in a function
description:
This code used to lint, but no longer does:

```r
lint(linters = vector_logic_linter(), text = "
foo <- function(x) filter(x, A && B)
")
```

This is likely a regression due to #2935

title: Combine rules related to pipes: pipe_linter
description:
We currently have 6 linters related to pipes in the suite:

```
nested_pipe_linter,readability consistency configurable
one_call_pipe_linter,style readability
pipe_call_linter,style readability
pipe_consistency_linter,default style readability configurable
pipe_continuation_linter,style readability default
pipe_return_linter,best_practices common_mistakes
```

I propose combining them all into one linter for simplicity: `pipe_linter()`. By default it:

 - Enforces `|>` as the preferred pipe [originally `pipe_consistency_linter`]
 - Prevents `return()` at the end of a `%>%` pipe [originally `pipe_return_linter`]
 - Requires pipes in multi-line pipes to terminate lines [originally `pipe_continuation_linter`]
 - Prevents passing symbols to `%>%` pipes [originally `pipe_call_linter`]

And optionally:

 - Blocks nested pipes [orginal `nested_pipe_linter`; will need some care for how to handle `allow_inline=` and `allow_outer_calls=` arguments]
 - Enforces a different pipe [original `pipe=` argument to `pipe_consistency_linter`]

This will be a default linter since it enforces the tidyverse guide section on pipes: https://style.tidyverse.org/pipes.html

title: add exception for `library_call_linter()` when `library()` is invoked within a function body
description: add an exception for library() calls inside functions -- e.g. for libraries calling library() on behalf of the user. The current logic seems tailored to scripts, but the linter will end up being used in packages too.

title: Make rev(sort(.)) -> sort(decreasing=TRUE) rule optional
description:
Follow-up to #2614 / #3066.

Observe:

```r
x = c(a = 2, b = 2, c = 1)
rev(sort(x))
# b a c 
# 2 2 1 
sort(x, decreasing=TRUE)
# a b c 
# 2 2 1 
```

In code like `y <- rev(sort(x))[N]`, the difference can break back-compatibility. Therefore, I think we should make this lint optional, though I lean towards enabling it by default -- use cases for which this difference matters should probably be more intentional about their choice, including possibly marking `# nolint`. WDYT @Bisaloo / @IndrajeetPatil?

title: Handling imports from roxygen comment
description:
The linter indicates an object_user_linter issue for functions that have been imported using roxygen import statements. This doesn't happen on RStudio, only on VSCode. For context, I am working on a golem project.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25822124/175294041-11b48a77-1295-4735-8790-812c379a75ae.png)

title: Support cli functions in `extract_glued_symbols()`
description:
``` r
# glue::glue passes
lintr::lint(
  text = "foo <- function() { x <- 1; glue::glue('{x}') }",
  linters = lintr::object_usage_linter()
)

# cli functions lint
lintr::lint(
  text = "foo <- function() { x <- 1; cli::cli_h1('{x}') }",
  linters = lintr::object_usage_linter()
)
#> <text>:1:21: warning: [object_usage_linter] local variable 'x' assigned but may not be used
#> foo <- function() { x <- 1; cli::cli_h1('{x}') }
#>                     ^

# This is valid cli usage
x <- 1
cli::cli_h1('{x}')
#> 
#> ── 1 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

<sup>Created on 2023-10-31 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

title: Find unreachable code with implicit returns
description:
The current logic was written for explicit returns. With implicit returns, there can still be unreachable code (code after `stop()` will be caught in either case), especially comments, e.g.

```r
function(x) {
  x
  # remove or refactor this
}
```

While we're at it, make sure implicit returns are properly accounted for in the other various part of `unreachable_code_linter()`.

title: Remove version-specific ...names() workaround when depending on R>4.1.2
description:
Follow-up to #2503. `...names()` doesn't work as expected in R4.1.1 and R4.1.2, so we have an ugly workaround that will be simplified by just using `...names()`.

For reference, this is the item on `...names()` in the R4.1.3 BUG FIXES, fixed specifically by r81283.

title: lint_dir(pattern=) should be configurable by .lintr
description:
In {data.table}, for historical reasons we use the extension .Rraw for test files, thus [we have to run](https://github.com/Rdatatable/data.table/blob/014c82fd7b04e6e41da9680d41b25620a11f46b6/.github/workflows/lint.yaml#L31):

```r
lintr::lint_package(pattern = "(?i)[.](r|rmd|rraw)$")
```

(we don't use any of the other extensions in the default `pattern=` so we exclude them for simplicity)

This is fine in CI, but makes it hard to run interactively as we have to remember to add a strange regex to every execution of `lint_package()`.

Instead it would make sense if `pattern=` could be set by the config -- this is something that is reasonable to be fixed at a repo level and would allow the easy-to-remember approach of "always run `lint_package()`" to apply even locally.

title: Un-braced nested if/else gives false positive for unreachable_code_linter
description:
Found in {bit64}:

```r
lint(linters = unreachable_code_linter(), '
function(x, ...){
    if(is.null(env))
        has.cache <- FALSE
    else if (exists("nunique", envir=env, inherits=FALSE))
        return(get("nunique", envir=env, inherits=FALSE))
    else
        has.cache <- TRUE
}
')
# <text>:7:5: warning: [unreachable_code_linter] Remove code and comments coming after return() or stop().
#     else
#     ^~~~
```

https://github.com/r-lib/bit64/blob/cb4552b8345550d158cc7ae9b937b009f4dcd200/R/cache.R#L358-L363

title: New linter for `...names()` instead of `names(list(...))`
description: Since R version 4.1.3 there is the base R function `...names()` for the pattern `names(list(...))` with the benefit of being more concise and performant.

title: Gitlab / CodeClimate report
description:
Gitlab supports the consumption of a so called "codequality report" artifact, so that it can display static code checker results in a structured way, e.g. in merge requests, see https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/testing/code_quality/#import-code-quality-results-from-a-cicd-job.

This reports needs to be in a [specific JSON format](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/testing/code_quality/#code-quality-report-format) which is a subset of the [CodeClimate format](https://github.com/codeclimate/platform/blob/master/spec/analyzers/SPEC.md#data-types).

Linter like

- [ESLint](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/testing/code_quality/#eslint)
- [Stylelint](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/testing/code_quality/#stylelint)
- [MyPy](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/testing/code_quality/#mypy)
- [Flake8](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/testing/code_quality/#flake8)
- [Pylint](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/testing/code_quality/#pylint)
- [Ruff](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/testing/code_quality/#ruff)
- [golangci-lint](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/testing/code_quality/#golangci-lint)
- [PMD Copy/Paste Detector](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/testing/code_quality/#pmd-copypaste-detector)

already support that format.

Would you be interested in a contribution that adds support in the form of a function that consumes an "lints" object and returns a JSON string in the mentioned format?

title: Use skip_unless_r, eventually
description:
Just merged upstream: 

https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/pull/2094

This can replace our skip_if_not_r_version helper, but we should probably let it bake in CRAN for a cycle or two before refactoring. 

Filing as an earmark.

title: Lint expect_lint(x, NULL, linter)
description:
Follow-up to #2737 to prevent back-sliding.

I don't think this needs to be an exported linter -- we can leave it as an _ad hoc_ linter only used in our CI suite.

title: seq_linter() could optionally lint all 1:<non-literal> usage
description:
I think that a large portion of `1:<non-literal>` usages should be replaced by `seq_len(<non-literal>)`. In practice it's often as simple as:

```r
size <- length(x)
for (i in 1:size) { }
```

`1:10` should still be allowed as `seq_len(10)` is probably overkill.

I'm tempted to turn this on by default, but I'm OK with a more conservative approach to leave this under an option that's off by default.

title: Lint `deparse(substitute(x))` for `deparse1(substitute(x))`
description: Since R 4.0.0 the pattern `deparse1(substitute(x))` seems to be recommended over `deparse(substitute(x))`. See the PR for examples: https://bugs.r-project.org/show_bug.cgi?id=17671 but this most likely will have many false positives.

title: Single-indent multi-line function definitions
description:
The "Good" "Single-indent" example of "Multi-line function definitions" from the tidyverse style guide (https://style.tidyverse.org/functions.html#multi-line-function-definitions) currently generates a lint from `indentation_linter`:

``` r
code <-
'long_function_name <- function(
    a = "a long argument",
    b = "another argument",
    c = "another long argument"
) {
  # As usual code is indented by two spaces.
}'
cat(code)
#> long_function_name <- function(
#>     a = "a long argument",
#>     b = "another argument",
#>     c = "another long argument"
#> ) {
#>   # As usual code is indented by two spaces.
#> }
lintr::lint(code)
#> <text>:2:4: style: [indentation_linter] Indentation should be 2 spaces but is 4 spaces.
#>     a = "a long argument",
#>   ~^
```

<sup>Created on 2025-03-10 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

This occurs both with v3.2.0 from CRAN and commit https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/commit/a2b8d6fec967e037e736ba81eb7fca83333438c7 from GitHub.

In contrast, moving `) {` onto the line of the last argument produces no lint:

``` r
code <-
'long_function_name <- function(
    a = "a long argument",
    b = "another argument",
    c = "another long argument") {
  # As usual code is indented by two spaces.
}'
cat(code)
#> long_function_name <- function(
#>     a = "a long argument",
#>     b = "another argument",
#>     c = "another long argument") {
#>   # As usual code is indented by two spaces.
#> }
lintr::lint(code)
#> ℹ No lints found.
```

<sup>Created on 2025-03-10 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

title: Skip eval=FALSE chunks
description:
Resurrection of #581.

[As noted there](https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/issues/581#issuecomment-732421520), we can't get a fully general solution, as run-time usage of `opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)` is very hard to detect.

Still, I think it's feasible for us to look at chunk-level options as an improvement over status quo. The key will be using `knitr:::parse_params()`:

https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/e8aae19fcc7443b8a212c8dc65ba2b83894f1fe0/R/parser.R#L174

which takes as input a string like `"x, eval = stop('haha')"` and outputs a key-value list like `list(label = "x", eval = quote(stop('haha')))`.

Parsing chunk params is also something we want for #773.

At a glance, using `eval = FALSE` is a _very_ common way to tell `knitr` to skip R chunks:

https://github.com/search?q=filename%3ARmd+%22eval+%3D+FALSE%22

It looks like GH search can't help us find "```r" usage; I also don't see any usage of `opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)`:

https://github.com/search?q=filename%3ARmd+%22opts_chunk%24set%22%2C+%22eval+%3D+FALSE%22

So I think this issue is pretty high-impact & value, even if imperfect.

title: library_call_linter() should exempt header boilerplate in Rmd
description:
_Originally posted by @MichaelChirico in https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/pull/2152#discussion_r1323530530_

It's very common to start an Rmd vignette with an `include=FALSE` header setting up metadata:

    ```{r setup, include=FALSE}
    knitr::opts_chunk$set(...)
    ```

    ```{r first_visible_cell}
    library(my.pkg)
    ```

But `library_call_linter()` lints this. The right approach is probably to exclude certain calls preceding the first `library()`.

I've also wondered if `commandArgs(TRUE)` / options parsing _must_ come after the `library()` calls.

title: New linter `length_unique_linter`
description:
I would put that as a separate linter.

The closer analogue is `nested_ifelse_linter()`, whose primary recommended alternatives are `data.table::fcase()` and `dplyr::case_when()`.

But in that case, there _are_ ways to avoid the nested `ifelse()` using base functions, so the user doesn't _strictly_ need any new packages to fix the issue.

For `length(unique(.))`, there's no improvement in {base} (AFAIK).

Doesn't mean we shouldn't offer such a linter (since it'll be optional for users to turn on anyway), just by way of explaining why we didn't write that so far (it's certainly crossed my mind).

_Originally posted by @MichaelChirico in https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/pull/2051#issuecomment-1668881627_

title: Extend namespace_linter() for using '::' for functions already imported in the NAMESPACE
description:
```r
#' @importFrom pkg foo
pkg::foo()
```

The latter usage of `foo()` could be linted as `pkg::` is not needed.

Such a linter could help backsliding after clean-ups like #2031

title: New lint: `pkg_namespace_usage_linter`
description:
As a package maintainer I would like to know whether my _declared_ imports in the DESCRIPTION file are actually _used_ in the code. 

I managed to find a great third-party package [checkglobals](https://github.com/JorisChau/checkglobals/) that does similar thing and this is a dummy script executed on one of those packages
``` r
x_deps_in_desc <- desc::desc_get_deps() |> subset(x = _, type %in% pkgdepends::as_pkg_dependencies("hard")$direct) |> _$package
x_deps_in_code <- as.data.frame(checkglobals::check_pkg()) |> _$package |> unique()
setdiff(x_deps_in_desc, x_deps_in_code) # this should be empty
#> [1] "R"             "GenomeInfoDb"  "GenomicRanges" "scda"         
#> [5] "teal.logger"   "teal.reporter"
search() # just to show no side effects
#>  [1] ".GlobalEnv"        "package:stats"     "package:graphics" 
#>  [4] "package:grDevices" "package:utils"     "package:datasets" 
#>  [7] "package:methods"   "Autoloads"         "tools:callr"      
#> [10] "package:base"
```

This obviously does not follow how lints are written but I can move it forward. More importantly, I would like to ask how does it fit `lintr` as a whole? This feels more like a validation on the package level as opposed to individual scripts? How to report issues as I cannot point to the script line of code that is wrong but rather DESCRIPTION file. 
I am interested in hearing your thoughts on that. The bottom line is that I can create my own GHAction for that but from my perspective I would like to avoid creating so many testing functionalities and I would like to reuse an open engine of `lintr` if possible.

(CC @m7pr)

title: Lint `rev(sort(x))` pattern in `sort_linter()` in favour of the more efficient alternative
description:
As mentioned in the docs for `rev()`:

> Note that this is no longer needed (nor efficient) for obtaining vectors sorted into descending order, since that is now rather more directly achievable by [sort](http://127.0.0.1:24379/help/library/base/help/sort)(x, decreasing = TRUE).

``` r
x <- rnorm(1e5)

bench::mark(
  sort(x, decreasing = TRUE),
  rev(sort(x))
)[1:5]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   expression                      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc
#>   <bch:expr>                 <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>
#> 1 sort(x, decreasing = TRUE)   2.16ms   2.25ms      402.    1.15MB
#> 2 rev(sort(x))                  2.4ms   2.52ms      391.    2.29MB
```

But, currently, we don't lint it:

``` r
library(lintr)
lint(text = "rev(sort(x))", linters = sort_linter())
```

<sup>Created on 2024-06-19 with [reprex v2.1.0](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

title: Add globbing support to exclusions
description:
Maybe we should look into allowing wildcard exclusions based on file names?

```
exclusions: list("*.Rmd" = "library_call_linter"))
```

seems readable and concise for your usecase @IndrajeetPatil. WDYT?

_Originally posted by @AshesITR in https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/issues/2161#issuecomment-1719762111_

title: Better support for linting a general vector of files
description:
Sometimes, we want to lint a vector of files that's not neatly captured by `lint_dir()`.

Currently, there's three ways to do so:

 1. Use `lint_dir()` with non-default `patterns=`. This is not very flexible -- `patterns=` is passed to `dir(patterns=)`, which only operates on `basename()`.
 1. manually loop over the vector with `lint()`. This sacrifices several things handled by `lint_dir()`, like a progress meter, possible parallelization (#485), `flatten_lints()` merging results, etc.
 2. Use a `.lintr` config to set exclusions. This works well for simple packages/projects, but is not fully general and very clunky for interactive use cases.

One use case I have in mind is linting the R sources. `lint_dir()` includes lots of files that we'd typically not want to lint, e.g. test scripts for the R parser that intentionally use bad R syntax, and the concatenated source `all.R` files. It's very hard to get `lint_dir()` to ignore those `all.R` files especially, which is very inefficient, so the best way to lint the R sources currently is to filter `list.files()` by hand, then `lintr:::flatten_lints(lapply(filtered_files, lint, ...))`.

I can see ~two~ three (3rd thanks to @JSchoenbachler) options for improving this situation:

 1. `lint_dir()` gets an argument specifying a vector of files, e.g. `files=`, user can specify either `path=` or `files=` and the rest, including `lint_package()` is unchanged.
 2. `lint()` accepts a vector of file names in `filename=`.
 3. A new `lint_files()` function.

I can see arguments for both; I'm currently leaning towards option (1) because the code change will be very small & will make it easier to plug in to parallelization in the future. The main advantage of option (2) is not growing the argument surface of any functions. (3) is also a new function, but we could have `lint_dir()` call it so that all of the logic around combining lints over multiple files is still in one place.

Filing issue here for feedback/discussion.

title: Lints() constructor to vectorize Lint()?
description:
Now that we have a series of consistency checks built into `Lint()`:

https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/f8bb91e7f0fd749f9a28523006a4cedd369c2688/R/lint.R#L374-L395

It may make sense to offer a vectorized interface for constructing lints so these consistency checks can be vectorized for efficiency, rather than running the checks lint-by-lint.

title: Integration with roxygen2: data structure for get_source_expressions()
description:
There are a number of linters it would be nice to write regarding roxygen2 documentation, e.g. ensuring `@param` entries are in sync with the declaration (of course `@inheritParams` makes this hard to to completely, but certainly `@param X` should only happen when `X` is indeed a parameter.

We could also apply the rest of the lint suite directly to code in `@examples`.

Parsing the roxygen markup is easy enough: `roxygen2::parse_file()`. The key will be integrating this result with our existing data structure from `get_source_expressions()`, which I don't see a super clean way to do while also ensuring we keep the link between which doc entry corresponds to which source expression.

As a reminder, the current structure is laid out here: https://lintr.r-lib.org/reference/get_source_expressions.html#value.

We also likely want to keep the data structure back-compatible unless we want this to become a version 4.0.0 thing.

So filing this issue first for design discussion.

title: Make `backport_linter()` more informative by default
description:
The default for the `r_version` argument of `backport_linter()` is `getRversion()`, which, in most case, won't provide any useful insights.

A possibly better default in the case of R package, or any project with a `DESCRIPTION` file, would be to extract the stated minimum R version and use it.

This means that `backport_linter()` would now automatically warn you if you use a function that has been defined in an earlier R version that what you declared in `DESCRIPTION`.

This can be done with a handful of base R function:

```r
depends <- read.dcf("DESCRIPTION", "Depends")

depends_list <- trimws(unlist(strsplit(",")))

depends_r <- grep("R ", depends_list, value = TRUE)
min_r_version <- gsub("^R \\(>=?\\s(.+)\\)", "\\1", depends_r)
```

An alternative that seems less generic but still more informative than the default could be to use the tidyverse policy of supporting `oldrel-4`. This can make sense since the rest of the lintr already defaults to the tidyverse policy.

title: lint_dir() should be cognizant of read permissions
description:
`lint_dir()` currently just looks at `dir(recursive = TRUE)` and attempts to run `lint()` on all the included files.

This is usually fine for packages, but less so for maintaining an analysis codebase where ownership permissions may be mixed.

The current behavior is clunky because linting can fail mid-way & lose progress. It would be better to skip (possibly warning) files where the correct read permissions are not available:

```r
lint_dir()
# ...........................Error in file(con, "r") : cannot open the connection
# In addition: Warning message:
# In file(con, "r") :
#   cannot open file '...': Permission denied
```

title: New linter to recommend using `%in%`
description:
I sometimes see code like the following:

```r
x == "a" | x == "b"
```

It would be good to recommend using `%in%` in this situation. `%in%` is more readable and more efficient.

``` r
l <- sample(letters, 1)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  l == "a" | l == "e" | l == "i" | l == "o" | l == "u" | l == "y",
  l %in% c("a", "e", "i", "o", "u", "y"),
  times = 1e4,
  check = "identical"
)
#> Unit: nanoseconds
#>                                                             expr  min   lq
#>  l == "a" | l == "e" | l == "i" | l == "o" | l == "u" | l == "y" 1337 1448
#>                           l %in% c("a", "e", "i", "o", "u", "y")  853  938
#>      mean median     uq   max neval
#>  2214.408   1518 2129.5 29833 10000
#>  1526.725    989 1268.0 37533 10000

l <- sample(letters, 10)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  l == "a" | l == "e" | l == "i" | l == "o" | l == "u" | l == "y",
  l %in% c("a", "e", "i", "o", "u", "y"),
  times = 1e4,
  check = "identical"
)
#> Unit: microseconds
#>                                                             expr   min    lq
#>  l == "a" | l == "e" | l == "i" | l == "o" | l == "u" | l == "y" 1.685 1.856
#>                           l %in% c("a", "e", "i", "o", "u", "y") 1.143 1.240
#>      mean median    uq    max neval
#>  2.583897  1.931 2.450 39.678 10000
#>  1.799001  1.295 1.493 43.415 10000
```

<sup>Created on 2022-12-23 with [reprex v2.0.2.9000](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

title: Lintr should lint Roxygen documentation examples
description:
Example code should be well formatted.

I hand't though about this until I started using 1.0.1, and it noticed a lot of trailing line spaces in the Roxygen comments, but I noticed that there aren't any checks for the actual example code.

For example:
```r
#' show head and return summary
#'
#' @param bar an object
#'
#' @return summary of \code{bar}
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
#' ThisIsATerribleVariable = 6:20
#' foo( ThisIsATerribleVariable )
#' 
foo <- function(bar){
  print(head(bar))
  return(summary(bar))
}
```
I would expect `lintr` to flag line 9 for  `snake_case` and `<- not =`, and line 10 for space around code in parentheses. In stead, all that I get is line 11, for trailing whitespace.

title: if_switch_linter counts expressions incorrectly if the argument doesn't use '{'
description:
```r
l = if_switch_linter(max_branch_expressions = 2L)
lint('
  switch(x,
    a = foo(c, d, e),
    b = bar(f, g, h)
  )
', l)
# <text>:2:3: warning: [if_switch_linter] Prefer repeated if/else statements over overly-complicated switch() statements. Disable this with a comment: `# nolint` (one line) or `# lintr: disable` (multiple lines). See go/tidy-style#linting for more.
#   switch(x,
#   ^~~~~~~~~
```

The lint logic is written with `switch(a = { ... }, b = { ... })` in mind, whereas in this case the number of expressions is just 1.

title: Should implicit length to Boolean coercion in conditional expressions produce a lint?
description:
This is a pattern I often see in the wild and find difficult to read (especially the negative variant) given the implicit coercions it relies on.  Should it produce a lint?

``` r
library(lintr)

lint(
  text = "if (length(x)) return(TRUE)",
  linters = linters_with_tags(NULL)
)

lint(
  text = "if (!length(x)) return(FALSE)",
  linters = linters_with_tags(NULL)
)

# etc.
```

<sup>Created on 2022-11-04 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

The suggested replacements could be, respectively:

```r
if (length(x) > 0L) return(TRUE)
if (length(x) == 0L) return(FALSE)
```

The conditional expressions could be: `if`, `else if`, `ifelse`
The length functions in conditional expressions could be: `c("length", "nrow", "ncol", "NROW", "NCOL", "dim")`

title: Recommend `if (nzchar(x))` instead of `if (nchar(x))`
description:
I am seeing some cases where automatic integer to bool conversion is used and `nchar(x)` is used directly in an `if` clause, where `nzchar()` would be both faster and clearer.

This should likely be part of `nzchar()` linter.

title: Linting for pipes in `pdf()` or `postscript()`
description:
E.g. 

```R
postscript("|lp -dlw")
pdf("|lp -o landscape", paper = "a4r")
```

Motivated by the following report https://bugs.r-project.org/show_bug.cgi?id=19087 and https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/pull/264. This seems like something lintr could flag.

title: Prefer `parent::*` to `parent::expr` where possible
description:
If we know the type of the parent node (or don't care about it), `parent::*` is faster than `parent::expr`:

Here is comparison data for 
```r
x <- get_source_expressions("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Rdatatable/data.table/master/inst/tests/tests.Rraw")
xml <- x$expressions[[length(x$expressions)]]$full_xml_parsed_content
```

```r
system.time(xml_find_all(xml, "//SYMBOL_FUNCTION_CALL/parent::expr"))
#   user  system elapsed 
#   2.02    0.00    2.02 
system.time(xml_find_all(xml, "//SYMBOL_FUNCTION_CALL/parent::expr/parent::expr"))
#   user  system elapsed 
#  3.903   0.000   3.904 
system.time(xml_find_all(xml, "//SYMBOL_FUNCTION_CALL/parent::*"))
#   user  system elapsed 
#  1.989   0.000   1.989 
system.time(xml_find_all(xml, "//SYMBOL_FUNCTION_CALL/parent::*/parent::*"))
#   user  system elapsed 
#  3.877   0.000   3.877 
```

_Originally posted by @AshesITR in https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/issues/2496#issuecomment-1864963361_

title: New lint to not use `{}` in generic
description:
Based on Hadley's suggestion:
https://github.com/hadley/adv-r/blob/dc49c3872c3530ac08716fd4f4c235b01266a4ce/S4.Rmd#L345-L352

> It is bad practice to use `{}` in the generic as it triggers a special case that is more expensive, and generally best avoided.
>

> # Don't do this!
>  setGeneric("myGeneric", function(x) {
>  standardGeneric("myGeneric")
> })
> ```

Would it be a good idea to create a lint for this rule?

Linking with:
https://github.com/insightsengineering/teal.code/issues/109

title: roxygen2 change causing update in manual link resolution
description:
https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/33efecf7f4aee58fbc9d4f2e1f3fda5ae908ed42/R/any_is_na_linter.R#L3

See https://github.com/r-lib/roxygen2/issues/1725

How do we want to handle this? For now, it's causing the `repo-meta-tests` check to fail.

 - We could disable the check that roxygen2 comments & man/ contents are in sync
 - We could manually specify `base::anyNA()` in the manual
 - We could manually write out the `\code{\link[=anyNA]{anyNA}()}` Rd link
 - We could un-link `anyNA()` and just leave it like `` `anyNA()` `` (Rd: `\code{anyNA()}`)

Since there are a number of options I'm first filing this as an issue. At a glance using `base::anyNA()` will be the best, possibly with a TODO to revert it in the future.

title: paste_linter should not warn inside expression() in a plot
description:
This suggestion is actually misleading, as only `paste()` and not `paste0()` is allowed when `expression()` is used within a plot, such as to generate title or axis labels:
```R
warning: [paste_linter] paste0(...) is better than paste(..., sep = "").
      main = expression(paste("Plateau test ", L[n], ",", L[x], " curves", sep =
                        ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

The rationale is that only a certain number of functions and operators are valid inside `expression()`:
https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/grDevices/html/plotmath.html

title: unnecessary_lambda_linter() misses '!' when suggesting removing a lambda
description:
```r
lint(text = "sapply(x, function(xi) !all.equal(xi, y))", linters = unnecessary_lambda_linter())
# <text>:1:11: warning: [unnecessary_lambda_linter] Pass all.equal directly as a symbol to sapply() instead of wrapping it in an unnecessary anonymous function. For example, prefer lapply(DF, sum) to lapply(DF, function(x) sum(x)).
# sapply(x, function(xi) !all.equal(xi, y))
#           ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

We could do `sapply(x, Negate(all.equal), y)`, I think, but that's hardly a strict improvement.

title: Exclude should ignore groups
description:


But this

title: absolute_path_linter() fails for unmarked UTF-8
description:
Reproducible example, assuming a UTF-8 session:

``` r
library("lintr")

tf <- tempfile()
writeLines('x <- c("\u00e4")', tf, useBytes = TRUE)

lint(tf, linters = absolute_path_linter())                   # OK
#> ℹ No lints found.

text_UTF8 <- readLines(tf, encoding = "UTF-8")
lint(text = text_UTF8, linters = absolute_path_linter())     # OK
#> ℹ No lints found.

text_native <- readLines(tf)  # should be fine in a UTF-8 session
lint(text = text_native, linters = absolute_path_linter())
#> Error in `lint_impl_()`:
#> ! Linter `linter()` failed in '/tmp/RtmpTmjsLz/file185f638e6615c':
#> Caused by error in `parse()`:
#> ! <text>:1:5: Unerwartete(s) ')'
#> 1: "ä")
#>         ^
```

Possibly related to #2836.

title: commas_linter() could allow spaces before commas to match air
description:
Possibly related/subsumes: #2442 

`air` prefers spaces _before_ a comma when doing vertical alignment, where {styler} prefers spaces _after_ a comma, e.g.

```
# Formatted by air
tibble::tribble(
  ~x       , ~y ,
  "another", 1:3 ,
  "b"      , 1211234
)

# Formatted by styler
tibble::tribble(
  ~x,        ~y,
  "another", 1:3,
  "b",       1211234
)
```

I suspect it's possible to just support this by default without an option by checking that, for a given possible lint on 'spaces before', all lines in that call with at least the same line length _also_ have a comma in the same position. It can let through a few false negatives but I think it will be rare.

Alternatively, we could just make this an option like `allow_before` that totally skips checking spacing before commas. This approach will let in a lot more "false negatives" in the sense that a formatter will make a change that the linter did not find.

title: Possibly remove <<- from the default valid operators in assignment_linter

Filing this issue for now so as not to introduce one more breaking change in the current release.

title: Inconsistent handling of `.data` by `object_usage_linter`
description:
The `.data` pronoun is flagged as an object without a visible binding when used in the definition of a named function but not when used in the definition of an anonymous function or outside of a function.

``` r
# No lint
lintr::lint(
  text = 'iris |> dplyr::filter(.data$Species == "setosa")',
  linters = lintr::object_usage_linter()
)
#> ℹ No lints found.

# No lint
lintr::lint(
  text = 'function() {iris |> dplyr::filter(.data$Species == "setosa")}',
  linters = lintr::object_usage_linter()
)
#> ℹ No lints found.

# Lint!
lintr::lint(
  text = 'fun <- function() {iris |> dplyr::filter(.data$Species == "setosa")}',
  linters = lintr::object_usage_linter()
)
#> <text>:1:42: warning: [object_usage_linter] no visible binding for global variable '.data'
#> fun <- function() {iris |> dplyr::filter(.data$Species == "setosa")}
#>                                          ^~~~~
```

title: New linter to suggest moving complex conditional expressions to boolean function/variable?
description:
## Preamble

Complex conditional expressions can make the code difficult to read because they interrupt the "flow" of the main program.

If one instead extracts them to a boolean function/variable, the new conditional expression much more readable and, as a side effect, the new function/variable introduces a reusable abstraction in the codebase.

## Example

Actual

```r
if (looks_like_a_duck(x) && 
    swims_like_a_duck(x) && 
    quacks_like_a_duck(x)) {
  ...
}
```

Suggested-1: boolean function

```r
is_duck <- function(x) {
  looks_like_a_duck(x) &&
    swims_like_a_duck(x) &&
    quacks_like_a_duck(x)
}

if (is_duck(x)) {
  ...
}
```

Suggested-1: boolean variable

```r
is_duck <- 
  looks_like_a_duck(x) &&
  swims_like_a_duck(x) &&
  quacks_like_a_duck(x)

if (is_duck) {
  ...
}
```

Note that this is the simplest cases, but one can imagine that the expression depend on different objects, and so the boolean function can be multi-parameter (e.g. `is_duck(x, y, z)`).

## Configurable

As for what constitutes a _complex_ conditional expression can be configurable. The default will be 2L. That is, any expression with more than two operands will set off this linter. But users can set this to a higher or a lower value (e.g. if someone prefers to _always_ use a boolean function in a conditional expression to improve readability).

title: Best practices linters from the R documentation
description:
#3036  and #3035 are cases of taking R's own documented best practices and converting them to linters. We might as well scale this up to the whole R codebase -- what else do .Rd files point us towards?

I threw gemini at the task; here's a digested version of its output.

----

  1. Performance & Efficiency Rules

 - [ ] Matrix Cross-Products: Use `crossprod(x, y)` instead of `t(x) %*% y` and `tcrossprod(x, y)` instead of `x %*% t(y)`. They are formally equivalent but significantly faster and more memory-efficient. (#3035)
 - [x] String Prefix/Suffix Checks: Use `startsWith(x, prefix)` and `endsWith(x, suffix)` instead of `grepl("^prefix", x)` or `substring(x, 1, nchar(prefix)) == prefix`. They are much faster and handle NA values more consistently. _(already have `string_boundary_linter()`)_
 - [x] Duplicate Detection: Use `anyDuplicated(x)` instead of `any(duplicated(x))`. It is more efficient and returns the index of the first duplicate. _(already have `any_duplicated_linter()`)_
 - [ ] Object Existence & Retrieval: Use `get0(x, ...)` instead of the pattern `if (exists(x, ...)) get(x, ...)`. It combines both operations efficiently. (#1970)
 - [ ] Factor-to-Numeric Conversion: To convert a factor `f` to its original numeric values, use `as.numeric(levels(f))[f]` instead of `as.numeric(as.character(f))` _(is there any other use case for this besides factors?)_.
 - [ ] Triangular Binning/Table: Instead of `table(cut(x, br))`, use `hist(x, br, plot = FALSE)`. It is more efficient and uses less memory.
 - [ ] Use `findInterval()` instead of `cut(..., labels = FALSE)`.
 - [ ] Matrix Transposition: Use `t(x)` instead of `aperm(x, c(2, 1))` for transposing matrices.
 - [x] Prefer `fixed = TRUE` when no regular expression is needed for a significant speedup. _(already have `fixed_regex_linter()`)_
 - [x] Prefer `perl = TRUE` over the default POSIX engine for better performance and more features. _(not clear to enforce this generically)_
 - [x] Avoid `useBytes = TRUE` unless working with raw byte data, as it can produce unexpected results in multibyte locales. _(can't be enforced statically)_

  2. Numerical Stability & Accuracy

 - [ ] Log-Scale Probabilities: Use the `log = TRUE` argument in density/distribution functions (e.g., `dbinom(x, size, prob, log = TRUE)`) instead of `log(dbinom(x, size, prob))`. This avoids underflow and provides better precision.
 - [ ] Solving Linear Systems: Use `qr.coef(qr(x), y)` instead of `solve(x) %*% y` for better numerical stability.
 - [ ] Principal Component Analysis: Prefer `prcomp()` over `princomp()`. prcomp uses singular value decomposition (SVD) on the data matrix, which is generally the preferred method for numerical accuracy. _(need to investigate / compare the two...)_
 - [x] Bessel Functions: Use `expon.scaled = TRUE` in `besselI` and `besselK` to avoid overflow/underflow when dealing with large arguments. _(can't be enforced statically)_

  3. Programming Best Practices

 - [ ] Always use braces `{ .. }` around statements in `if` and `for` blocks. _(via `?Control`; this is Tidyverse style too... could add to `brace_linter()`)_
 - [ ] Avoid newlines between `}` and `else` to prevent syntax errors in certain contexts. _(via `?Control`; we may enforce this already? need to check)_
 - [x] Use the null coalescing operator `%||%` (added in R 4.4.0) instead of `if (is.null(x)) y else x`. _(already have `null_coalescing_linter()`)_
 - [ ] For programming and inspection, use `formals(f)` instead of `args(f)`. _(via `?args`; need to investigate / compare the two...)_
 - [x] In grep, grepl, sub, gsub, etc., always name the arguments (except the first one, pattern) because the text vector x is not the first argument. _(via `?grep`; not sure about this one)_
 - [x] For S4 classes, use `as(object, value)` instead of directly assigning the class with `class(x) <- value`. _(can't enforce statically)_
 - [ ] Use `deparse1()` (added in R 4.0.0) instead of `deparse()` when a single string result is expected. (#2615)
 - [x] Avoid using `identical()` on Date objects, as their internal storage mode (integer vs. double) can vary; use `all.equal()` instead. _(can't enforce statically)_
 - [x] For data frames, prefer `row.names(df)` and `names(df)` over `rownames(df)` and `colnames(df)`. _(can't enforce statically)_
 - [x] Use `subset()` for extraction instead of complex `[` or `[[` indexing when possible. _(can't enforce statically, also, I'm pretty sure `subset()` is discouraged for packages by the Rd sources too)_
 - [x] Avoid matrix-style indexing (e.g., `df[matrix_index]`) on data frames. _(can't enforce statically)_
 - [ ] Dimnames Management: To set a single component of dimnames, use `rownames(A) <- value` or `colnames(A) <- value` instead of `dimnames(A)[[1]] <- value`, as the latter fails if the assigned value is `NULL`.
 - [x] Diagonal Matrices: Use `diag(x, nrow = length(x))` instead of `diag(x)` when x is a vector that could potentially have length one, to avoid accidentally creating an identity matrix of size x. _(can't enforce statically)_
 - [x] Environment Interaction: Use `mget()` for retrieving multiple objects from an environment simultaneously. _(can't enforce statically)_
 - [x] Connection Handling: Always close connections explicitly, preferably using `on.exit(close(con))` to ensure cleanup even if errors occur. _(we have `terminal_close_linter()`, which is close as we can get statically AIUI)_
 - [ ] Use `system.time()` instead of `unix.time()`.
 - [x] Use Sys.getenv() instead of getenv(). / Use double()/as.double() instead of real()/as.real(). / Use Sys.setenv() instead of Sys.putenv(). _(these functions don't even exist anymore, I'm not sure why they're even referenced in `?base-defunct`

title: Recommend `crossprod()` / `tcrossprod()`
description:
`?crossprod` says:

> This is formally equivalent to (but faster than) the call t(x) %\*% y (crossprod) or x %\*% t(y) (tcrossprod).

And indeed:

``` r
m <- matrix(1:90, nrow = 10, ncol = 9)
v <- 1:9

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  tcrossprod(v, m),
  v %*% t(m),
  check = "identical",
  times = 1e4
)
#> Unit: nanoseconds
#>              expr min   lq      mean median     uq    max neval
#>  tcrossprod(v, m) 196  245  579.2064    276  401.5  25760 10000
#>        v %*% t(m) 871 1013 1685.2116   1169 1925.0 131034 10000
```

title: object_length_linter and object_name_linter crash with normalizePath('') when lint('', text=...) called with empty filename
description:
## Description

When `lint('', text = ...)` is called with an empty string as `filename`, `object_length_linter` and `object_name_linter` crash on Windows with:

```
Linter `linter()` failed in '':
Caused by error in `normalizePath()`:
! path[1]="": The system cannot find the path specified
```

This happens because both linters call `find_package(source_expression$filename)`, which calls `normalize_path('', mustWork = TRUE)`, which fails on Windows when the filename is empty.

This is triggered in practice when the R language server (`languageserver`) calls `lintr::lint(path, text = content)` and the path is empty (e.g., for `untitled:` or `vscode-userdata:` URI schemes where `path_from_uri()` returns `""`).

## Minimal Reprex

```r
library(lintr)
txt <- c("x <- 1", "camelCase <- 2")

# Works fine:
lint(text = txt)

# Crashes (object_length_linter calls find_package -> normalizePath(""))
lint("", text = txt)
```

**Expected:** No crash; linters should handle empty filename gracefully when `text=` is provided.

**Actual:** Error in `normalizePath(path[1])` from `find_package()`.

## Root Cause

In `R/get_source_expressions.R`, `find_package()` calls `normalize_path(filename, ...)` without checking if `filename` is empty or `nzchar()`.

Both `object_length_linter` and `object_name_linter` pass `source_expression$filename` to `find_package()` unconditionally. When `lint()` receives `filename = ""` and `text = ...`, it sets `inline_data = TRUE` so `normalize_path("", mustWork = FALSE)` succeeds in `lint()`, but `find_package()` still calls `normalize_path("", mustWork = TRUE)`.

## Suggested Fix

Guard `find_package()` against empty filename at the top of the function:

```r
find_package <- function(filename, ...) {
  if (!nzchar(filename)) return(NULL)
  # ... rest of function
}
```

This is also related to #2847; the `inline_data` / `parse_settings` interaction means that `lint("", text=...)` defaults to `parse_settings = FALSE`, so even if `.lintr` disables these linters, the config is not read.

## Session Info

- lintr 3.3.0.1
- R 4.5.0 on Windows 10
- languageserver 0.3.16

title: `object_usage_linter` false positive: Variable assigned **and used** within `with` flagged as unused
description:
### MRE

```r
lint(
  "
  fn <- function(df) {
    with(df, {
      x <- b + c
      x
    })
  }",
  linters = list(object_usage_linter(skip_with = TRUE))
)
```

### Expected Behavior

No lint. `x` should not be considered as "assigned and not used" for two reasons: 1) It's inside a `with` statement 2) it is being used! In fact, it's the return value of the function as a whole.

### Actual Behavior
```
<text>:4:7: warning: [object_usage_linter] local variable 'x' assigned but may not be used
      x <- b + c
```

Lintr version: `lintr_3.3.0-1`

title: Add Shiny app support
description:
**Description:**
I use `lintr` daily, and it is a great tool for analyzing R scripts and packages. However, when performing static code analysis on Shiny apps, I encounter many false positives due to the unique structure and syntax of Shiny apps.

Here are a few examples of linters with false-positive instances:

| Linter                                                 | False-positive example                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [extraction_operator_linter]                           | `input$submit`, `output$plot`, `tags$head`, etc.                                                   |
| [cyclocomp_linter]                                     | Server and UI functions are flagged as too complex                                                |
| [unused_import_linter] + [undesirable_function_linter] | There is a disconnection when the app is split into multiple scripts (`global.r` / `app.r`, `server.r`, and `ui.r`) |

I can, of course, disable these linters to remove false-positive instances, but I find them important to use in the static code analysis of Shiny apps, and I manually go through each of them.

Is there a smarter way to do this currently? Do you have any plans to add Shiny app support in the future?

**Feature request:**
It would be great to have an option to lint a Shiny app, similar to linting an R package. Therefore, I propose adding dedicated Shiny app support to `lintr` to address this issue and provide more accurate feedback to Shiny developers.

**Other:**
Please feel free to reach out if you have any questions or need further information.

title: Don't require "nested" indentation for multiline formulas?
description:
First, thank you for this very useful package!

Is the following lint intended?

```r
txt <- "
y ~
  var_1 +
  var_2 +
  var_3
"
lintr::lint(
  txt,
  linters = lintr::linters_with_defaults(),
  parse_settings = FALSE
)
#> <text>:4:2: style: [indentation_linter] Indentation should be 4 spaces but is 2 spaces.
#>   var_2 +
#>  ^~~
```

`lintr` currently expects a "nested" indentation:

```r
txt <- "
y ~
  var_1 +
    var_2 +
    var_3
"
lintr::lint(
  txt,
  linters = lintr::linters_with_defaults(),
  parse_settings = FALSE
)
#> ℹ No lints found.
```

I think it is suboptimal because there is no "hierarchy" between the variables.

FWIW, there have been similar discussions for air here: https://github.com/posit-dev/air/issues/444.

title: Add check for duplicated index variables in nested `for` loops?
description:
When there are nested loops, it is easy to re-use the same index variables by mistake. Having a rule to detect this kind of case can be useful:

```r
for (i in 1:10)
  ...
  for (i in 1:10) { # -> re-use "i", probably a mistake
    ...
  }
  ...
}
```

This was a request on Bluesky that I implemented in Jarl, here are some tests in case you want to implement this in `lintr` and re-use those test cases: https://github.com/etiennebacher/jarl/blob/main/crates/jarl-core/src/lints/base/for_loop_dup_index/mod.rs

title: New lint equivalency fuzzer: swapping '->' and '<-'
description:
> One problem with `->` is it doesn't share operator precedence rules with `<-` (edit: [that's not precisely true](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/Syntax.html), it's something else about the parser that causes this, but the effect is the same), hence the need to `()`-wrap here:
> 
> ```r
> (function(x) {
>   x
> }) -> foo
> ```
> 
> It will also require a tiny bit of ingenuity to swap the AST entries vs. the simple cases like `@`↔️`$`, but comment injection was similarly nontrivial.
> 
> We can try it out and if there's too much nofuzz required we can give it up. 

 _Originally posted by @MichaelChirico in [#2191](https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/issues/2191#issuecomment-3125562605)_

Still, I suspect this will turn up some good true positive issues where we assume assignment is always `<-` or `=`, so I'm earmarking it for future work.

title: Lint consistency fuzz testing?
description:
One concern I have about the consistency cleanups in this release (#2039, #2046, #2190) is there's no mechanism to ensure future improvements/new linters continue to keep "up to code" & enforce the same consistency.

One approach that seems doable is to have a GHA that [fuzzes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuzzing) our test suite. For example, for #2190, that means:

 - Go through the suite and identify all `expect_lint()` calls using "function(...)" or `\(...)` in the `content=` argument (text matching should be enough, but we could also use `getParseData()` here...).
 - Randomly (or exhaustively?) switch all such usages to their opposite: `s/function/\/g` and `s/\/function/g`
 - Run the test suite
 - Any test failure means a linter is inconsistently handling `function(...)` and `\(...)`

Similar fuzzes could apply in the other cases:

 - Randomly swap `%>%` and `|>`
 - Randomly swap `$` and `@`

Some exceptions will need to be carved out, e.g. for cases where intentionally only one alternative is meant to be linted, and we might need some work to make the fuzzing robust to changes in an expected lint message. But overall this approach seems pretty doable to me.

If run with randomness, I'd also run it periodically, not on push/merge, since a failure might not be caught up-front & surfacing that failure on "someone else's" PR would be bad form.

title: Recommend `!is.unsorted()` instead of `identical(x, sort(x))` in `sort_linter()`
description:
Not a super common pattern:

https://github.com/search?q=language%3AR+%2Fidentical%5C%28%5Cw%2B%2C+sort%5C%28%5Cw%2B%5C%29%5C%29%2F&type=code

But there is a huge opportunity for optimization here:

``` r
x <- runif(1e5)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  identical(x, sort(x)),
  !is.unsorted(x),
  check = "identical"
)
#> Unit: microseconds
#>                   expr      min       lq       mean   median       uq      max
#>  identical(x, sort(x)) 4010.383 4313.883 4636.98955 4496.855 4761.682 7040.232
#>        !is.unsorted(x)   40.104   41.166   46.29157   42.666   46.807   86.509
#>  neval
#>    100
#>    100

x <- sort(x)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  identical(x, sort(x)),
  !is.unsorted(x),
  check = "identical"
)
#> Unit: nanoseconds
#>                   expr  min     lq    mean median     uq   max neval
#>  identical(x, sort(x)) 3612 3732.0 4094.85 3872.5 4033.0 22994   100
#>        !is.unsorted(x)  662  722.5  803.60  773.0  800.5  3131   100
```

title: Is it actually better to run file.exists() in a loop?
description:
https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/945c2a2edafe8d133adc2ac81b27154b41460203/R/settings_utils.R#L78-L82

I think this is written under the assumption that typically the first/second entry will give the config, thus it's "not worth" running `file.exists()` for the full vector of possible config locations.

But `file.exists()` is not all that expensive, is it? And this code is not executed 100s of times? So maybe it's simpler to just write this code in terms of checking the first `TRUE` entry on the `file.exists(<vector>)` result.

Should check the result quantitatively first, though.

title: fourth hanging_indent_style to match air?
description:
This is my air.toml file:

```
line-ending = "auto"
persistent-line-breaks = true
exclude = []
default-exclude = true
```

```
dt[,
```
