title: Bad error handling for invalid `Lint()`s
description:
When a linter returns a `Lint` with an invalid (`NA`) `column_number`, as has recently happened in some regex-based linters, the error message is extremely confusing:

```
Error in rep.int(character, length) : invalid 'times' value
Calls: <Anonymous> ... print.lint -> cat -> highlight_string -> fill_with -> paste0
Execution halted
```

IMO `Lint()` should do some mild verification during construction so that invalid `Lint()`s can't be created successfully.

Here are a bunch of checks we could add:

 1. No `NA`s are allowed anywhere.
 2. `1L <= column_number <= nchar(line) + 1L`.
 3. `line_number >= 1L`.
 4. `ranges` is a list of length 2 integer(ish) vectors, or `NULL`.
 5. `1L <= ranges[[i]][1L] <= ranges[[i]][2L] <= nchar(line) + 1L` for all `i`.

WDYT?

title: spaces_inside_linter()/commas_linter() could optionally allow `[ , ]` instead of `[, ]`
description:
Some authors (usually myself included) prefer making the empty first argument to `[` more visible by leaving an intentional blank space. Compare:

```r
DT[ , .N, by = grp] # throws both spaces_inside_linter()+commas_linter()

# tidyverse guide compliant versions (also idempotent in styler)
DT[, .N, by = grp]
DT[,
  .N,
  by = grp
]
DT[,
  j = .N, # making it clearer this isn't i=
  by = grp
]
```

I find it's easier to miss `[,` when scanning code & so prefer the first option in my own code; it would be nice to support this exception with an option.

title: False positive in object_usage_linter() for infix operators in glue strings

#   ^~~~~~
```

The problem is we only look for `SYMBOL` or `SYMBOL_FUNCTION_CALL` in the parse tree of the glue expression:

https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/2813b6dcd29edb06676481df9cf879fd2c11e76c/R/object_usage_linter.R#L225

#2068 already fixed this by using `all.vars()` instead.

title: Introduce `undesirable_loop_variable_linter()`?
description: If you are coming from other programming languages (like C++ or JavaScript), you would expect that the loop variable name binding will be destroyed once the execution goes out of scope. E.g., here is a JavaScript example. Note that `elem` doesn't change its value after the loop finishes executing. If you write R with the same expectation, you are in for a surprise. ``` r elem <- -4 vec <- 1:3 for (elem in vec) { print(elem) } #> [1] 1 #> [1] 2 #> [1] 3 print(elem) #> [1] 3 ``` Created on 2023-01-12 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) As mentioned in the docs for `for` loop: > When the loop terminates, `var` remains as a variable containing its latest value. Although, in the minimal example shown here, it might be easier to see this problem, in a script of reasonable size, it won't be. And, given the difficulty of naming things, it is likely that users can re-use a name. So I am wondering if `{lintr}` should dissuade users from engaging in such practice.

I know a linter like this would be helpful to me at least, so I thought I'd suggest it here. Roughly speaking, a lintr user would add a machine-readable file containing data for each:

1. Legacy term, e.g. `purchase_order`
2. Replacement term, e.g. `sales_order`
3. Optional notes about when or why the legacy term was deemed undesirable

The `legacy_term_linter()` would flag legacy terms in the code base and the lint message would provide the context:

> Legacy term `purchase_order` detected: use `sales_order` instead.

title: keyword_quote_linter() could get an allow_strings argument to allow "" quoting (not just backticks)
description:
Follow-up to #2030.

Currently, the linter has the following behavior:

```r
01; c("a" = 1)   # lints
02; c(`a` = 1)   # lints
03; c("a b" = 1) # no lint
04; c(`a b` = 1) # no lint

05; "a" <- 1     # lint
06; `a` <- 1     # lint
07; "a b" <- 1   # lint
08; `a b` <- 1   # no lint

09; x$"a"        # lint
10; x$`a`        # lint
11; x$"a b"      # lint
12; x$`a b`      # no lint
```

This should _especially_ lint using `"` / `'` to write function calls:

```r
"%%"(10, 2)
# [1] 0
```

This argument would allow customization on which of 3, 7, and 11 throw lints.

My thought for an API is

`keyword_quote_linter(allow_strings = c("formals", "assignment", "extraction"))` for cases 3, 7, and 11 respectively.

I would lean towards `allow_strings = character()` by default for consistency, and because `substitute(c("a b" = 1))` converts the quotes to backticks on printing:

```r
c("a b" = 1)
# c(`a b` = 1)
```

(for both assignment and extraction, `substitute()` leaves the delimiters alone)

title: `unnecessary_concatenation_linter` wrongly complains about usage with magrittr's assignment pipe operator `%<>%`
description:
Consider the following reprex:

``` r
tmp_file <- tempfile(fileext = "R")
writeLines(con = tmp_file,
           text = "
library(magrittr)
x <- 1:2
x %<>% c(3)
x
")

lintr::lint(filename = tmp_file,
            linters = list(lintr::unnecessary_concatenation_linter()))
#> /tmp/RtmpyaBMnL/filee0674c13fd78R:4:8: style: [unnecessary_concatenation_linter] Unneeded concatenation of a constant. Remove the "c" call.
#> x %<>% c(3)
#>        ^~~~
```

<sup>Created on 2023-07-20 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

`x %<>% c(3)` above is the [magrittr way](https://magrittr.tidyverse.org/reference/compound.html) to write `x <- c(x, 3)`, so lintr should ideally allow `c()` with a single constant *if* it is preceded by the `%<>%` operator.

title: Introduce `unnecessary_argument_linter()`
description:
In multi-parameter functions, it often happens that some parameters are factored out of the code but are never removed from the function signature. 

A simple example of this would be a function like the following, where the parameter `arg1` is no longer needed because whatever relied upon it in the function body has already been removed, but the author forgot to update the signature.

``` r
library(lintr)

lint(
  text = "f <- function(x, arg1 = TRUE) mean(x)", 
  linters = linters_with_tags(NULL)
)
```

<sup>Created on 2022-10-25 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

This can be detected by checking if a symbol corresponding to this argument appears anywhere in the function body. Note that this logic (correctly) won't produce lints for deprecated parameters.

Exceptions should be made for 

- `S3` generics

```r
foo <- function(x, ...) {
  UseMethod("foo")
}
```

- `...`, which can sometimes be used to change function signature in a backward compatible way

```r
foo <- function(x, y1 = NULL, ...) { g(x, y1) } # old
foo <- function(x, y2 = NULL, ...) { g(x, y2) } # new; won't break, `y1 = ` will be absorbed by `...`
```

title: Detect broken configuration
description:
A lot of new users seem to stumble upon the quirkiness of the dcf format we use for `.lintr`.
I see three major pitfalls:

1. Indentation of multiline code is not intuitive

```
# Wrong
linters: with_defaults(
    line_length_linter = line_length_linter(120)
)

# Right
linters: with_defaults(
    line_length_linter = line_length_linter(120)
  )
```

2. Trailing newline is mandatory, but not reported as an error

```
# Wrong
linters: with_defaults(
    line_length_linter = line_length_linter(120)
  )
(EOF)

# Right
linters: with_defaults(
    line_length_linter = line_length_linter(120)
  )

(EOF)
```

3. The proper location of the `.lintr` config files sometimes causes confusion.

It would be nice of us to catch these and report a warning (or maybe even an error?) if the config file is malformed.

Regarding the location issue, maybe reporting the config file used (if any) would help diagnosing the problem more quickly.
I see a few options here as to when to report it:

1. Only if some option (`linter.verbose`, or `lintr.debug`?) is set.
2. Only if some argument (`verbose`, or `debug`?) is TRUE.
3. Always if running interactively.
4. Always at the start of a top-level call (lint_dir, lint_package or lint if the latter isn't called from within lint_*).

WDYT?
I think the most user-friendly version would be to use `getOption("lintr.???", default = interactive())` to decide whether to print this diagnostic info at the start of a top-level call.
If no config file is found, the info could be

  Using the default linter configuration. See vignette("using_lintr", package = "lintr") for customization options.

or something like that.

title: get0 linter
description:
A pattern we see occasionally looks like:

```r
if (exists("key", ...)) {
  value <- get("key", ...)
} else {
  value <- default()
}
```

With some minor variations thereof.

`base::get0()` is a more concise and efficient alternative in this case:

```r
value <- get0("key", ..., ifnotfound = default())
```

The problem comes from getting the logic here right... it's easy to see a `get0()` replacement manually, but tough to design a rule that will catch enough cases for it to be worth it.

In our code, I did a simple pass like this:

```
//IF[
  following-sibling::expr[1]/expr/SYMBOL_FUNCTION_CALL[text() = 'exists']
  and following-sibling::expr[2]//SYMBOL_FUNCTION_CALL[text() = 'get']
  and following-sibling::ELSE
]
```

There were few enough hits that I could filter through the false positives manually. But if we want to productionize this we should try to exclude more false positives up front.

----

Originally inspired by https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/commit/1f7f974f0aa426b3044ce1c6acdcf2de2a53e1c5

title: Drop deprecated linters from individual tag pages
description:
Currently, we surface linters that may be deprecated on the tag descriptions' pages, e.g.

https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/fb294ccca4267c5b6530c7be886ebcdd34afec41/man/style_linters.Rd#L45

This is not ideal since users may attempt to use these without realizing they're deprecated if it's referenced on the tag page without context.

We could either annotate `(deprecated)` on the tag page, or simply omit these from the tag page.

I would opt for the latter.

There are two options:

 1. Amend the code generating the pages to skip if `deprecated` is among the tags
 2. Retain only the `deprecated` tag for such linters

We may still want to keep the tags recorded in inst/lintr/linters.csv for reference (it's still correct metadata about the linter), hence I lean towards option 1 on the assumption it's only a line or two of difference to implement it.

title: available_linters(tags = "deprecated") should "just work"
description:
I find the current behavior a bit strange:

```r
available_linters(tags = "deprecated")
# [1] linter  package tags   
# <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
```

Almost surely, that's not what the user wanted. The problem is `exclude_tags = "deprecated"` by default, so we need to also specify `exclude_tags = NULL`:

```r
nrow(available_linters(tags = "deprecated", exclude_tags = NULL))
# [1] 7
```

I see two options:

 1. Special case `"deprecated"` with an `if (missing(exclude_tags) && identical(tags, "deprecated")) exclude_tags <- NULL`
 2. Always run `exclude_tags <- setdiff(exclude_tags, tags)`, i.e., `exclude_tags` takes priority over `tags` if there's any collision

Either way, it will simplify the implementation for #1958.

Any thoughts?

title: New `lint_setequal()` linter
description:
This aims at encouraging the use of `setequal()` in place of some less clear patterns I've occasionally seen:

```r
identical(sort(x), sort(y))
identical(unique(x), y)
identical(unique(x), unique(y))
identical(sort(unique(x)), sort(unique(y)))
```

or any similar combination.

This linter could also use the same logic to encourage the use of `testthat::expect_setequal()`. Possibly also recommend using `testthat::expect_setequal()` over `testthat::expect_true(setequal())`?

If you agree this would be a good addition, I can work on a PR. Do you see any potential pitfalls I should be looking out for?

title: Avoid unnecessary implicit assignments in our own test suite
description:
Still not 100% sure this necessitates excepting `expect_warning()`

e.g. even in case the value needs to be re-used in a subsequent test, you can do
```r
# bad
expect_warning(prepared_thing <- my_setup_with_warning(), "setup warning")
expect_equal(funny_function(prepared_thing), funny_value) |>
  expect_warning("funny warning")

# good
my_setup_with_warning() |>
  funny_function() |>
  expect_equal(funny_value) |>
  expect_warning("setup warning") |>
  expect_warning("funny warning")
```

This is also how we structure our tests that expect warnings.

_Originally posted by @AshesITR in https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/issues/1777#issuecomment-1343414735_

title: Infix operator lint metadata is not helpful for object_usage_linter
description:
```r
lintr::lint("a <- function() {\n  1:10 %>% sum()\n}", lintr::object_usage_linter())
# <text>:1:6: warning: [object_usage_linter] no visible global function definition for ‘%>%’. Disable this with a comment: `# nolint` (one line) or `# lintr: disable` (multiple lines). See go/tidy-style#linting for more.
# a <- function() {
#      ^~~~~~~~~~~~
```

The linter anchors to the function definition, not to the usage of `%>%` itself. Similar goes for other infixes, e.g.

```r
lintr::lint("a <- function() {\n  1:10 %>% sum()\n}", lintr::object_usage_linter())
# <text>:1:6: warning: [object_usage_linter] no visible global function definition for ‘:=’. Disable this with a comment: `# nolint` (one line) or `# lintr: disable` (multiple lines). See go/tidy-style#linting for more.
# a <- function(x) {
#      ^~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

I guess this is `codetools`' fault, but is there something we can do to patch it up? Or maybe we have a bad XPath?

title: Strict test (warnings=errors) failing because of encoding issue
description:
Observed failure:

```
── Error (test-get_source_expressions.R:111): Warns if encoding is misspecified ──
Error in `grepl(pat, text, perl = TRUE)`: (converted from warning) input string 3 is invalid UTF-8

title: quote(expr =) should be allowed
description:
The "missing argument" form of `quote(expr =)` causes an `infix_spaces_linter` error. This syntax is suggested by http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Expressions.html#names

If the expression is rewritten as `quote(expr = )`, it causes a `spaces_inside_linter` error.

These errors can be avoided by `nolint` directive comments, but that feels excessive for recommended syntax.

```r
# Code showing both erring syntaxes, and the directive suppressing the issue.
original <- pairlist(path = quote(expr =))
modified <- pairlist(path = quote(expr = ))
avoided <- pairlist(path = quote(expr =)) # nolint: infix_spaces_linter.
```

```bash
# Sample output.
R -s -e 'lintr::lint_dir(".")'
# => examples.R:1:40: style: [infix_spaces_linter] Put spaces around all infix operators.
# => original <- pairlist(path = quote(expr =))

title: Generics defined in other files not detected by `object_name_linter()` and `object_length_linter()`
description:
R/generic.R

```r
my_generic <- function(x, ...) {
  UseMethod("my_generic")
}
```

R/other.R
```r
my_generic.other <- function(x, ...) {
  # code
}
```

Should not be linted by `object_name_linter()`, and `object_length_linter()` should only consider `"other"` for length computations.
I can see multiple options here:

* Inspect all visible functions whether they are generics
* Inspect the Package `NAMESPACE` file for `S3method(my_generic,<anything>)` to deduce `my_generic` must be an S3 generic

The former also works for non packages but is more expensive.
The latter should be easier, using `unique(parseNamespaceFile("package", "..")$S3methods[, 1L])` similar to `namespace_imports()`.

The SARIF file for my project comes back as follows:
``` r
sarif_output(lint_package())
```

``` json
{
  "$schema": "https://schemastore.azurewebsites.net/schemas/json/sarif-2.1.0-rtm.5.json",
  "version": "2.1.0",
  "runs": [
    {
      "tool": {
        "driver": {
          "name": "lintr",
          "informationUri": "https://lintr.r-lib.org/",
          "version": "3.0.2"
        }
      },
      "columnKind": "utf16CodeUnits",
      "originalUriBaseIds": {
        "ROOTPATH": {
          "uri": "<file path>"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```
Notice there is no `results` array inside `runs`.

#### Proposed solution
Include the `results` array inside each run in the SARIF file even if there are no issues returned by `lintr`. I believe it should work if it's an empty array in that case (i.e. `"results": []`).

#### Further reference
* [Context from `codeql-action` contributor regarding empty SARIF files](https://github.com/github/codeql-action/issues/390#issuecomment-786052405)
* [`codeql-action` check for empty `run.results`](https://github.com/github/codeql-action/blob/4acf201e5b7de54488c4ec1d4b3748145f0614da/src/upload-lib.ts#L217)

title: Different behaviour of `brace_linter()` inside and outside of function call
description:
When outside a function call, `brace_linter()` lints both the opening and the closing braces:

``` r
lint(text = "1:4 %>% { sum(.) }", linters = brace_linter())
#> <text>:1:9: style: [brace_linter] Opening curly braces should never go on their own line and should always be followed by a new line.
#> 1:4 %>% { sum(.) }
#>         ^
#> <text>:1:18: style: [brace_linter] Closing curly-braces should always be on their own line, unless they are followed by an else.
#> 1:4 %>% { sum(.) }
#>                  ^
```

<sup>Created on 2022-12-10 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

When inside a function call, `brace_linter()` lints only the opening brace for the same expression:

```r
lint(text = "local(1:4 %>% { sum(.) })", linters = brace_linter())
#> <text>:1:15: style: [brace_linter] Opening curly braces should never go on their own line and should always be followed by a new line.
#> local(1:4 %>% { sum(.) })
#>               ^
```

<sup>Created on 2022-12-10 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

Is this expected?

---

Making sure they produce identical results:

``` r
library(lintr)
library(magrittr)

identical(
  1:4 %>% { sum(.) }, 
  local(1:4 %>% { sum(.) })
)
#> [1] TRUE
```

}

  ...
}
```

title: New linter for assignments within conditional expressions
description:
In the wild, I have come across cases where variables are assigned within conditional expressions and their value is then immediately used as a condition and/or inside their scope. I think this makes the code difficult to understand, and we should lint it.

WDYT?

Here is a reprex with a simple assignment, but you can imagine far more complex assignments and the difficulty to understand the code increases with the complexity of the assignment.

``` r
library(lintr)

if (x <- 1L) print(x)
#> [1] 1

# currently, this doesn't generate any lints
lint(
  text = "if (x <- 1L) print(x)",
  linters = linters_with_tags(tags = NULL)
)
```

<sup>Created on 2022-11-25 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

The suggested alternative here in the lint message would be the following (i.e. do variable assignment outside the expression and then use the variable instead):

```r
x <- 1L
if (x) print(x)
```

title: Should patterns like `ifelse(x, 1, 0)` be linted in `redundant_ifelse_linter()`?
description:
## Description

> `ifelse(x, 1, 0)` is a false positive.
>
> It's a perfectly valid, logical way of expressing this (and arguably even superior to `as.numeric(x)` because it describes the intended semantics rather than implicitly relying on an implementation detail).

``` r
library(lintr)

lint(
  text = "ifelse(x, 1, 0)",
  linters = redundant_ifelse_linter()
)
#> <text>:1:1: warning: [redundant_ifelse_linter] Prefer as.numeric(x) to ifelse(x, 1, 0) if really needed.
#> ifelse(x, 1, 0)
#> ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

title: New linter: recommend `sort(x)` over `x[order(x)]`
description:
I think it would be nice to have a linter to recommend using `sort(x)` to sort a vector instead of `x[order(x)]`:

- it is more readable
- it is faster, especially for longer vectors

``` r
library(microbenchmark)

x <- sample(LETTERS, 1e3, replace = TRUE)

microbenchmark(
  sort(x),
  x[order(x)],
  check = "identical"
)
#> Unit: microseconds
#>         expr     min       lq     mean   median       uq      max neval
#>      sort(x) 529.036 544.6405 585.4106 559.5975 597.4515  907.008   100
#>  x[order(x)] 811.534 836.0540 899.0072 865.4155 904.8205 1453.345   100

x_long <- sample(LETTERS, 1e5, replace = TRUE)

microbenchmark(
  sort(x_long),
  x_long[order(x_long)],
  check = "identical"
)
#> Unit: milliseconds
#>                   expr       min        lq      mean    median        uq
#>           sort(x_long)  59.78242  61.85322  64.85112  63.69153  66.59794
#>  x_long[order(x_long)] 150.68092 160.44464 168.89652 164.85925 175.08799
#>        max neval
#>   86.98432   100
#>  207.92772   100
```

<sup>Created on 2022-08-26 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1.9000)</sup>

## Possible issues

`sort()` and `order()` are both generic and it is theoretically possible that some packages only provide S3 methods for one of them. In this case, they could not be strictly equivalent. However, I would say it's likely a bug in the package.

title: New linter: discourage the use of anonymous functions for trivial cases
description:
# Example

## Discouraged

```r
lapply(l, function(x) mean(x)))
```

## Recommended

```r
lapply(l, mean)
```

# Scope

- to limit the risk of false positive, I'm thinking to limit this to the `apply()` family function (+ `replicate()`), at least as a first step. Or do you think it wouldn't be much more difficult and riskier to do this in all contexts?
- ideally, this should detect also both tidyverse (`~ mean(.x)`) and base (`\(x) mean(x)`) lambda functions
- I'm thinking to limit it to cases with a single argument, i.e. exclude:

  ```r
  lapply(l, function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))
  ``` 

  even though the anonymous function could be removed here as well by forwarding the `...` because users might find it clearer to not forward them.

title: Proposed linter for mixing logical operators without grouping
description:
Consider:

```r
x | y & z
# or
x & y | z
```

I think this is a common pitfall for users not well-versed in logical operator precedence rules (myself included -- I had to look up the precedence once again while writing this post 😸).

At least "`&&` evaluates before `||`" appears consistent across languages from what I've seen; this Q&A hints that this order was chosen "to reduce the number of parentheses" (would love a citation on that), while also highlighting an interesting language (Fortress) which declines to set arbitrary operator precedences and instead enforces parentheses in any uncommon combinations:

https://softwareengineering.stackexchange.com/q/391263/221381

The above would lint unless the user adds parentheses:

```r
x | (y & z)
(x & y) | z
```

would be the logical equivalents. This would also apply to `&&` / `||`.

Related: in the Google suite, we have a linter for `!(x == 2)` --> `x != 2`. To me, the precedence of `!` is clear enough not to need extra parentheses when combined with `&&`/`||`, so I didn't include it here.

title: Re-evaluate if code to deal with a broken `NAMESPACE` is needed by `namespace_linter()`

https://developer.r-project.org/blosxom.cgi/R-devel/NEWS/2022/06/04

That should make it easier for `get_source_expressions()` to work -- instead of (or perhaps in addition to) parsing error messages, we can use the error class.

This is an experimental r-devel feature, so definitely not worth working on before our release.

---

I think they'd still like to hear comments from the lintr team about possible changes.  This is only in R-devel, and it won't be released for 10 months, so there's lots of time to try it out.

title: Conflicting lintr rules with alist and explicitly missing arguments
description:
This is pretty niche but shows up a conflicting pair of rules:

```
> lintr::lint("alist(a =)\n")
<text>:1:9: style: Put spaces around all infix operators.
alist(a =)
        ^~
> lintr::lint("alist(a = )\n")
<text>:1:10: style: Do not place spaces around code in parentheses or square brackets.
alist(a = )
         ^
> lintr::lint("alist(a =, b = NULL)\n")
<text>:1:9: style: Put spaces around all infix operators.
alist(a =, b = NULL)
        ^~
> lintr::lint("alist(a = , b = NULL)\n")
<text>:1:11: style: Commas should never have a space before.
alist(a = , b = NULL)
```

So for arguments that are "explicitly missing" there is no way of satisfying the default set of linter rules - we must and cannot have a space following the `=`, for cases that are within or at the end of an argument list.

The above behaviour is triggered in both the cran version (2.0.1) and current github (2.0.1.9000, eece3c178257e5d7d2a4c7820187af662448635d)

title: More `fixed_regex_linter` features
description:
There are some more cases where regexes can be optimized away:

For regex detection functions, we can safely replace

 * `grepl("^static_rx", x)` by `startsWith(x, "static_rx")`
 * `grepl("static_rx$", x)` by `endsWith(x, "static_rx")`
 * `grepl("^static_rx$", x)` by `x == "static_rx"`

For substitution functions, we can replace

 * `gsub("^static_rx$", "replacement", x)` by `(function(.) { .[. == "static_rx"] <- "replacement"; . })(x)`

title: Write an XPath for extended known-literal expressions
description:
Follow-up to https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/pull/957#discussion_r830463257

There are a few places that would benefit from some shared logic about what constitutes a "literal expression" along the lines of these:

```
const_exprs <- c(
  '"a"',
  '1',
  '1+1i',
  'c("a")',
  'c("a", 1)',
  'c("a", 1+1i)',
  'rep("a", 2)',
  'rep("a", n)',
  'rep(c("a", "b"), 5)',
  'c(rep("a", 10), rep("b", 10))'
)
```

but excluding non-constant expressions like:

```
non_constant_exprs <- c(
  'a',
  'a + 1',
  'foo(1)',
  'foo(c(1, 2))'
)
```

I think `c()` and `rep()` are the most common ways to build constant expressions, so we can limit it to combinations of those. Note that I consider `rep(1:3, n)` as being "constant" here, as the variable part is "constant enough" for the places where we'd use this:

 - `strings_as_factors_linter` which looks for `data.frame`s declared with known-character columns
 - `expect_{type,length,named,s3_class}_linter` which look for literal exprs in the 1st argument
 - `yoda_test_linter` which does the same

title: How to list and include all available linters?
description:
# Synopsis

Correct me if I missed this, but I don't think currently the docs/functions make it easy to:

- list names of all available linters
- include all available linters while linting (a package, e.g.)

# Listing all available linters

It should be possible for the users to easily generate a list of names of available linters. 

Currently, we make this easy only for default linters:

``` r
library(lintr)

names(default_linters) # or `names(default_settings$linters)` will also work
#>  [1] "assignment_linter"                "brace_linter"                    
#>  [3] "commas_linter"                    "commented_code_linter"           
#>  [5] "cyclocomp_linter"                 "equals_na_linter"                
#>  [7] "function_left_parentheses_linter" "infix_spaces_linter"             
#>  [9] "line_length_linter"               "no_tab_linter"                   
#> [11] "object_length_linter"             "object_name_linter"              
#> [13] "object_usage_linter"              "paren_body_linter"               
#> [15] "pipe_continuation_linter"         "semicolon_linter"                
#> [17] "seq_linter"                       "single_quotes_linter"            
#> [19] "spaces_inside_linter"             "spaces_left_parentheses_linter"  
#> [21] "T_and_F_symbol_linter"            "trailing_blank_lines_linter"     
#> [23] "trailing_whitespace_linter"       "vector_logic_linter"
```

<sup>Created on 2022-07-28 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

But we have many other linters, which are not included in `default_linters` (why?!), and can be seen only* in the [reference](https://lintr.r-lib.org/reference/index.html#individual-linters).

This means that if I wanted to include all available linters, I need to manually inspect the list of default linters and the website, note that down which are not included and then add them to my `.lintr` file. That is cumbersome.

(* There is `lintr:::rd_linterlist()` to list all available linters, but it is not in a form that is useful, and it is not exported.)

So should we implement and export a new `all_linters` list, similar to `default_linters`?

# Linting a package with all available linters

If we implement and export `all_linters`, it also solves the second issue, which is to lint a package will all available linters. Because a user can just do:

```r
with_defaults(..., default = all_linters)
```

I also think that this should be the default, but I am guessing there are good reasons why only certain - and not available - linters were chosen for the default list.

x <- rep(c(TRUE, NA, FALSE, FALSE), 1000)

identical(

)
#> [1] TRUE

# currently doesn't lint
lint(
  text = "sum(is.na(x)) != 0L",
  linters = any_is_na_linter()
)
```

title: object_usage_linter doesn't match R CMD check
description:
As seen here: https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/pull/931#discussion_r826188056

Basically our `tools::checkUsage()` call doesn't match that of `R CMD check`. In this case, it's because the default `checkUsage()` doesn't set `skipWith=TRUE`, so objects seen inside `with()` calls can trip the linter.

My understanding is the main goal of `object_usage_linter` is to help match `R CMD check`, so we should adjust our code to match.

But maybe we think of this as a bit more general, and could expose an option instead (e.g. `match_r_check`, I would set `TRUE` by default).

title: Bug with "@import"ed data packages
description:
To reproduce:

In RStudio File -> New Project -> New Directory -> R Package
Package name = "temptanic"

This adds a package skeleton with `R/hello.R`. Running `lintr::lint_package()` flags a single whitespace lint in hello.R (irrelevant to the issue)

Add an R script to the package that imports the {titanic} package (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/titanic/index.html).

```
# dummy-imports.R

#' @import titanic
#'
NULL
```

Delete the initial NAMESPACE
Document the package - we see `import(titanic)` in NAMESPACE

Lint the {temptanic} package:

```
lintr::lint_package()
.Error in data.frame(pkg = ns, fun = getNamespaceExports(ns), stringsAsFactors = FALSE) : 
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 1, 0
```

(The same thing happens whether or not {titanic} is added to {temptanic}::Imports or Suggests)

Note the following:

```
> getNamespaceExports("titanic")
character(0)
```

As such, data.frame(pkg = "titanic", fun = getNamespaceExports("titanic"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)  complains due to mismatched argument lengths.

title: `object_usage_linter()` should set `useFancyQuotes=FALSE`
description:
Compare:

```r
str <- "foo <- function() {\n  x\n}\n"

options(useFancyQuotes = FALSE)
lintr::lint(text = str, linters = lintr::object_usage_linter())
# <text>:2:3: warning: [object_usage_linter] no visible binding for global variable 'x'.
#   x
#   ^
options(useFancyQuotes = TRUE)
lintr::lint(text = str, linters = lintr::object_usage_linter())
# <text>:2:3: warning: [object_usage_linter] no visible binding for global variable ‘x’.
#   x
#   ^
```

I think we should follow suit of `testthat` and turn off quotes here -- makes the lint appear differently depending on global options & it's harder to manipulate the message with non-ASCII characters.

The fix is pretty trivial to implement; filing here first as a gut check that this is the right approach.

title: Shouldn't the "lint-changed-files" GHA fail for PRs that add new lints?
description:
Currently, when working on a PR, the contributor needs to keep manually checking if they have added any new lints. 
Even if they check that they haven't, something might change during code review, and a lint might be added. Now if they forget to re-check, the reviewer needs to point this out, which is additional work for the reviewer.

So I was wondering if we can instead modify the "lint-changed-files" GHA so that it **fails** when any new lints are detected. Build failures will ensure that neither the contributor nor the reviewer will have to do this manually, and it'd be hard to miss the newly introduced lint. WDYT?

title: Build release and development versions of package website
description:
We need to start having separate versions of the website for the release and development package versions, so that the users are not confused by why the output they see doesn't match with what's on the website. 

We can only do this after the next release of the package. If we do it now, IINM, the release website will disappear.

We just need to add the following to `_pkgdown.yml`.

```yml
development:
  mode: auto
  version_label: default      # optional
  version_tooltip: "Version"  # optional
```

For more, see:
https://pkgdown.r-lib.org/articles/how-to-update-released-site.html

title: Deprecation message for "with_defaults" is misleading
description:
The deprecation message for `with_defaults` urges users to use `linters_with_defaults`. For most uses, I imagine that is the correct replacement. But the deprecation causes some confusion in settings where an old-style config looked like:

```
linters: with_defaults(
    assignment_linter = NULL,
    undesirable_operator_linter(
      with_defaults(
        "<-" = "Use =, not <-, for assignment.",
        default = default_undesirable_operators
      )
    )
  )
```

Here, when `lintr::lint_package()` is called, two deprecation messages are printed to the console. Both suggest using `linters_with_defaults` in place of `with_defaults`. But when defining the undesirable-op list, `linters_with_defaults` is not the appropriate replacement for `with_defaults`. Here, the recommendation should be `modify_defaults`.

Could we modify the deprecation warning to print 
```
Warning message:
Function with_defaults was deprecated in lintr version 3.0.0. Use linters_with_defaults or modify_defaults instead.
```

title: expect_lint_free() fails when Check is launched from RStudio, but not when launched by devtools::check()
description:
I've set up a test for a package using `testthat` that calls `lintr::expect_lint_free()`. When running this test through RStudio (ie. ctrl+shift+T), the test passes. When running `devtools::check()`, the test (which runs as part of R CMD check) passes. But, when running Check from RStudio (ie. ctrl+shift+E), the test fails with the following error:

```
> library(testthat)
> library(LintRErrorTest)
> 
> test_check("LintRErrorTest")
── 1. Error: Package Style (@test_lint.R#4)  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
invalid 'path' argument
1: lintr::expect_lint_free() at testthat/test_lint.R:4
2: lint_package(...)
3: normalizePath(path, mustWork = FALSE)
4: path.expand(path)

══ testthat results  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[ OK: 0 | SKIPPED: 0 | WARNINGS: 0 | FAILED: 1 ]
1. Error: Package Style (@test_lint.R#4) 
```

This can be reproduced as follows:

- Create a new package using RStudio's File -> New Project -> R Package
- Run `usethis::use_testthat()` to start using `testthat`
- Create the file `tests/testthat/test_lint.R` with the following content:

```r
if (requireNamespace("lintr", quietly = TRUE)) {
  context("linting package")
  test_that("Package Style", {
    lintr::expect_lint_free()
  })
}
```

- Run tests using either ctrl+shift+T or `devtools::test()`. There will be a test failure caused by a trailing whitespace in a comment in the default contents of `hello.R`. Remove this trailing whitespace if desired.
- Run `devtools::check()`. This will give a warning about a non-standard license, and a test failure caused by the trailing whitespace if you didn't fix it above.
- Run Check from the RStudio IDE (ctrl+shift+E). This will fail with the `invalid 'path' argument` error above.

I have tested this using R 3.6.1 running on Ubuntu 18.04.3 LTS. I currently have `testthat` version 2.2.1 installed. The same behavior occurs with both `lintr` 2.0.0 from CRAN and version 2.0.0.9000 installed using `devtools::install_github`

title: Add argument `scope = c("function", "variable", "constant", "class", ?)` to `object_name_linter()`
description:
This would allow a user to define custom naming conventions per scope if desired.
e.g. we use `snake_case` for functions and variables, `SNAKE_CASE` for constants and `CamelCase` for classes.
IIUC, google style mandates `CamelCase` for functions.

The way this would work if a user wanted to would be
```
linters_with_tags(
  tags = "default",
  object_name_linter(scope = c("function", "variable")),
  constant_name_linter = object_name_linter("SNAKE_CASE", scope = "constant"),
  class_name_linter = object_name_linter("CamelCase", scope = "class")
)
```

Definition of the scopes would be:
 * function = assignment targets of `//FUNCTION` exprs
 * constant = assignment targets of exactly one known-constant expr
 * class = assignment targets of `R6::R6Class()` exprs
 * argument = targets of `//SYMBOL_FORMALS`
 * variable = everything else

title: line length linter gives incorrect warnings with UTF-8 characters
description:
I've noticed that lintr fails on a file that contains a line like this:

```
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

(a #, followed by a space, followed by [U+2500](https://www.compart.com/en/unicode/U+2500), for a line length of 120).

I run something like

``` r
lintr::lint("filename.R", linters = c(line_length_linter(120)))
```

but get

```
filename.R:1:121: style: [line_length_linter] Lines should not be more than 120 characters.
# ââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââââ
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

setting the linter to 356 works, 355 fails. This sort of makes sense if the text is not being loaded as UTF-8 (1 char + 1 char + 118 * 3 char = 356).

Digging into this, is seems like the source of the issue may be in `get_source_expressions()` and the call to `base::srcfile`. On my system I have `getOption("encoding") == "native.enc"` (I am pretty certain that this is the default shipped with R as I have never had to change this previously), but setting `options("encoding" = "UTF-8")` causes the issue to go away.

I've tested this both on Windows and Mac OS, both with same results, using R 4.2.0 and lintr 3.0.0.9000, below is a subset of my session info. This feels like it's just a general text encoding issue so happy for this to be classed as out-of-scope.

title: Feature request: include linter name in warnings
description:
## Request

Consider the following code:

```r
library(lintr)
f <- tempfile(fileext = ".R")
writeLines("do_thing <- T", f)
lintr::lint(
    filename = f
    , linters = list(
        "tf" = lintr::T_and_F_symbol_linter
    )
    , cache = FALSE
)
```

On `{lintr}` 2.0.1 installed from CRAN and on the latest version from GitHub (https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/commit/801fac322613121f32ae916af379161a838e3b27, installed with `remotes::install_github("r-lib/lintr")`), this produces the following output (the `(...)` is mine, just to make the path a bit more readable):

```text
(...)/T/RtmpIvPGWZ/fileb817b0f6442.R:1:14: style: Use TRUE instead of the symbol T.
do_thing <- T
            ~^
```

As a user of `{lintr}`, I'd like to see the linter name printed in the output, like this:

```text
(...)/RtmpIvPGWZ/fileb817b0f6442.R:1:14: style: [T_and_F_symbol_linter] Use TRUE instead of the symbol T.
do_thing <- T
            ~^
```

## Motivation

I learned tonight from @MichaelChirico that as of `{lintr}` 3.0.0, it'll be possible to use a comment like the following to say "ignore warnings from a specific linter on this line" (https://github.com/microsoft/LightGBM/pull/5249#discussion_r889447818).

```r
x <- T  # nolint: T_and_F_symbol_linter`
```

I totally see the value in being specific there and would like to do that. But since the linter name isn't printed in the warnings from `lintr::lint()`, figuring out the right value to add in that comment will require some trial-and-error or searching in this package's source code.

## References:

As an example, `flake8` also supports such targeted comments (https://flake8.pycqa.org/en/3.1.1/user/ignoring-errors.html#in-line-ignoring-errors), and I've found it really helpful that it prints in its output exactly the code that should be added to `# noqa` comments.

```shell
echo "x = (1,2,3,y)" > ./out.py
flake8 ./out.py
```

```text
./out.py:1:7: E231 missing whitespace after ','
./out.py:1:9: E231 missing whitespace after ','
./out.py:1:11: E231 missing whitespace after ','
./out.py:1:12: F821 undefined name 'y'
```

Example suppressing one specific warning:

```shell
echo "x = (1,2,3,y)  # noqa: E231" > ./out.py
flake8 ./out.py
```

```text
./out.py:1:12: F821 undefined name 'y'
```

Thanks for your time and consideration!

title: Use expr[1][SYMBOL_FUNCTION_CALL] consistently
description: #1340 and its solution highlights the importance of the point raised by @AshesITR in #1310 -- we should use `expr[1]` where possible when specifying XPaths on `<expr>` nodes. This will almost surely have a notable performance implication for edge cases like `c(...)` where `...length()` is huge, but will likely have a good benefit even in the more common case where `...length()` is, say, dozens rather than 100s or 1000s.

title: unneeded_concatenation_linter() can throw on valid usages
description:
```
lint("c(matrix(1:10, 2, 5))\n", unneeded_concatenation_linter())
# <text>:1:1: style: Unneeded concatenation of a constant. Remove the "c" call.
# c(matrix(1:10, 1, 5))
# ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

`c()` can be used as here to concisely drop the dimensions on a matrix, so we can't just throw a lint on all `c(<expr>)` cases.

We have considered whether this usage should always be replaced by a more declarative version like `as.vector()` instead; perhaps we could do so with a linter parameter. In any case, this new lint marks a departure from 2.0.1 behavior.

Note that the new behavior _is_ good in some cases, e.g. it newly finds `c(1 - alpha / 2)` and `c(1:10)`, but I'm not sure there's a maintainable way to always catch these.

title: Rename of default= to defaults= is hard to debug (linters_with_defaults)
description:
Just discovered this hard-to-debug issue:

```
# pre-3.0.0 usage

writeLines(names(my_linters))
# no_tab_linter
```

OK, we get a warning:

> Warning message: Function with_defaults was deprecated in lintr version 2.0.9001. Use linters_with_defaults instead.

So we switch:

```
my_linters <- linters_with_defaults(default = list(), no_tab_linter())
writeLines(names(my_linters))
# assignment_linter
# ...
# default
# ...
# vector_logic_linter
```

i.e., `default=` is taken as part of the `...` arguments, and we don't start from a blank (`list()`) override.

Probably we should allow `default=` to work in `linters_with_defaults()`, with warning.

(Or perhaps this pluralization was an oversight?)

title: Adding SARIF result format support for lintr

If you agree, we will be happy to looking into necessary code changes in this repo and also creating a starter workflow in the GitHub starter workflow repo to make it available as a GitHub code scanner.

( Does the tool already has a flag logically like --format, if so we are looking at adding sarif to that list, if not let us know preferred way in R langue to provide arg what output format user want.
Feel free to let me know if have any guidance, thanks! )

I see previous related request #991 and #807 . Linking here.

Thanks,
Shaopeng

title: Provide support for GitHub's Code Scanning API
description:
> GitHub recently released the Code Scanning API, which allows users to upload SAST scan results directly to GitHub. This allows developers to scan code on pull requests and use branch protection rules to disallow code contributions if they do not pass. 
>
> We've written a [detailed integration guide](https://partner.github.com/integration-resources/2021/03/09/pattern-integrating-with-code-scanning.html) that outlines how to upload a SARIF report to GitHub and run the project out of GitHub actions. If you'd be interested to add this to your project we can recommend LintR when we see projects written in R on GitHub automatically. Users would be able to use their free actions minutes and the code-scanning api on any open source project written in R.
>
> If you'd be interested to add Lintr to the collection of OSS scanners on GitHub I'd really appreciate it! Happy to send out a swag kit to you or whoever does the work, too. It'll definitely help people find the tool. 
> 
> If you don't have time or interest, no worries! We know being an OSS maintainer is sort of a thankless job sometimes and we appreciate you working on GitHub. I have your project in a backlog of projects that sometimes our team will pick up from. I'll try to see if we can make the code contribution directly, too.

title: Improve warning message for `fixed_regex_linter`
description:
> For static regular expression patterns, set `fixed = TRUE`. Note that this includes regular expressions that can be expressed as fixed patterns, e.g. [.] is really just . and \\$ is really just $ if there are no other regular expression specials. For functions from the 'stringr' package, the way to declare a static string is to wrap the pattern in stringr::fixed(). If this is being used in a dbplyr context (i.e., translated to sql), replace the regular expression with the `LIKE` operator using the `%LIKE%` infix function. Lastly, take care to remember that the `replacement` argument of `gsub()` is affected by the `fixed` argument as well.

I have a few questions/comments around  this warning, especially the second sentence.

1. "Note that this includes" - what is "this"? Why does "this" "include" something? Is this supposed to say that "the previous statement" "holds true"/"applies"/... to "regular expressions that can be expressed as fixed patterns"?
2. What does "[.]" apply to? Is that to mean that folks shouldn't use "[H]ello world", but "Hello world"? Or is this to discourage people from actually writing "[.]" and writing "." instead? I suppose it's the former, but then the use of regular expressions in statements about regular expressions is really making it unclear.
3. Why is "\\$ ... really just $ if there are no other regular expression specials"? To my understanding, `$` is an end-of-expression placeholder when `fixed = FALSE` (or omitted), and it's a literal dollar sign when `fixed = TRUE`. What do "other regular expression specials" have to do with that?
4. The part of the message in 3 feels to me like it has been added to explain *why* lintr warns about something. However, it seems to warn about everything, irrespective of any regular expression specials - e.g., expressions such as `grepl("b", "abc")`. [Is that for performance? Because I find this much more readable than `grepl("b", "abc", fixed = TRUE)`, and I am not aware of any good alternative in R.] Anyway, I wonder why lintr explains why it warns about something specific if it warns about pretty much everything.

title: `object_usage_linter()` tries too many assignments
description:
Seen in our own package when running `lint_package()`:

```
..........Warning in formals(fun) : argument is not a function
Warning in body(fun) : argument is not a function
Warning in formals(fun) : argument is not a function
Warning in body(fun) : argument is not a function
...................................................Warning in formals(fun) : argument is not a function
Warning in body(fun) : argument is not a function
................................................................................................................................................
```

The reason is the XPath for `object_usage_linter()` finds e.g.

```r

title: Who lints the linters?
description:
Although there is a `.lintr` file in the lintr root, linting is not done as part of the current travis-CI workflow (or the soon to be introduced GHA CI workflow).

If people are keen to integrate lintr into their dev workflow, they're probably going to look at lintr as a good example of how to set this up. For those who read docs, the current docs explain how to set up lintr for running on Travis; they might need expanding to explain how to use lintr on GHA / other providers. For those who don't read docs, it would be good if `{lintr}` had exemplary lint-running code that they can copy/paste into their own projects (or perhaps a `use_lintr` hook could be constructed for `{usethis}` that makes setting up linting trivial).

Nonetheless, the current linting setup fails:

With master: f878ec99839d36289fcb14b4d811986933b93174 
if we run `Rscript -e "devtools::load_all(); lint_package()"` in the `lintr` root, we get the following:
```
Loading lintr
Error: Malformed file!
Execution halted
```

If we run `Rscript -e "devtools::load_all(); lint_dir('R')"` we get a long list of lints. (and also for `lint_dir("tests")`)

Some of these lints 

- are due to bugs in lintr (some fixed in recent but unmerged PRs: #441, #546
- are due to the "exclusions" not being updated when example/test code is added that is designed to fail the linters (@AshesITR 's recent directory-exclusion PR should ease fixing this kind of stuff)
- would have been fixed if linting had been a consistent part of the lintr PR workflow.

Should we fixup the lintr PR process so that linting is always run?
And if we do, how do we change the current code base so that linting the current code comes back green?

What we shouldn't do is a monolithic PR using `{styler}` or something that fixes hundreds of `function(arg=123)` to `function(arg = 123)`; when these wholesale-change commits introduce bugs they are hell to fix.

I'd suggest we rewrite the .lintr:

- exclude all test & doc directories for now
- use the smallest collection of the default linters that come back green on `<lintr>/R`
- apply these linters to any newly submitted PR
- then do individual PRs to gradually add further default-linters back in

An alternative would be to write up a .lintr that defines the linters that we definitely do want to apply to lintr and write up a CI workflow script that applies these linters to _just_ those files that were modified in a submitted PR; and if a lint crops up on a line that was touched by the PR author then linting should return red from CI.

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lintr/vignettes/creating_linters.html

Feels off. Two major shortcomings:

 - It doesn't mention anything about cacheing lints
 - It doesn't mention anything about parsing with the XML tree

I think it would make sense to update the vignette to show how to make a lint cache-friendly (distinguishing between the `full_parsed_content` and expression-level input), as well as to give some insights about how to get going making XPath-based logic for linting.

https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/c68c11e269bf2b5c15335cbfde163f05734417a9/tests/testthat/test-open_curly_linter.R#L35-L37

But not matched by the new `brace_linter`:

```
lint("a <- function() {  \n}", brace_linter())
```

I think the new behavior is better -- `trailing_whitespace_linter()` is the one designed to lint in this case.

OTOH, `open_curly_linter()` is being marked as deprecated -- is it worth making such a change?

This came up working on #1186. Linting on whitespace also makes it difficult to convert to XPath since the XML tree is unaware of the whitespace.

title: Auto-gernerate linter list for README

An approach to this could be:

2. Add a single-line description to `linters.csv` (so the CSV structure would be `linter,description,tags`)
3. Use this information in README.Rmd to generate a descriptive list

An added benefit would be that these one-line descriptions could also be put into `?linters`.
In lintr 2.0.1, `?linters` included these one-line descriptions since all linters were `@describeIn`'d there.
The new structure put this information on the individual linter help pages.

WDYT @MichaelChirico, @jimhester?

Alternatively, this could also become a `release_bullet()`, but it would require manual curation without an easily C&P-able template.

title: Noisy warnings from new abbreviated linter exclusions
description:
I've been seeing this a lot lately, finally got a reprex:

```
lintr::lint(text = "a = 1 # nolint: implicit_integer.", linters = lintr::assignment_linter())
# <text>:1:3: style: Use <-, not =, for assignment.
# a = 1 # nolint: implicit_integer.
#   ^
# Warning message:
# In add_exclusions(exclusions, nolints[i], linters_string, exclude_linter_sep,  :
#   Could not find linter named ‘implicit_integer’ in the list of active linters. Make sure the linter is uniquely identified by the given name or prefix.
```

That is, the code (1) throws a lint and (2) has a `#nolint` directive specifying a linter that's not in the current set of `linters`.

This makes running one or a few linters on code that's generally covered by more linters quite noisy. Is there anything we can do here? Should "list of active linters" be expanded to "list of known linters"?

title: Performance: Avoid `//*[self::...]` constructs.
description:
I've benchmarked `//*[self::... or self::...]` vs. `//... | //...` and found a huge difference performance-wise:

```r
xml <- xml2::read_xml(xmlparsedata::xml_parse_data(parse(text = "a <- 2\nb <- 3 + 4\nc <- 5 %% 6")))
bench::mark(
  xml2::xml_find_all(xml, "//*[self::OP-PLUS or self::SPECIAL[text() = '%%']]"),
  xml2::xml_find_all(xml, "//OP-PLUS | //SPECIAL[text() = '%%']")
)
```

On my laptop yields median times:
```
xml2::xml_find_all(xml, "//*[self::OP-PLUS or self::SPECIAL[text() = '%%']]")   59.5us
xml2::xml_find_all(xml, "//OP-PLUS | //SPECIAL[text() = '%%']")                 41.4us
```

That's a 33% faster for zero effort.

title: Possible improvement for 3.0.0 breaking change
description:
Reported by downstream here:

https://github.com/microsoft/LightGBM/issues/5228

Slightly simpler reprex:

```
lintr::lint(text = "print(1)", linters = lintr::assignment_linter)
# Error: `fun` must be a function taking exactly one argument.
# In addition: Warning message:
#  The use of linters of class 'function' was deprecated in lintr version 2.0.1.9001. Use linters classed as 'linter' (see ?Linter) instead.
```

Can we not do `fun()` for the user in this release after issuing "please use a linter" warning?

Also, I'm wondering if the warning message can't be improved:

> The use of linters of class 'function' was deprecated in lintr version 2.0.1.9001. Use linters classed as 'linter' (see ?Linter) instead.

I think the most likely scenario where a user encounters this warning is just like the above -- they've got a script using the un-called form, or they've grown used to supplying it themselves interactively. So we should add this to the end, right?

> For example, if you supplied `lintr::assignment_linter`, please use `lintr::assignment_linter()` instead.

title: undesirable_operator_linter doesn't handle `=` as expected
description:
I think it's safe to assume that a user specifying `undesirable_operator_linter(list(`=` = NA))` is targeting equals-assignment (even though `assignment_linter()` is more appropriate for this). But HEAD doesn't quite match that:

```
lintr::lint(linters = lintr::undesirable_operator_linter(op = list("=" = NA)), text = "
a = 1
foo <- function(a = 1) { a }
foo(a = 2)
")
```

makes two lints:

```
<text>:2:3: warning: Operator `=` is undesirable.
a = 1
  ^
<text>:4:7: warning: Operator `=` is undesirable.
foo(a = 2)
      ^
```

The latter is a false positive IMO -- there's basically no way to avoid the `=` (well, there's positional arguments, but we can easily write a signature such that `=` is required)

title: Is `isS3stdGeneric()` the right way to detect S3 generics?
description:
When checking if a function is an S3 generic (after getting it from the `NAMESPACE` file for example), [a call to `isS3stdGeneric()` is used](https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/blob/0397cb777e42ac25fcda8f7245edaadbf56f6fc0/R/namespace.R#L42) to tell if the function is an S3 generic. This works well for standard generics (when the first expression in the body calls `UseMethod()` [1]), but doesn't work so well if there is any sort of pre-processing in the generic (e.g.[`vctrs::vec_ptype_full`](https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/blob/master/R/ptype-abbr-full.R#L33-L38) which runs some dots checking before calling `UseMethod`)

```
> isS3stdGeneric(vctrs::vec_ptype_full)
[1] FALSE
```

I've looked a bit and haven't yet found a function that will find both standard and non-standard S3 generics. Would it be better / ok to fall back to the prior check of `is.function(fun)`? Or have an option to do that?

[1] - https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/utils/html/isS3stdGen.html

title: Make R/ conform to `cyclocomp_linter`
description:
Final part of #584.

The current target is to use `cyclocomp_linter(15)`. It's currently enabled at `cyclocomp_linter(29)`.

At current `master`, We get the following functions triggering the `cyclocomp_linter`:

 - [ ] CC=17 R/closed_curly_linter.R:6:1:closed_curly_linter
 - [ ] CC=16 R/commas_linter.R:5:1:commas_linter
 - [ ] CC=16 R/get_source_expressions.R:340:1:fix_tab_indentations
 - [ ] CC=18 R/get_source_expressions.R:393:1:fix_eq_assigns
 - [ ] CC=29 R/lint.R:25:1:lint
 - [ ] CC=18 R/namespace_linter.R:9:1:namespace_linter
 - [ ] CC=16 R/open_curly_linter.R:4:1:open_curly_linter
 - [ ] CC=17 R/path_linters.R:104:1:split_path
 - [ ] CC=19 R/sprintf_linter.R:4:1:sprintf_linter

Because each of these is more than a whitespace change/trivial refactor, each function should be addressed in its own PR.

PS One worry I have is that this one is more likely to be a high barrier for contributed PRs, as the linter's advice is not particularly actionable (my cyclomatic complexity is 16... OK... what exactly do I do now?). For the vast majority of people contributing PRs, any bot pestering them about the "cyclomatic complexity" of their PR is going to be confusing to say the least. Do we really want to send contributors on a chase to figure out what cyclomatic complexity is, and then how to apply it to their code?

One alternative would be to keep the threshold much lower during dev (say 29, like currently), and then have a pre-release task to address cyclomatic complexity among the maintainers before release.

Any thoughts?

title: `lint_dir` doesn't vectorize properly.
description:
I can't really provide a good reprex since it relies on having a specific filesystem constructed.

Note that there's no vectorization test: https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/master/tests/testthat/test-dir_linters.R

Note below: `<project-dir>` has been clipped and redacted. 

```
> lintr::lint_dir(c("R", "test/R"))
.........................
Error in .rs.normalizePath(marker$file, mustWork = TRUE) : 
  path[1]="/Users/<project-dir>/R//Users/<project-dir>/R/build_report.R": No such file or directory
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In while (!has_config(path, config)) { :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
2: In while (!has_config(path, config)) { :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
```

It looks like either `lint_dir` needs to be explicitly non-vectorized and `stop()` if given a char vector over length 1 in the path argument, or it needs to vectorize arguments and handle multiple directories.

description:
`xml2::xml_text(xml2::xml_find_first(xml, "/x/path"))` is equivalent to `xml2::xml_find_chr(xml, "string(/x/path)")`, looking a bit cleaner.
We could refactor our codebase to use the more concise idiom.

title: xml_nodes_to_lints' offset= could just be used to land the cursor after the linted symbol?
description:
In `T_and_F_symbol_linter` and now (#1160) `implicit_integer_linter`, we've got a case where `offset=` is only needed to land the RStudio marker "to the right" of where the lint is hitting, so that the cursor is conveniently where we can type a fix and be done.

For `T_and_F_symbol_linter`, that's easy, because for both cases, we offset by 1 (`T` -> move right by one, `F` -> move right by one).

But for `implicit_integer_linter`, this won't work, because the landed symbols can have variable width (`1` -> move right by one, `10` -> move right by two).

So I think we need a different API for this case than `offset`.

Will a boolean flag suffice? `xml_nodes_to_lint(postposition = TRUE)`? (name?)

That will certainly cover the two use cases we have thus far.

PS, any different thoughts about restricting `ranges[1] <= column_number <= ranges[2]` for this case?

title: Always populate xml_parsed_content and full_xml_parsed_content (perhaps with xml_missing)
description:
Just confirmed that

```
xml2::xml_find_all(xml2::xml_missing, "//a")
# {xml_nodeset (0)}
```

so most of our linters will just work with the replacement.

Unfortunately

```
xml2::xml_find_first(xml2::xml_missing, "//a")
```

is an error, so we may have to guard the code against attempting `xml_find_first()` on missing documents.

title: Export `xml_nodes_to_lint()`?
description:
Used in most linters by now, because it's a very useful helper for XPath-based linting.
Since we already export `with_id` and `ids_with_token` as helpers for the parse data based approach, I think we could also export `xml_nodes_to_lint()`.

Also thinking about the function name: Shouldn't this be either vectorized (on nodesets or lists of nodes) or singular (`xml_node_to_lint()`)?

cc @MichaelChirico

shiny::tags$b("Hi", )
```

shiny::tags$b("Hi", )
                  ^
```

title: Google linters for 3.0.0 release
description:
Splitting off a subset of #884 as a TODO list for 3.0.0 release; the rest of the linters can be done after that.

- [x] `AnyDuplicatedLinter` - Require usage of anyDuplicated() > 0 over any(duplicated(.)) #986
- [x] `AnyIsNALinter` - Require usage of anyNA over any(is.na(.)) #975
- [x] `ClassEqualsLinter` - Block comparison of class with == #989
- [x] ~`StopPasteLinter`~ `condition_message_linter` - Block usage of paste() and paste0() with messaging functions using ... #999
- [x] ~`MultipleStopifnotLinter`~ `ConsecutiveStopifnotLinter` - Force consecutive stopifnot() calls into just one #1005 
- [x] `ElseSameLineLinter` - Require else to come on the same line as the preceding brace #1002
- [x] `ExpectComparisonLinter` - Require usage of expect_gt(x, y) over expect_true(x > y) (and similar) #955 
- [x] `ExpectIdenticalLinter` - Require usage of expect_identical(x, y) where appropriate #958 
- [x] `ExpectIsLinter` - Redirect away from deprecated testthat::expect_is() #946 
- [x] `ExpectLengthLinter` - Require usage of expect_length(x, n) over expect_equal(length(x), n) #950 
- [x] `ExpectNamedLinter` - Require usage of expect_named(x, n) over expect_equal(names(x), n) #949 
- [x] `ExpectNotLinter` - Require usage of expect_false(.) over expect_true(!.) #945 
- [x] `ExpectNullLinter` - Require usage of expect_null(x) over expect_equal(x, NULL) and similar #887 
- [x] `ExpectS3ClassLinter` - Require usage of expect_s3_class() or expect_s4_class() where appropriate. #943
- [x] `ExpectS4ClassLinter` - Require usage of expect_s4_class(x, k) over expect_true(is(x, k)) #943 
- [x] ~`ExpectTrueFalseAndConditionLinter`~ `conjunct_test_linter` - Force && conditions in expect_true(), expect_false() to be written separately #948 
- [x] `ExpectTrueFalseLinter` - Require usage of expect_true(x) over expect_equal(x, TRUE) #947 
- [x] `ExpectTypeLinter` - Require usage of expect_type(x, type) over expect_equal(typeof(x), type) #924 
- [x] `FixedRegexLinter` - Require usage of 'fixed=TRUE' in regular expressions where appropriate #1021 
- [x] `FunctionBraceLinter` - Require multi-line functions to use braces #987
- [x] `IfelseCensorLinter` - Block usage of ifelse where pmin or pmax is more appropriate #1007
- [x] `IfElseMatchBracesLinter` - Require both or neither if/else branches to use curly braces #983
- [x] `InnerCombineLinter` - Require c() to be applied before relatively expensive vectorized functions #1012 
- [x] `LiteralCoercionLinter` - Require usage of correctly-typed literals over literal coercions #995
- [x] `NestedIfelseLinter` - Block usage of nested ifelse() calls #996
- [x] `NumericLeadingZeroLinter` - Require usage of a leading zero in all fractional numerics #992
- [x] `OuterNegationLinter` - Require usage of !any(.) over all(!.), !all(.) over any(!.) #988

title: Add/export a readable wrapper for testing whether a linter is on an expression or the whole file
description:
We've got (minor perturbations of) this little idiomatic piece at the top of basically every linter:

https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/23b06bdd4d8a28d94fa42eab4aebb58f8b108238/R/cyclocomp_linter.R#L13-L15

https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/23b06bdd4d8a28d94fa42eab4aebb58f8b108238/R/line_length_linter.R#L13

https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/23b06bdd4d8a28d94fa42eab4aebb58f8b108238/R/missing_argument_linter.R#L11

This is too obscure to a first-time reader. We should add a wrapper of this expression that makes it clear what's being done/why, and also export it for use in custom downstream linters.

title: Remove redundant `_linter` suffix from auto names?
description:
The new `# nolint: xxx.` feature makes it more likely for linter names to appear in source code.
I would therefor suggest we remove the redundant `_linter` suffix from the names to make most lint exclusions look more natural.
Compare:

```
my.bad.name <- function(a, b) { # nolint: object_name_linter.
  # Very long comment explaining why the name came to be and needs to stay # nolint: line_length_linter.
  a + b
}
```

to

```
my.bad.name <- function(a, b) { # nolint: object_name.
  # Very long comment explaining why the name came to be and needs to stay # nolint: line_length.
  a + b
}
```

wdyt?

cc @MichaelChirico @jimhester

title: Allowing lone curly braces in some cases
description:
I think the curly brace alone is the most readable in some cases. Particularly I came across this writing a `switch` where the default is multiline:

```
# file: brace.R
switch(x,
  "a" = do_something(x),
  "b" = do_another(x),
  { # default
    do_first(x)
    do_second(x)
  }
)
```

```
lintr::lint('brace.R')
/private/tmp/brace.R:4:3: style: Opening curly braces should never go on their own line and should always be followed by a new line.
  { # default
  ^
```

Is there any option to turn off this failure for this case? This alternative I think is not very readable:

```
switch(x,
  "a" = do_something(x),
  "b" = do_another(x), {
    do_first(x)
    do_second(x)
  }
)
```

There was also a request for exceptions in a case like `with` (though I would still use EOL-`{` in that case personally):

https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/issues/188#issuecomment-275643515

title: conjunct_stopifnot_linter could be generalized (in particular, to include assert_that)
description:
`assertthat::assert_that()` falls under basically the same lens as `conjunct_stopifnot_linter()` -- code like

```
assertthat::assert_that(A && B)
```

is usually more informative if tested separately:

```
assertthat::assert_that(A)
assertthat::assert_that(B)
```

(similar proviso applies if `msg=` argument is used as for the named test version of `stopifnot()`).

raising now since this generalization is best served by renaming the function, so we might want to do that before 3.0.0 -- we don't have to implement the new logic yet, just to land on a name if we decide to include the `assert_that` case.

conjunct_test_linter() should optionally skip keyword arguments to stopifnot()
description:
Follow-up to #1011 

consider

```
stopifnot(
  `x is a logical scalar` = length(x) == 1 && is.logical(x) && !is.na(x),
  `y is a logical scalar` = length(y) == 1 && is.logical(y) && !is.na(y), 
)
```

Converting each of these conditions to their own test might be tedious, so I think it should be optional.

I think the option to lint keyword usage should be `TRUE` by default (i.e., only optionally exclude such usage)

title: False positive for yoda_test_linter finding STR_CONST in $ expressions
description:
A pattern seen several times in `IOHanalyzer`:

https://github.com/IOHprofiler/IOHanalyzer/blob/93fdf6400f64c63c26c956086469d7a27c31ab05/tests/testthat/test_DataSetList.R#L42

```
expect_equal(get_FV_sample(dsl[1],12)$"run.5",13)
```

Here, the `STR_CONST` for `"run.5"` is at the same parse level that we check for constants in the first expression.

title: False positive for yoda_test_linter in magrittr pipeline
description:
A pattern seen a lot in `formula.tools`:

https://github.com/decisionpatterns/formula.tools/blob/45b6654e4d8570cbaf1e2fd527652471202d97ad/tests/testthat/test-lhs.r#L13

```
lhs( NA ~ . )   %>% expect_equal(NA) 
```

IMO this is not the best way to write tests, but nevertheless we shouldn't trigger a lint with `yoda_test_linter()`.

title: Check relevance of false positive in yoda_test_linter
description:
This is a known false positive in `yoda_test_linter()`:

```
expect_equal(1, 1)
```

This should be linted (it's a placeholder that shouldn't really be checked in "to prod"), but currently the message is confusing.

We should check the practical relevance of this concern, though, before investing in a workaround.

title: Ensure linter logic allows for R>=4 raw strings
description:
Some linters (e.g. current `paste_sep_linter` and `paste_to_string_linter`) rely on assumptions about `STR_CONST` nodes that are designed with R<4 in mind, where `R"(a string)"` is not available.

We should take a pass over linters to ensure robustness to this new style of literal strings.

title: Add `allow_multiple_spaces = TRUE` to `infix_spaces_linter()` to fully replace `assignment_linter()`
description:
Since @f-ritter's original use-case was disallowing these, I think we should also support that rule via an argument (`allow_multiple_spaces = TRUE`). WDYT?

title: object_usage_linter and $ operator
description:
Hi, excuse me if I'm posting an inappropriate issue, it's my first issue on Github.

I noticed a strange behavior of object_usage_linter and $ operator when used inside and outside functions.

File "test.r":
```
print.list.item <- function(list.argument) {
    item <- list.argument$item1
    print(item)
}

my.list <- list(item1 = "item1")
my.list.2 <- list(item2 = "item2")

my.list.2$item2 <- 1

print.list.item(my.list)
```

Then I get:
```
> lint("test.r")
C:\[...]\test.r:2:27: warning: no visible binding for global variable 'item1'
    item <- list.argument$item1
                          ^~~~~
```

If I remove the line that uses the $ operator outside the function, like this:

File "test.r":
```
print.list.item <- function(list.argument) {
    item <- list.argument$item1
    print(item)
}

my.list <- list(item1 = "item1")
my.list.2 <- list(item2 = "item2")

print.list.item(my.list)
```

`lint("test.r")` returns no problems.

Is it a bug in lintr, or it is my coding style that should be different?

title: Refactor semicolon_terminator_linter for consistency?
description:
`semicolon_terminator_linter` strikes me as a bit "off" w.r.t. the style elsewhere in the package

 1. The name `semicolon_linter` seems better to me
 2. The signature `function(semicolon = c("compound", "trailing"))` looks odd. I think we are aligning more on toggling these types of things with `allow*`-style arguments, e.g. `function(allow_compound = FALSE, allow_trailing = FALSE)` would be equivalent to the current signature.

Are either of these worth doing?

Of course, we can use a deprecation cycle to make the changes more gradually.

      fun = function() {
        a = 1
      }
    "),

```

title: Use .Rin files to test 4.0+ features?
description:
Happened to be reading the section on tests and was reminded that R supports .Rin files:

https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-exts.html#Package-subdirectories

We might be able to use these to do proper tests of `|>` without violating the R dependency requirement -- on R<4.1, the .Rin file just produces a vanilla script that always passes. Otherwise, it runs some `|>`-related tests (or anything that has a parser dependency, really).

Run namespace_linter in a subprocess? Optionally?

> Note that using `check_exports=TRUE` or `check_nonexports=TRUE` will load packages used in user code so it could potentially change the global state.

We could avoid this by running the linter in a subprocess, right? Is it worthwhile to do so?

description:
A number of linters need to evaluate code to work properly, such as retrieving namespace exports and some of the object usage linters.

unloading namespaces is not always possible, so it is probably easier to run the linters in a separate R process with **callr**.

title: Should the named arguments being on separate lines be considered a lint?
description: Here is an example code: ```r mean( x = c(1, 2, 3, NA, 5), na.rm = TRUE ) ``` The _Tidyverse style guide_ says [nothing](https://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#argument-names) about whether the parameter name and the argument provided to it should be on the same lines: And `{styler}` will [not change](https://github.com/r-lib/styler/issues/734) styling for this code: ``` r styler::style_text( "mean( x = c(1, 2, 3, NA, 5), na.rm = TRUE )" ) #> mean( #> x = #> c(1, 2, 3, NA, 5), #> na.rm = #> TRUE #> ) ``` Created on 2022-04-02 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1) But I am wondering how intentional such a usage might be in the wild, and if this should be considered a lint?
