title: ... should come 2nd in lint_dir()
description:
Now, if we want to run `lint_dir()` for only a specific linter, we have to somewhat awkwardly pass the default argument to `relative_path`:

```
lintr::lint_dir("/path/to/dir", TRUE, lintr::specific_linter())
```

I think this goes against the tidyverse design principle where `...` is considered "data":

https://design.tidyverse.org/args-data-details.html

Since the next release is a major version bump, I think we can make the change now and try and fix whoever's broken, hopefully few if any people rely on this anyway.

title: Ability to edit style_regexes or alternative approach
description:
So, I might have a bit of a weird use case but I was wondering if you could add an argument to be able to provide my own list for `style_regexes` for the `object_name_linter`?

Our lab uses `data.table` which outputs NOTES while checking the package if you reference column names: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/43662416/when-using-data-table-in-a-package-r-cmd-check-notes-no-visible-global-functio

We currently solve this by adding a line like the following at the beginning of our functions:

```
column_referenced1 = column_referenced2 = NULL
```
(For a real example, see here: https://github.com/hugheylab/seeker/blob/3735fdc0459257bf2601a00b64f2bff633c3b1f1/R/array_utils.R#L241)

This is a fine workaround, but unfortunately some of the `data.table` columns we deal with don't match the same standard we want to use for our other object names.

I know I can provide multiple object name styles, but I'd really like to be able to add a custom style that will ignore the style when it's ultimately followed by `= NULL` kinda like this:

```
style_regexes = lintr:::style_regexes
style_regexes$snake_case_null  = rex(start, maybe("."), some_of(lower, digit), any_of("_", lower, digit), " = NULL", end)
```

Or is there an alternate approach you think I should take to accomplish this?

title: Ungraceful failure when using multi-assign operator `%<-%` from `zeallot` (`keras`)
description:
**Description**: `lintr` fails with the following error:

```
Error in rep.int(character, length) : invalid 'times' value
Calls: <Anonymous> ... print.lint -> cat -> highlight_string -> fill_with -> paste0
```

This happens when the linted file contains the multi-assign operator `%<-%` from the `zeallot` package.

Related to: #763 , #742 , #355 ?

**Steps to reproduce**

1. Put the following code into `foo.R`.

```
foo <- function() {
  a <- b <- NULL
  c(a, b) %<-% list(1, 2)
  return(NULL)
}
```

2. Run `R -e "lintr::lint('foo.R')"`

`sessionInfo()`
```
R version 4.1.1 (2021-08-10)
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)
Running under: Ubuntu 20.04.3 LTS

Matrix products: default
BLAS/LAPACK: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/openblas-pthread/libopenblasp-r0.3.8.so

locale:
 [1] LC_CTYPE=en_US.UTF-8       LC_NUMERIC=C              
 [3] LC_TIME=en_US.UTF-8        LC_COLLATE=en_US.UTF-8    
 [5] LC_MONETARY=en_US.UTF-8    LC_MESSAGES=C             
 [7] LC_PAPER=en_US.UTF-8       LC_NAME=C                 
 [9] LC_ADDRESS=C               LC_TELEPHONE=C            
[11] LC_MEASUREMENT=en_US.UTF-8 LC_IDENTIFICATION=C       

attached base packages:
[1] stats     graphics  grDevices utils     datasets  methods   base     

loaded via a namespace (and not attached):
[1] compiler_4.1.1
```
While this session is relevant to my use case, I also tested on R version `4.1.2` and `4.0.4` using `rocker/r-ver` images, `install.packages("lintr")` (also need `apt-get install libxml2`).

**Expected behavior**

When the previous code is run after installing the development version with `devtools::install_github("jimhester/lintr")`, `lintr` produces its expected behavior.

```
/home/foo.R:3:1: warning: no visible global function definition for ‘%<-%’
```

**Fix**: install the development version of `lintr`.

**Significance:** You may ask if this is an issue since there is a fix in the development version. I would say yes for three reasons. First, I wanted to give visibility to an error that took time to track down. Second, the multi-assign operator from `zeallot` is often use in `keras` because of the parallel with `python` multi-assign. `keras` tutorials use it [often](https://tensorflow.rstudio.com/guide/keras/examples/mnist_mlp/), including in functions, for example, [`gradient_ascent` here](https://tensorflow.rstudio.com/guide/keras/examples/deep_dream/). With the popularity of `keras`, this error may show up more often. Finally, it is good practice to limit reliance on (potentially unstable) development version, especially for a package that is so important to CI.

description:

Perhaps this might be of interest to lintr users, as an alternative to the https://github.com/r-lib/actions lintr action.

I'd be happy to add it to the `README.md` with a PR.

title: some no proper `no visible binding` by `object_usage_linter`
description:
For the next code:
```r
library(dplyr)
library(magrittr)
test <- function(data) {
  f <<- function(y) class
  data %T>% {
      print(summary(.))
  } %>%
    head()
}
```
I get
```r
lintr::lint('file.r')
/home/iago/Downloads/rep.r:7:3: warning: no visible binding for '<<-' assignment to ‘f’
  f <<- function(y) class
  ^
/home/iago/Downloads/rep.r:9:21: warning: no visible binding for global variable ‘.’
      print(summary(.))
```
So it seems to not understand global assignments of anonymous functions inside functions (but if the assignment is previously done outside the `test` function, there is no warning), and also the `.` used in `magrittr` pipe workflow.

Further, usually I write such code as follows:
```r
library(dplyr)
library(magrittr)
test <- function(data) {

title: Adding type hints to the AST?
description:
R is dynamically typed, which limits the scope of some linters / makes some linters impossible to write.

Nonetheless, there are some functions in R whose output we can type with certainty, e.g.

* `as.{raw,logical,integer,double,complex,character,list}` converters
* `lapply()` --> `list()`
* `paste()`/`paste0()`/`sprintf()`/`file.path()`/`gsub()` --> `character()`
* `grepl()`/`any()`/`all()`/`&&`/`||`/`&`/`|`/`xor()`/`%in%`/`nzchar()`/`==`/`!=`/`>=`/`<=`/`>`/`<` --> `logical()`
* `which()`/`grep(value=FALSE)` --> `integer()`
* ...

We could patch this sort of information as a "type hint" into the `utils::getParseData()` `data.frame()` (as a new column) and/or the `xml_parse_data()` XML tree (as XML attributes) to make it available to linters.

The downside is:

 1. Extra maintenance burden of these new structures
 2. (Part of 1 really, but worth emphasizing) Incrementing/scoping a list of functions to include
 3. Performance impact to building these augmented structures
 4. Always going to be incomplete as probably most nodes will just have missing data -- just the nature of a dynamically-typed language

What do the other maintainers think of the benefit/cost of this?

title: suggestion: # nolint like exclussion for path problems
description:
I'm getting lots of false positive when using the portable file paths linter.

- string of a regex pattern: e.g. `"\\.jpg$"`
- string with git refs. e.g. `"origin/main"`, `"refs/heads/branch"`
- constructing long URL with paste to stay belong the long line limit.

```
paste(
  "https://github.com/r-lib/lintr/blob/master/.github",
  "workflows/lint-changed-files.yaml", sep = "/"
)
```

The current solutions are IMHO subpar:
- turning the portable file paths linter off. Then we no longer check for portable file paths.
- replacing all the false positive with `file.path(..., fsep = "/")` or `paste(..., sep = "/")`. This make the code much less readable.
- adding `# nolint` to the false negative. This turns off all checking.

A more elegant solution could be something like adding `# nolintpath` which only excludes the path related linters.

title: False positive for "no visible binding for global variable" check
description:
It seems like the "no visible binding for global variable" check is producing false positives in a very specific scenario.

If I try to use `$` subsetting both inside and outside functions in a script this check will treat the name after the `$` inside the function body as a global variable.

Here's the simplest runnable example:
```R
fun <- function() {
  df2 <- data.frame(y = "another string")
  df2$y
}

my_list <- list()
my_list$b <- "a string"
fun()
```

Saving the above R code to a file named `test.R` and running the linter gives the following results:
```
> lintr::lint("test.R")
/home/tcabj/gresb-scoring/test.R:3:7: warning: no visible binding for global variable ‘y’
  df2$y
```

I experimented a bit and found that any of the following changes makes the error go away:
1. Moving the code inside the function body outside it
2. Removing the line `my_list$b <- "a string"`
These two characteristics of the code snippet seem to be what causes the error to occur.

My environment details:
- lintr version 2.0.1
- R version 4.0.4
- WSL2  Ubuntu 20.04.2 LTS

title: New match_symbol_usage argument to undesirable_function_linter
description:
We have a function `foo()` that we'd like to lint. However, `foo()` comes from the package `foo`, which is still OK, so we have the following unfortunate situation:

```
library(foo) # triggers a lint, but shouldn't
foo::foo()  # triggers a lint, as it should
```

The issue is that `undesirable_function_linter` by default also looks for `SYMBOL` usage of input functions, which is good for catching usage within `sapply`, `purrr::map`, etc.

So we can add a new argument to toggle whether `SYMBOL` is included, and run linting with

```
with_defaults(
  undesirable_function_linter(c("return")), # match_symbol_usage = TRUE by default
  undesirable_function_linter(c("foo"), match_symbol_usage = FALSE)
)
```

Happy to file the PR if that sounds like a good idea.

title: A new linter checking duplicate arguments
description:
It is almost always a mistake to call a function with duplicate arguments, i.e. arguments of the same name, like the following:

```r
foo(bar1 = 1, bar1 = 2, bar3 = 3)
```

Therefore, in most cases, it might make sense to check all function calls and ensure there are no duplicate arguments.

One use case of duplicate argument is to produce some table that actually needs duplicate headers for demonstration in documents, e.g.

```r
data <- data.frame(
  mean = 1:5,
  sd = 0.5,
  mean = 2:6,
  sd = 1,
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

title: Make sure `README.md` lists all available linters (missing: `backport_linter`, `pipe_call_linter`, note on misencoded files)
User-defined S3 methods & `object_name_linter`
description:
This has been raised in a few issues (which I think have all been closed). But it isn't an issue that has really been solved.

If a newly minted package defines a generic and an S3-method based on that generic:

```
#' drink_me
#' @description empty
#'
#' @export
drink_me <- function(x, ...) {
  UseMethod("drink_me")
}

#' drink_me for most things
#' @export
drink_me.default <- function(x, ...) {
  1
}

#' drink_me for lists
#' @export
drink_me.list <- function(x, ...) {
  NULL
}

#' drink_me for data.frames
#' @export
drink_me.data.frame <- function(x, ...) {
  NULL
}
```

then, IMO, the expected behaviour when running `lint_package(linters = object_name_linter("snake_case"))` is for no lints to be thrown. Only the name of the generic should be subject to the snake-case linter.

But the `.<className>` suffix throws a lint because of there being multiple dots in the `drink_me.data.frame`

To reproduce
- open rstudio
- make new package ~/temp/temppkg using rstudio package template
- delete the NAMESPACE
- add the above code to drink.R
- document()
- Use devtools::load_all("path/to/lintr") to load current lintr master
- `lint_package(linters = object_name_linter("snake_case"))`
- Note the lint on `drink_me.data.frame`
- ... then
- load the temp package using devtools::load_all()
- Run lint_package again
- note that the lints are present whether or not the package-under-development is loaded.

This is an issue that arose while experimenally running `lint_package(linters = object_name_linter(c("snake_case", "camelCase", "symbols")))` on {targets} (https://github.com/ropensci/targets)

title: Consistent handling of Encoding
description:
Currently, we use `readLines()` when linting, which assumes the system encoding when parsing files.

This results in uncovered lines w.r.t. fixing column numbers of UTF-8 Multibyte characters (at least on Windows, cf. #739) and in bugs when the file encoding doesn't match the system encoding (cf. #541)

lintr should

 * get a new setting `encoding` with a smart default (see below) overridable in the usual ways.
 * respect this setting in `get_source_expressions()`
 * Update the tests to force `UTF-8` encoding where necessary

The smart default for encoding should pick the first valid option of this list:

1. The `Encoding` field in a package `DESCRIPTION`
2. The `Encoding` field from the `.Rproj` file in a project directory
3. `UTF-8`

This default is system-independent and thus should be safe to use.

title: [Discussion] High-level API for excluding specific linters
description:
@AshesITR sorry for the delay -- have been moving across the country since early December, finally getting settles with a good enough setup to do a review.

Some higher-level thoughts:

 1. Another good follow-up would be the option to _force_ exclusions to use a list, i.e. generic `# nolint` is not allowed. Specifying the linter makes "lint creep" far less likely, and makes it easier to search out all instances of a specific lint to boot.
 2. The `: <linters>.` syntax looks a bit odd for `nolint: start: <linters>.` because the `:` is repeated. I still don't have a good alternative I'm happy with thought so not making it a blocker...
 3. Somewhat related, some people might like to namespace-tag the linter exclusions, e.g. I keep my custom lints in a package `myLinter` and it makes it clearer to readers to see `# nolint: lintr::seq_linter, myLinter::power_linter`. Probably another follow-up issue to file.
 4. Another power feature I think was mentioned at some point is non-overlapping range exclusions, e.g. `1:# nolint start: linterA` ... `5:# nolint start: linterB` `6: ...` `7: # nolint end: linterA` ... `12: # nolint end: linterB`. I think the logic is partway there to supporting this, but it's not necessary to get this merged.

_Originally posted by @MichaelChirico in https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/issues/660#issuecomment-769675032_

title: lintr fails when parser generates "error: unexpected input" from unicode character token
description:
Reproducible example:
```r
> lintr::lint(text="x <- 2 × 3")
# Error in nchar(content$text, "chars") : 
#   invalid multibyte string, element 7
```

The problem seems to be that, when the R parser finds an unexpected token that starts with or is a multibyte Unicode character, it halts the parse (fine) and returns _just the first byte of that character_ as the text for the offending token (bad). The first byte of a multibyte UTF-8 character alone is an invalid character and triggers the error.

I'm still investigating this bug. The source seems to be at least in `utils::getParseData()` or deeper, depending on what is the expected behavior. Anyway, whether or not there is an issue in base functions, I'll submit a pull request with a workaround tomorrow.

title: linter weighting?
description:
Sometimes we get multiple lints on a given line. If a display tool is limited to showing only one lint, right now, there's no systematic way to prioritize which is shown.

This might be important if there are multiple overlapping lints that point to slightly different fixes, e.g.

 - `expect_lt_linter` looks for `expect_true(x < 5)` to be `expect_lt(x, 5)`
 - `expect_eq_linter` looks for `expect_true(abs(x - y) < 1)` to be `expect_equal(x, y, tolerance=1)`

Any code failing `expect_eq_linter` also fails `expect_lt_linter`, but the former "has higher priority" since we'd rather fix that one than do `expect_lt(abs(x-y), 1)`*.

It should be possible to set up an API for adding weights to the linters (probably through the `.lintr` config so that this can be customized, default is equal weighting) -- I guess the main question is whether this would be in scope for `lintr` or delegated to an add-on?

\*One could extend `expect_eq_linter` to also look for usage like `expect_lt(abs(x-y), 1)`, which is basically OK, though slightly inconvenient to users who might fix code only for it to still be broken. Matryoshka linting 😃

title: Replacement functions are incorrectly marked as errors
Add text argument to lintr::lint
description:
In languageserver, we have to pass the file content to `lintr::lint()` (since the file is often being edited but not saved, and we do provide live diagnostics on user input) but also want it to behave as if the content is from a filename so that the following cases could work:

* `linter_file` is respected (https://github.com/REditorSupport/languageserver/issues/235)
* `object_usage_linter` detects its package (https://github.com/REditorSupport/languageserver/issues/238)
* Exclusions in `.lintr` not working (https://github.com/REditorSupport/languageserver/issues/282)

One bad solution is to write a temp file inside the user workspace (e.g. original file `test.R` and we write a temp `test.Rtmp`) but Language Server Protocol seems to discourage any change in user workspace directly rather than via LSP communication.

Therefore, I'm wondering if we could add a `text` argument so that we could use 

```r
lintr::lint(filename, linters = NULL, cache = FALSE, ..., parse_settings = TRUE, text = NULL)
```

by supplying both `filename` and `text`:

```r
lintr::lint(filename, text = text)
```

so that both are respected and `lint` wouldn't have to read the file again if `text` is supplied.

title: Improve symbol detection
description:
Currently, symbol-based linters use the parse data to determine of some token is a symbol or not.

When combined with the dollar operator, this can cause some confusing false positives, e.g. #582, #657.

It would be nice if we had a helper function that can find out whether a specific symbol is part of a dollar-operator (-chain) call and

* skip such symbols in `T_and_F_symbol_linter`.
* optionally skip such symbols in `object_name_linter`.

Note that for `object_name_linter` we could introduce some false negatives if variables are written to environments via a dollar-assignment instead of into lists or data.frames (where one might not consider them variable names)

These false negatives will be near impossible to discern from true negatives without running the code, since that would require type information on the dollar-accessed object.

Another, possibly even more useful, option for `object_name_linter` would be to allow separate linters.
A use-case would be to prescribe a different naming convention for data.frame column names than for variable names.
I use this in practice to easily distinguish which symbols in a dplyr call come from the data and which come from the surrounding environment.

What do you think about this? It could be implemented by adding a new argument to `object_name_linter`s builder function, e.g.

```r
object_name_linter(style = c("symbols", "snake_case"), dollar_style = style)
```

I'm also interested in suggestions for the possible argument name (`colname_style` might be misleading for cases where the user is not dealing with column names, I'm not very satisfied with `dollar_style` either, though).

title: Hit 99% code coverage
description:
As of this writing we're at 97.09%:

https://codecov.io/gh/jimhester/lintr/tree/master/R

99% would be 2450 of 2475 expressions on current HEAD, an increase of 47 lines covered.

Alternatively we can mark about the same number of lines as `# nocov` to get there.

I think that's a good ambitious target to hit for release, but don't let this issue be too much of a blocker.

---

quoting from #739 

Going through the files with coverage < 100%:

 - [ ] namespace.R is covered by #740, so we can leave it alone
 - [ ] namespace_linter.R has an uncovered lint that should trigger only if a package is installed, but loading its namespace fails. IDK how we would test that at all. I'd be fine with # nocov'ing ll 93--104
 - [ ] cache.R has gaps where we check for specified paths to not mess up loading settings.
 - [ ] We could add a test that self-lints lintr with caching enabled, I think. WDYT?
 - [ ] make_linter_from_regex.R could need a test with a custom linter created on-the-fly. The uncovered parts are the builder code.
 - [ ] get_source_expressions.R has a few blind spots. The first one is for parser errors without location information. We manually try to find location information for the attempt to use zero-length variable name case. Other cases aren't tested and I don't even know about them. I'd be fine with # nocov'ing ll 101 -- 109 since those are a fallback Lint if we missed a parse error without location information.
 - [ ] The next is in fix_column_numbers() and should be tested.
 - [ ] Finally fix_eq_assigns() has a blind spot I think could be reached if there are multiple eq-assignments to be fixed.
 - [ ] tree-utils.R has no tests for simplify = FALSE in children() and parents().
 - [ ] path_linters.R has in a few holes in split_path()
 - [ ] object_usage_linter.R seems to have an unreachable early return (IMO we should check full_xml_parsed_content for consistency across all file-level XPath-based linters. IINM coverage will increase if it's added to the test for #740.
 - [ ] comments.R the travis_build_info() seems bugged because "" %||% NULL will always be "", so travis_build_info() will never return NULL, even if !in_travis().
 - [ ] backport_linter.R has a blind spot when a backport lint spans multiple lines.
 - [ ] seq_linter.R: I'm unsure how to reach the uncovered line 29. IINM, the XPath expression guarantees existence of the children. Maybe 1:1 triggers it?
 - [ ] settings.R has a miss because ~/.lintr doesn't exist. I think we can safely # nocov l 97.
 - [ ] comment_linters.R has a miss in parsable(). I don't think this is reachable, seems okay to remove it.
 - [ ] lint.R has a miss for lint(cache = TRUE) and checkstyle_output() if attr(lints, "path") exists. I didn't even know about the attribute. Is this still relevant or should we remove it?
 - [ ] expect_lint.R has no failure test case for expect_lint_free().
 - [ ] utils.R has no test for xml_nodes_to_lint() where the lint spans multiple lines.
 - [ ] methods.R has no test for rstudio_source_markers() if there are no lints.

https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/blob/fa05ceb2bf967ddad9230e25879b95084c80b0dc/R/lint.R#L287

title: How about the infix space linter has a feature to exclude any infix tokens?
description:

title: Feature: allow turning off specific linters per-line
description:
It might be useful to disable only a specific linter on a per-line basis, e.g.

```r
`%||%` = function(x, y) {
  if (is.null(x)) y else x
}
```

produces two default lints: `object_name_linter` and `assignment_linter`.
One may actively decide that `%||%` is an acceptable name here and not want to generally disable `object_name_linter`.

Currently, this can only be achieved by # nolint'ing the entire line
```r
`%||%` = function(x, y) { # nolint
  if (is.null(x)) y else x
}
```
but unfortunately this also kills the `assignment_linter`

It would be very useful to have a way to only exclude some linters on a line (or in a block).
A syntax might be a space-separated list of linters to be disabled, e.g.

```r
`%||%` = function(x, y) { # nolint object_name_linter
  if (is.null(x)) y else x
}
```

I realize this would require work in the way exclusions are specified. Especially the line-based specification in `.lintr` files or the `exclusions` argument requires thought.

One solution would be one more level of (optional) nesting

```r
exclude: list(
    "my_file.R" = list(
      1,
      "2" = "object_name_linter",
      "4" = c("line_length_linter", "commented_code_linter")
    )
  )
```

title: "Curly-braces... own line" exception to the rule: function stubs
description:
The curly brace messages make sense in virtually every case. Today I ran into a complaint from the linter about function stubs. For instance:

```
x <- function() { }
```

This is clearly aesthetically preferable to
```
x <- function() {
}
```

Why would you use a function stub? 

1. Mocking out an API. 
2. Writing a unit test for any function that takes a function as an argument -- in my particular case I have an error handler which inspects the formals of a function but doesn't care about the function itself, so function stubs are ideal. I use it because I have a function that allows the user to override some default calculations by providing an external function with identical formals.

So given this, I choose to use single line inline braces as shown in the first example. The other place the one-line inline braces might come up in R is single statement conditionals -- especially flow control like break/next in the `if(cond) { next }` format. However, you can solve that by ditching braces entirely -- the following is valid:

```
if(cond) next
```

Unfortunately, there is no equivalent for function stubs. The following is not legal:
```
x <- function()
```

I know you guys don't generally like error reports that boil down to "I like your style guide, except I don't like this part, so make an exception for me". So apologies in advance if that's what this comes off as. But I think this is an interesting corner case that might be worth adjusting the grammar of the rule. Totally reasonable if you disagree.

Any thoughts?

title: Likely false warnings from switch fall-through lines
description:
Hi,

If you use the fall-through syntax for the switch command, such as in the example below, you trigger warnings in lintr which I don't think are resolvable:

```
a <- "dog"

# Check how many legs
switch(a,
  "bird" = {
    # Two legs
  },
  "cat" = ,
  "dog" = ,
  "horse" = {
    # Four legs
  }
)
```

In the line `"cat" = ,` if you place a space between the = and the , you will get the warning:

`Commas should never have a space before.
`
If you don't, you'll get the warning:

`Put spaces around all infix operators.`

I suspect that this is a special case that `= ,` as a sequence is excepted (unless I'm missing something).

title: lint workflows
description:
I've been looking to update the `readme` CI section. I realised the install package step was missing from the `r-lib/actions` lint workflow (confirmed by this [issue and solution](https://github.com/r-lib/actions/pull/216) that were merged after I configured the GHA workflows).

This might be a bit meta, but if my understanding is correct, I might have misconfigured the GHA workflows. I think a package needs to be installed for `lintr::lint_package()` to do its thing. For the standard `.lint` GHA workflow - for any other package but {lintr} - the steps are simple: 
* install the CRAN version of {lintr}
* install the package
* lint the package

For {lintr} this is a bit trickier since we can only have one version of a package installed at any one time. Possible issues:
* The first workflow - `lint.yaml` - installs {lintr} from CRAN, which means it's linting that version of the package. 
* The second workflow - `lint-changed-files.yaml` - installs the dev version (`main`) and, as a consequence, that's the version that gets linted.  

I think both workflows should install the version in the branch subject of the pull request, namely with a step that installs the branch version of the package, something like

```
    - name: Install package
         run: R CMD INSTALL .
```

A side-effect would be that the `.lint` workflows configured for {lintr} should not be an inspiration for other package developers.

description:

For example, if one uses `trimws(whitespace=)`, then it is only compatible with R >= 3.6.0. However, developers using R >= 3.6.0 might not be aware of this until some user or CI using R < 3.6.0 complains.

I don't know a simple way to find how compatible the functions I use in package development are unless I carefully go through the [R News](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-devel/NEWS.html), [R News 3.x](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-devel/NEWS.3.html), etc.

I'm wondering if there's a way to make this process work in a more automatic manner, e.g. create a linter that checks the usage of functions are compatible with declared version requirement? Or suggest the use of `backport` instead?

title: undesirable_function_linter() should look for function calls only
description:
I think the `undesirable_function_linter()` should only look for function calls. The context is that I want to use lintr to keep watch for base file system functions creeping into usethis (https://github.com/r-lib/usethis/issues/531, https://github.com/r-lib/fs/issues/85). I can *almost* do what I want with the `undesirable_function_linter()`.

But it reports tons of false positives, i.e. warns when it should not.

`dir()` is one of the functions I'm linting for. But throughout the package, below both `R/` and `tests/`, the name `dir` is frequently used for the path to a directory. So the linter reports dozens of false warnings.

Here's a small reprex with current lintr vs. after the change in my PR (#557):

``` r
library(lintr)

lint_this <- function(this, ...) {
  file <- tempfile()
  on.exit(unlink(file))
  writeLines(this, con = file, sep = "\n")
  lint(file, ...)
}

linter <- undesirable_function_linter(fun = c("dir" = NA))

# warning is correct: I'm calling dir()
lint_this('dir(".")', linter)
#> /private/var/folders/pv/l2mbh7j90y5_vslh_1wyqxj00000gn/T/RtmpQbfI18/file121123553fe9e:1:1: warning: Function "dir" is undesirable.
#> dir(".")
#> ^~~

# warning is WRONG: I'm defining an object named 'dir'
lint_this("dir <- 1:3", linter)
#> /private/var/folders/pv/l2mbh7j90y5_vslh_1wyqxj00000gn/T/RtmpQbfI18/file121121d71526c:1:1: warning: Function "dir" is undesirable.
#> dir <- 1:3
#> ^~~

devtools::load_all("~/rrr/lintr")
#> ℹ Loading lintr

linter <- undesirable_function_linter(fun = c("dir" = NA))

# warning is correct: I'm calling dir()
lint_this('dir(".")', linter)
#> /private/var/folders/pv/l2mbh7j90y5_vslh_1wyqxj00000gn/T/RtmpQbfI18/file121127ada3f8d:1:1: warning: Function "dir" is undesirable.
#> dir(".")
#> ^~~

# lack of warning is correct: I'm defining an object named 'dir'
lint_this("dir <- 1:3", linter)
```

<sup>Created on 2020-11-01 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0.9001)</sup>

title: Need a better way to skip when XML parse fails
description:
Split off from #546.

Right now we have to use this workaround:

```
(!length(source_file$full_parsed_content) || is.null(source_file$xml_parsed_content)) return(list())
```

This is pretty arcane & unreadable IMO -- hard to know without being pretty experienced with `lintr` internals what's going on here. And with lints, it's tough to just wrap that into a helper function because now that's something we need to export for downstreams to use as well I think.

Both checks are needed because

 1. We want to skip on the last expression (where `full_parsed_content` is present) and
 2. We can't use `!is.null(source_file$parsed_content)` because there are cases where `parsed_content` is present (e.g. in some parsing error situations, as fixed in #560) but `xml_parsed_content` is not. lastly
 3. We can't skip based on `xml_parsed_content` because that element has the same name for the full file & individual expressions.

I think the easiest solution is to rename `xml_parsed_content` to `full_xml_parsed_content` to be consistent with `parsed_content` :arrow_right: `full_parsed_content`. There is some (?) breakage potential here in the event that some downstream logic depends on `xml_parsed_content` being the name for the full file, but I think it's worth the change for consistency & readability.

title: Windows tests regression
description:

title: Allow exclusion of directories
description:

Currently, one can only exclude single files, so there is no practical way to lint projects using `renv`.

A remedy would be support for excluding entire directories from linting.

title: Exclusions read from .lintr are depedent of the current working directory
description:
Hi, I recently started using lintr and it's pretty great. Thank you to everyone involved!

I bumped into an issue related with the `exclusions` extracted from `.lintr` files. It seems that the lint report depends on the current working directory of the R console.

Running the following script while the working directory was in the root of the project (`lintr/`)
```R
> lint_package(".")
```
does not show `inst/example/bad.R` in the report (since it's path is in `.lintr`). Then, if I run
```R
> setwd("..")
> lint_package("lintr")
```
the file `inst/example/bad.R` shows in the report.

There is a similar issue with `lint()`. I added a file `lintr/inst/example/.lintr` with the content
```
exclusions: list("bad.R")
```
Then, I ran the commands
```R
> setwd("lintr/inst/example")
> lint("bad.R")
```
and `bad.R` did not show up in the report (as expected). However, that was not the case when I ran
```R
> setwd("..")
> lint("example/bad.R")
```

Furthermore, when run directly from the console, it seems that `lint_dir()` always ignores the exclusions in `.lintr`.

Can you clarify if any of these contrasting behaviors are expected, or what the expected behaviors should be?

Thank you
João

title: Missing function argument linter
description:
Although R allows missing argument in the following forms:

```r
fun(x =)
fun(x=1,,2)
fun(1,)
```

such examples are almost always not intended in practice. For example, when editing the following list:

```r
x <- list(
  a = 1,
  b = 2,
  c = 3
)
```

Removing `c` only will result in the following:

```r
x <- list(
  a = 1,
  b = 2,
)
```

This is syntactically correct but will produce error at runtime.

A missing function argument linter will be useful to detect all these cases where `(,`, `,,`, `,)` or `=)` appear.

For matrix/array or data frame subsetting like `mat[1,]`, `arr[,1,2]`, `df[, "col"]`, since using `[` is not parsed as `SYMBOL_FUNCTION_CALL`, then the linter would by default not complain such usage.

title: Invalid "\" crashes lintr
description:
If the source code contains any invalid use of `\`, then `lintr::lint()` will stop working:

```r
col <- c("a", \)
```

The case could be simplified to the following:

```
> parse(text = "\\")                                                                                                        
Error in parse(text = "\\") : <text>:1:1: unexpected input
1: \
    ^
Backtrace:
1: parse(text = "\\")

> lintr::lint("\\\n")                                                                                                       
Error in read_xml.raw(charToRaw(enc2utf8(x)), "UTF-8", ..., as_html = as_html,  : 
  StartTag: invalid element name [68]
Backtrace:
1: read_xml.raw(charToRaw(enc2utf8(x)), "UTF-8", ..., as_html = as_html, 
2: read_xml.character(xmlparsedata::xml_parse_data(pc))
3: xml2::read_xml(xmlparsedata::xml_parse_data(pc))
4: FUN(X[[i]], ...)
5: lapply(X = top_level_expressions(parsed_content), FUN = get_single_source_expression, 
6: get_source_expressions(filename)
7: lintr::lint("\\\n")
```

Looks like it is caused by xmlparsedata writing invalid XML and lintr does not handle such case.

Before error occurs, `pc` got the following value:

```
  line1 col1 line2 col2 id parent token terminal text
1     1    1     1    1  1      0    \\    FALSE   \\
```

`xmlparsedata::xml_parse_data(pc)` produces the following XML with invalid tokens:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" standalone="yes" ?>
<exprlist>
  <\ line1="1" col1="1" line2="1" col2="1" start="3" end="3">\
  </\>
</exprlist>
```

title: Not-installed package linter

title: Namespace linter
description:
#547 implements a `missing_package_linter()` which checks if all packages loaded by `library()`, `require()`, `loadNamespace()`, and `requireNamespace()` are installed.

Apart from that, we could also check the usage of `ns::obj` and `ns:::obj` as they also used to access objects in a namespace (provided by package).

We could implement a separate linter (as suggested at https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/pull/547#issuecomment-719822505) to check if 

1. The package `ns` in `ns::obj` and `ns:::obj` are installed.
2. The `obj` in `ns::obj` is exported from namespace `ns`.
3. The `obj` in `ns:::obj` exists in namespace `ns`.

While checking 1 does not load any new package, checking 2 and 3 might load the package being checked. I'm not sure if we allow loading extra packages from user code?

title: print methods are tab-agnostic
description:
```
writeLines('\t\t1:length(x)', tmp <- tempfile())
lintr::lint(tmp, seq_linter)
# /tmp/RtmpmKh1Cr/file344e46549f77bf:1:3: warning: Avoid 1:length(...) expressions, use seq_len. Disable this with a comment: `# nolint` (one line) or `# lintr: disable` (multiple lines). See go/tidy-style#linting for more.
#                 1:length(x)
#   ^
```

Would subbing `'\t'` for `' '` in `lintr:::print.lint` be enough?

```
cat(sep = "", crayon::bold(x$filename, ":", as.character(x$line_number), 
        ":", as.character(x$column_number), ": ", sep = ""), 
        color(x$type, ": ", sep = ""), crayon::bold(combined_message), 
        "\n", x$line, "\n", highlight_string(combined_message, 
            x$column_number, x$ranges), "\n")

title: infix operators don't conform to tidyverse standards
description:
I have found a difference between `lintr` and [`styler`](https://github.com/r-lib/styler). `styler` will correct the following

```r
(10 ^ (x - 1)) + 1
```

to

```r
(10^(x - 1)) + 1
```

This gives the following `lintr` errors:

```
Put spaces around all infix operators.
Place a space before left parenthesis, except in a function call.
```

Looking at the current tidyverse style guide, [`styler` is correct here](http://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#spacing). To get around this you can use

```r
styler::style_pkg(".", math_token_spacing = list(one = c("'^'", "'+'", "'-'", "'*'", "'/'")))
```

A similar issue exists with

```r
break ()
```

which gets corrected to 

```r
break()
```

by `styler`. I am not sure which is correct with regards to the tidyverse here.

title: Rmd: Markdown fenced code blocks with language identifier cause `Error: Malformed file!`
description:
## Problem

Consider the following reprex:

````r
example_file <- tempfile()

readr::write_file(path = example_file,
                  x = '# Rmd example file

## R code chunk

The following is linted fine:

```{r}
print ("hi" )
```

## Plain code block

The following fenced code block _without_ a language identifier is not linted (also fine!):

```
print ("hi" )
```

## Code block with language identifier

The language identifier of the following code block triggers a \'malformed file\' error (bad!):

```r
print ("hi" )
```
')

lintr::lint(filename = example_file)
#> Error: Malformed file!
````
<sup>Created on 2020-07-03 by the [reprex](https://reprex.tidyverse.org/) package (v0.3.0)</sup>

Markdown code blocks with a language identifier are valid R Markdown syntax and should simply be excluded from linting.

## Possibly related

If I understand it correctly, R Markdown files should be supported by lintr as of https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/commit/50ab86db4ebc7272d95990f8d15b3fabe0278936 fixing https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/issues/32.

In https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/issues/252, a similar issue was raised which has been solved by https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/commit/fdd19507481fddcc8ec200463c5b8c73bc58e949, _assumedly_ without properly handling language identifiers. I'm not familiar with lintr's internals and didn't dive into the code, but I guess the R code extraction logic in https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/blob/master/R/extract.R is erroneous. Maybe @russHyde or @jimhester could have a look at this?

Maybe also related: https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/issues/322

title: Local object usage linter specifies line of the *function* - not the file
description:
The linter for object (variable) usage returns a lint specifying the offending line of the **function**, not the line of the **file**. This causes confusion in passing an `exclusions` argument to downstream functions (e.g. `expect_lint_free()` or even `lint_file()`). For example from the README instructions:

```
exclusions: list("inst/doc/creating_linters.R" = 1, "inst/example/bad.R", "tests/testthat/exclusions-test")
```

The desired exclusion is **line 1** of file `creating_linters.R`, however if the lint in question is the object usage linter, it will exclude `line1` of the **function**. This could be particularly confusing if there are numerous functions in the same file and is inconsistent with other linters. This may be coming from `codetools::checkUsage()` and may be related to #445. Minimal example:

```
myfile.R

#' Function Blah
#'
#' This function has a 2 failing lints: 1) path unused, 2) infix spaces.
#'
#' @examples
#' myfun()
#' @export
myfun <- function() {
  path <- search()        # `path` unused; line2 of function; line9 of file
  n <- purrr::map_dbl(search(), function(.x) length(ls(.x)))
  mean(n, na.rm=TRUE)     # spaces around infix
}
```

Specified like this:
```
lintr::lint_file("myfile.R", exclusions = list("myfile.R" = 2))
```
Would be more consistent if specified by line of the **file**:
```
lintr::lint_file("myfile.R", exclusions = list("myfile.R" = 9))
```

I ran  the script in the readme (https://github.com/jimhester/lintr#project-configuration) to make a `.lintr` config for `installr` (https://github.com/talgalili/installr).
This gave the following .lintr:
```
linters: with_defaults(
    trailing_whitespace_linter = NULL, # 983
    line_length_linter = NULL, # 807
    object_name_linter = NULL, # 309
    commas_linter = NULL, # 253

    object_usage_linter = NULL, # 18
    object_length_linter = NULL, # 16
    closed_curly_linter = NULL, # 8
    function_left_parentheses = NULL, # 7
    cyclocomp_linter = NULL, # 2
    seq_linter = NULL, # 1
    dummy_linter = NULL
  )
exclusions: list(
    ...
)
```

Then, without modifying the .lintr file, I ran `lint_package()` on the same package.

This flagged up 7 lint failures  of the form "Remove spaces before the left parenthesis in a function call."

This seemed a bit weird, since all default linters have been NULLed out in the .lintr file. It appears to relate to a mismatch between the function-name `function_left_parentheses_linter` and the stated-name of the linter within that function `function_left_parentheses`.

```
          Lint(
            filename = source_file$filename,
            line_number = parsed$line1,
            column_number = parsed$col1,
            type = "style",
            message = "Remove spaces before the left parenthesis in a function call.",
            line = line,
            linter = "function_left_parentheses" # --- here
            )
```

`default_linters` uses the function-name to distinguish linters;
The results from as.data.frame(lint_package()) use the `$linter` entry returned by a call to `Lint(...)`.

Should the `Lint( ... linter = "", ...)` entry be equal to the name of the linter function for each linter?

I ran this to find any `linter = "..."` strings where the string did not end with `_linter`
```
# in lintr directory
grep "linter = " R/*.R | grep -v "_linter\""
```

... and checked the idenitified files, the only linters where the function-name and the linter-name in Lint() are mismatched are in `function_left_parentheses_linter` and in `get_source_expressions` (where an error string is returned).

title: Behavior of lintr before/after calling library
description:
Hi,

I use neovim with ale + Nvim-R and it got me wondering about how lintr works.

Let's say that I have the following file called `test.R`:

```
library(purrr)

n <- 10
map(1:n, function(x) rnorm(x))
myfun <- function(n) {
  map(1:n, function(x) rnorm(x))
}
```

If I start a new R session and call `lintr::lint("test.R")`, I get a marker related to the second map ("no visible global function definition"), whereas if I call `library(purrr)` first, I do not get a marker.

1. Why do I never get a marker for the first `map`?
2. In the second case (i.e., if I call `lintr::lint` after `library`), how does `lintr` "knows" that `map` is "available"?

While I ask the first question by curiosity, I ask the second question because, as mentioned, I use ale and Nvim-R. In this context, although I often load packages in the R session opened with Nvim-R, the markers for missing global function definitions never disappear after loading the appropriate packages. 

This is obviously expected since, to the best of my knowledge, there is no connection between ale and Nvim-R. But I am trying to understand where `lintr` looks for the information about the loaded namespaces with the final goal to get ale to use the current Nvim-R session to make the markers related to global function definitions from packages that are loaded disappear.

I am not sure whether I explained clearly the issue, my apologies if not.

title: Robustness linters
description:
Suggestions from @hadley
- [ ] Require drop = FALSE whenever [ is used with two or more args
- [ ] Require na.rm argument for any function that has it (to force you to
  think about missing values during development)
- [x] Don't use of require()/library() inside a function
- [x] Don't change global state: setwd(), options(), par() etc.  Could
  have next package robustr that contained alternatives (i.e. the with_*
  functions from devtools)
- [ ] Always turn partial matching warning options on (not really code
  linting, but related)
- [ ] Avoid functions that use NSE (with(), subset(), transform() etc)
- [ ] Avoid functions that return different types of output (e.g. sapply())
- [x] `TRUE` and `FALSE` instead of `T` and `F`.
- [ ] `return()` calls at the end of functions (result of last statement is always returned, so the explicit `return()` is redundant (and also slower as it requires an additional function call).
- [x] use of `1:length(x)` in for loops (dangerous if length(x) can be 0) as `1:0` returns `c(1, 0)`, should use `seq_len(length(x))` instead.
- [ ] Iterative appending to vectors within loops rather than pre-allocation the vectors and filling. (the former is quadratic in time complexity, as R has to keep re-sizing the vector on every assignment.

``` r
# bad
for (i in seq_len(10)) {
  x <- c(x, i)
}

# good
x <- integer(10)
for (i in seq_len(10)) {
  x[i] <- i
}
```

title: Hadley Style linters
description:
All from http://r-pkgs.had.co.nz/style.html  Most should be pretty straight forward, some are a little tricky.
- [x] line length (80 120? + characters)
- [x] variable names
  - [x] no camelCase
  - [x] no multiple dots
  - [x] very long variable names?
- [x] Spacing
  - [x] infix operators have spaces around them
  - [x] commas space after, none before
  - [x] space before left parentheses
  - [x] no spaces inside parentheses or square brackets
- [x] Curly braces
  - [x] Open never on own line
  - [x] Open always followed by a new line
  - [x] Closing always on new line, unless an else
  - [ ] Code inside curly braces should be indented appropriately
- [x] no tab characters
- [ ] Functions
  - [ ] verbs where possible
  - [ ] `return()` only for early returns (never at the end of a function)
- [ ] Comments
  - should be a `#` followed by a space, or roxygen `#'`
- [x] only double quotes
- [x] `<-` not `=` for assignment

title: Don't run lintr during covr run
description:
Running `lintr` can take quite some time for large packages, so I think it is a good idea to exclude it from being run during a code coverage check (where it is useless?), e.g. when using `covr`. When lintr is invoked in testthat using `expect_lint_free`, the test is skipped if `NOT_CRAN` is not `"true"`. Therefore, when using `package_coverage()` to get coverage data locally, lintr is excluded.

Travis seems to set `NOT_CRAN` to `"true"`, however, so I assume lintr is run twice there and is leading to longer Travis build times.

I suggest also checking for the `"R_COVR"` environment variable in `expect_lint_free`, and skipping linting it is set to `"true"`.

title: Regular expression captures break expect_lint()
description:
```
> expect_lint("cat('hello')", "double-quotes", lintr::single_quotes_linter)
As expected

> expect_lint("cat('hello')", "double-quotes (with parentheses)", lintr::single_quotes_linter)
Error: Don't know how to convert 'data.frame' to expectation.
```

The first `expect_lint()` call behaves as expected. The second does not; it errors instead of reporting that the "message" does not match.

The problem in the second case is the presence of parentheses in the regular expression, which are interpreted as captures. Captures have no reasons to be used in this context and they cause trouble at [expect_lint.R line 60](https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/blob/master/R/expect_lint.R#L60) because `re_matches` then returns a data.frame instead of a logical. Potential solutions would be to somehow escape captures in "value" just before the call to `re_matches`, or to force `re_matches` to return a single logical.

Best, 

Florent

title: Enhancement: make lint() accept string input
description:
Jim suggested improving the `lint()` function by making it accept a character **string** through the 'filename' option: https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/pull/233#issuecomment-297761852 . `lint()` would work in string mode if 'filename' contains a trailing newline character.

```R
lintr::lint("a = b\n")
```

It seems to be partially implemented in `lint()`; the code seems to be there, but as far as I can tell is not tested nor documented.

The 'filename' argument does not seem ideal for this purpose, but if we found a better alternative, we would need to deprecate 'filename', which is also not ideal. Besides, 'filename' is the first argument and can therefore be omitted in the majority of cases.

In my eyes, the main issue with this enhancement proposal is that it makes it impossible to pass strings without newlines, and therefore to test the trailing newline linter. Perhaps the requirements should be relaxed and a newline character should be detected anywhere in the string?
```R
lintr::lint("NULL\na = b")
```

Alternatively, string input may be passed in a list object containing lines of text.

```R
lintr::lint(list("a = b"))
```

title: Question about performance regression (master vs v1.0.1)
description:
I lately tried to upgrade from jimhester/lintr@a769c0b to https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/commit/5431140ffea65071f1327625d4a8de9688fa7e72. The master branch, https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/commit/5431140ffea65071f1327625d4a8de9688fa7e72 (vs  jimhester/lintr@a769c0b) looks it has fixed many bugs and now finds many instances that I have observed and thought should be caught time to time in R code base in a project.

The problem is, it now takes about 7ish mins, (it was 2ish mins before) in my local. It is not the problem with v1.0.1 (it also takes 2ish mins).

To verify this, I filtered out new litners in the master branch, https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/commit/5431140ffea65071f1327625d4a8de9688fa7e72 (vs  v1.0.1):


Assuming from the doc, v1.0.1 looks missing the linters below (vs master, https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/commit/5431140ffea65071f1327625d4a8de9688fa7e72):

```
nonportable_path_linter: check that file.path() is used to construct safe and portable paths.
pipe_continuation_linter: Check that each step in a pipeline is on a new line, or the entire pipe fits on one line.
extraction_operator_linter: check that the [[ operator is used when extracting a single element from an object, not [ (subsetting) nor $ (interactive use).
implicit_integer_linter: check that integers are explicitly typed using the form 1L instead of 1.
object_name_linter: check that object names conform to a single naming style, e.g. snake_case or lowerCamelCase.
semicolon_terminator_linter: check that no semicolons terminate statements.
todo_comment_linter: check that the source contains no TODO comments (case-insensitive).
T_and_F_symbol_linter: avoid the symbols T and F (for TRUE and FALSE).
undesirable_function_linter: report the use of undesirable functions, e.g. options or sapply and suggest an alternative.
undesirable_operator_linter: report the use of undesirable operators, e.g. ::: or <<- and suggest an alternative.
unneeded_concatenation_linter: check that the c function is not used without arguments nor with a single constant
```

I manually disabled the linters above but the elapsed time looks almost the same, 7ish mins. So, it looks existing linters have some problem with performance regression.

I wonder how much it helps but I tried to disable everything except for each linter [here](https://gist.github.com/HyukjinKwon/1f852bcdcc2a13f396dfd2d6a88bea16) with the code base here, https://github.com/apache/spark/tree/master/R

To cut it short, are there any advices to avoid the slowdown between master branch and v1.0.1, or dose anyone know roughly why?

I would like to use the master one as it detects many meaningful instances but the slowdown is a concern.

title: Sync Up Documentation with Releases
description:
Hey folks - I observed a failure in linting that recently came up, and it stemmed from the fact that the naming styles went from `lowerCamelCase`/`UpperCamelCase` to `camelCase`/`CamelCase.`  The README lists the options, but refers to a style regex that then no longer exists:
```
object_name_linter: check that object names conform to a single naming style, e.g. snake_case or lowerCamelCase.
```
I think it'd be reasonable to include the available regex styles in that bullet point. At minimum it should have the name for `lowerCamelCase` updated to match the most recent version of the code.

```
style_regexes <- list(
  "CamelCase" = rex(start, maybe("."), upper, zero_or_more(alnum), end),
  "camelCase" = rex(start, maybe("."), lower, zero_or_more(alnum), end),
  "snake_case"     = rex(start, maybe("."), some_of(lower, digit), any_of("_", lower, digit), end),
  "dotted.case"    = rex(start, maybe("."), one_or_more(loweralnum), zero_or_more(dot, one_or_more(loweralnum)), end),
  "lowercase"   = rex(start, maybe("."), one_or_more(loweralnum), end),
  "UPPERCASE"   = rex(start, maybe("."), one_or_more(upperalnum), end)
)
```

title: Function `%||%` fails on R-devel due to `_R_CHECK_LENGTH_1_LOGIC2_`
description:
R-devel introduces as new features:
"Experimentally, setting environment variable `_R_CHECK_LENGTH_1_LOGIC2_` will lead to warnings (or errors if the variable is set to a ‘true’ value) when && or || encounter and use arguments of length more than one. " (https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-devel/NEWS.html)

The `lintr` function `%||%` will fail this upcoming check, e.g., 
```
x <- c("", "", "object_name_linter", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "")
y <- c("", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "")
lintr:::`%||%`(x, y)
```
with message 
```
Error in is.null(x) || is.na(x) : 
  'length(x) = 11 > 1' in coercion to 'logical(1)'
```

Expected result (as obtained with R v3.5.2):
```
> lintr:::`%||%`(x, y)
 [1] ""                   ""                  
 [3] "object_name_linter" ""                  
 [5] ""                   ""                  
 [7] ""                   ""                  
 [9] ""                   ""                  
[11] ""                  
```

Suggested fix: replace 
`if (is.null(x) || is.na(x) || length(x) <= 0) {...` 
with
`if (is.null(x) || anyNA(x) || length(x) <= 0) {...` 
(`anyNA` was introduced in R v3.1.0 (https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/NEWS.html) which is earlier than the `lintr` required R version 3.1.1).

title: How to add a long custom linter to .lintr
Passing lints to the lint function
description:
In the `lint()` help page, the arguement

```
linters | a list of linter functions to apply see linters for a full list of default and available linters.
```

This is correct. However, it needs to be a **named** list. So

```
lint("X.R", list(lint1 = T_and_F_symbol_linter))
```
is OK, but 
```
lint("X.R", list(T_and_F_symbol_linter))
```
this doesn't (and doesn't raise an error message).

title: Ambiguous files in cache cause lint crash
description:
Hi Jim,

I obtained a "Marker line is unspecified or invalidNA" error when using lintr with caching. I managed to find out what is causing this problem. It is reproducible using these steps:
1. Create two packages, "A" and "B", that have the identically-named files "tests/testthat.R". Let us assume that "A/tests/testthat.R" and "B/tests/testthat.R" are identical, except that "A/tests/testthat.R" has some trailing newlines.
2. In package A, run `expect_lint_free(cache=TRUE)`. This runs fine, yields a few lints because of the trailing newlines, and generates a "~/.R/lintr_cache/testthat.R" file.
3. In package B, run `expect_lint_free(cache=TRUE)`. This operation crashes with "Marker line is unspecified or invalidNA". I imagine this is because lintr sees the "~/.R/lintr_cache/testthat.R" file and wrongly assumes that it belongs to package B. Since there are some lints at line numbers after last line of file "B/tests/testthat.R", mayhem ensues...

My conclusion is that the cache should differentiate files belonging to different packages. This is important because many packages use the same names, e.g. "testthat.R"  or "zzz.R".

But the problem is probably not limited to identically-named files between packages. When I create a file "A/R/more/testthat.R", issue a `clear_cache()` and re-run `expect_lint_free(cache=TRUE)`, there is a single "~/.R/lintr_cache/testthat.R" file, meaning that the two "testthat.R" files in package A were likely cached in the same location, one of them overwriting the other.

A straightforward solution would be to create a subfolder for each package, and further subfolders mimicking the folder structure of the respective packages, i.e. 

Source file | Cache file
------------ | -------------
A/tests/testthat.R | ~/.R/lintr_cache/A/tests/testthat.R
A/R/more/testthat.R | ~/.R/lintr_cache/A/R/more/testthat.R
B/tests/testthat.R | ~/.R/lintr_cache/B/tests/testthat.R


Cheers,
Florent

title: Lint fails with Rmd chunks using {lang} engine format
description:
This issue is related to #32, where lintr should ignore non-R chunks as it lints. `lintr` currently only ignores chunks that have the following chunk header: `{r engine = "LANG"}`, vs. the newer and now more common `{LANG}` Refer [here](https://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/authoring_knitr_engines.html), and the discussion on knitr issue #963 [here](https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/963).

Currently, if you use the `{LANG}` language engine syntax, `lintr` will do 2 things:

1. attempt to lint the chunk and throw an error for the user
2. not lint any R code after that chunk.

Below is a minimal reprex, using the .Rmd test case in `lintr` as a base and adding a chunk with `{python}`.

````
text <- c('# Test #

          Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consetetur sadipscing elitr, sed diam nonumy eirmod
          tempor invidunt ut labore et dolore magna aliquyam erat, sed diam voluptua. At
          vero eos et accusam et justo duo dolores et ea rebum. Stet clita kasd gubergren,
          no sea takimata sanctus est Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet.
          
          ```{r}
          a = 1
```

          Test
          ====
          
          Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consetetur sadipscing elitr, sed diam nonumy eirmod
          tempor invidunt ut labore et dolore magna aliquyam erat, sed diam voluptua. At
          vero eos et accusam et justo duo dolores et ea rebum. Stet clita kasd gubergren,
          no sea takimata sanctus est Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet.
          
          ```{r}
          b <- function(x) {
          d = 1
          }
          
          ```
          
          ```{r engine="python"}
          a=[]
          
          a[0]=1
          ```
          
          ```{python}
          a=[]
          
          a[0]=1
          ```


​          
          ## Same code chunk as above, but lintr will not ouput this
          ```{r}
          
          b <- function(x) {
          d = 1
          }
          
          ```
          ')
  tmp <- tempfile()

  writeLines(text, tmp)

  lintr::lint(tmp)
````
The results of the lint are below:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/12430096/40795946-84166e9a-64d1-11e8-8ed6-c1c09280c48e.png)


The part of the code that would require an edit is [here](https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/blob/15fd8ee6685248b7f477c949c1e78dc13350cd15/R/extract.R#L31).

I _think_ the fix to this would involve adding another `&&` condition that checked that the chunk began with `r` and does NOT have `engine` following it. Or perhaps more simply, found any chunk that began with anything other than `r` and ignored it. Happy to try a fix on this and submit a PR if that would be useful.

title: Accept multiple styles in object_name_linter
description:
```
> library(lintr)
> txt <- c("var_one <- 1", "varTwo <- 2", "var.three <- 3")
> linter <- object_name_linter(c("snake_case", "lowerCamelCase"))
```
Current behavior:
```
> expect_lint(txt, list("should be snake_case", line_number=3), linter)
Error in vapply(x, `[[`, character(1), "message") : 
  values must be length 1,
 but FUN(X[[1]]) result is length 2
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In if (!matches_styles(name, style)) { :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
2: In if (!matches_styles(name, style)) { :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
3: In if (!matches_styles(name, style)) { :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
```

Proposed: 
```
> expect_lint(txt, list("should be snake_case or lowerCamelCase", line_number=3), linter)
> 
```

I realize it's usually far better to pick one naming style and stick to it, but today I'm writing a package whose interface is dictated by two incompatible upstream APIs, so I'd like to allow "snake_case or dotted.case, but no others". Since users would need to explicitly opt into it by specifying multiple styles, I submit that this change doesn't pose too much of a moral hazard :)

Since `matches_styles` already returns a vector, I think this should be easy to implement and I can take a stab at it if y'all are OK with the concept.

title: File Exclusions Passed to lint_package() Not Ignored
description:
Hello Jim,

I've been running into an issue trying to lint a package while passing file exclusions via the `...`. From my understanding, the `...` should be passed from `lint_package()` -> `lint()` -> `exclude()`, which is where I want my exclusions `list()` to end up. It's a little difficult to provide a `reprex` but here is an example.

```{r}
library(lintr)
lint_package(".", exclusions = list("inst/examples/bad_lint.R"))
```
The problem is that the list of excluded files are **not** being ignored. I have traced the issue to `lintr:::exclude()`, and it stems from the fact that the filenames in the `df` object (e.g. df$filename[1]) are written as full *absolute paths*, whereas the filenames being passed via the `...` are provided as *relative path(s)*. So during the `vapply()` step, the filenames (paths) do not match, and it doesn't know to exclude these "matching" files (i.e. `file %in% namex(excl)` evaluates to `FALSE`).

To work around this I have been able to:
1. use absolute paths in the original call, which is a bit tedious and doesn't appear to be what you had in mind considering the `relative_path =` argument defaults to `TRUE`.
2. I saw in the package README.md where you suggest configuring with a `.lintr` file with the exclusions supplied there in Debian Control Format. This DOES work! The paths do not get misaligned, so it's a slightly different behavior with passing via the `...`

**Questions**:
1. Am I using `lint_package` with exclusions as you intended?
2. I have some inconveniently long paths, so specifying relative paths (which from your examples you intended to be the case) would be ideal. Besides the package level config with `.lintr`, do you have any suggestions?

I realize there is a lot more going on under the hood, so I am sorry if this is not a simple work-around. I'd appreciate any advice. BTW, I absolutely **love** `lintr`, thank you so much for putting it together. I have been trying unify our group around common code style and practices for years ... I am hoping pre-commit hooks with `lintr` will get us there! ;)

Thank you so much,
Stu

title: extract_r_source fails when knitr pattern chunk.end doesn't match any lines
description:
I have an R source file which causes lintr to throw its hands in the air and fail with an error. The problem is in the `extract_r_source` function.

**To reproduce:**

```
lines <- c("# This single comment `r length(x)` with some inline code is enough.\n")
temp <- tempfile(fileext = '.R')
cat(lines, file = temp)
tryCatch(lint(temp, with_defaults()), finally = unlink(temp))
# Error in rep.int(NA_character_, max(ends - 1)) : invalid 'times' value
# In addition: Warning messages:
#1: In max(ends - 1) : no non-missing arguments to max; returning -Inf
#2: In rep.int(NA_character_, max(ends - 1)) :
#   NAs introduced by coercion to integer range
```

The error is from https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/blob/master/R/extract.R#L17. 

If some knitr patterns are found but the `chunk.end` pattern doesn't end up matching any lines of code, an error is thrown by `rep.int` since `-Inf` gets passed as its `times` parameter. Leading up to the error:
- `pattern` is not `NULL`.
- `ends` and `starts` are `integer(0)` since no matching lines of code were found by `grepl`
- calling `max(integer(0) - 1)` returns `-Inf`
- `rep.int(NA_character_, -Inf)` throws the error above.

```R
# TODO 1

  # TODO 4
  x * 2 # TODO 5
}

```
In this first example (above), only TODO 3-5 are returned as COMMENT tokens in `source_file$parsed_content`. 

```R
a <- 1; b <- 2;
foo <- function(a, b) {
  c <- a + b; cat(c);
}
```
In this second example, only the two semicolons within the function are returned as ';' tokens. The two first are missing.

Ideally, one would want to have all needed tokens exposed, and the overcomplicated linters simplified.

The variable `parsed_content` in `get_source_expression()` seems to contain all tokens, but later in the same function, variable `expressions` seems to have dropped some of them. This illustrates that the issue is likely in lintr.

title: Bug in as.data.frame.lints() [patch]
description:
Still following the tutorial at https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lintr/vignettes/creating_linters.html

A Lint object is created as:

```
Lint(
  filename = source_file$filename,
  line_number = parsed$line1,
  column_number = parsed$col1,
  type = "style",
  message = "Use <-, not =, for assignment.",
  line = source_file$lines[parsed$line1]
  )
```

According to the help page for Lint, the linter parameter appears optional:

```
Lint(filename, line_number = 1L, column_number = NULL, type = c("style",
  "warning", "error"), message = "", line = "", ranges = NULL,
  linter = NULL)
```

All good then!

Except that further down the line when executing lint() with a small test case, I get an error message:

```
 Error in vapply(x, `[[`, character(1), "linter") : 
  values must be length 1,
 but FUN(X[[1]]) result is length 0 
10. vapply(x, `[[`, character(1), "linter") 
9. data.frame(filename = vapply(x, `[[`, character(1), "filename"), 
    line_number = vapply(x, `[[`, numeric(1), "line_number"), 
    column_number = vapply(x, `[[`, numeric(1), "column_number"), 
    type = vapply(x, `[[`, character(1), "type"), message = vapply(x,  ... 
8. as.data.frame.lints(lints) 
7. as.data.frame(lints) 
6. exclude(lints, ...) 
5. lint("./R/try_style.R", linters = semicolon_linter) at debugme.R#2
4. eval(substitute(expr), envir, enclos) 
3. evalq({
    library(lintr)
    lint("./R/try_style.R", linters = semicolon_linter)
}, envir = envir) at debugme.R#1
2. env$fun() 
1. debugSource("C:/qc/zoe_home/S001_BaseKit/debugme.R")
```

The problem is that as.data.frame.lints should accept a linter value of NULL but doesn't.

A small example reproduces the crash:

```
lints <- structure(list(Lint(
   filename = "xyz",
   line_number = 1,
   column_number = 10,
   type = "style",
   message = "Use <-, not =, for assignment.",
   line = "asdfasdfasdfasdf"
   )), class = "lints")
lintr:::as.data.frame.lints(lints)
```

If you add a "linter = 'my_linter'", then there is no crash anymore.

Cheers,
Florent

title: expect_lint() escaping issue
description:
Consider a file "doublebackslash.R" that contains a single double-backslash string:

And the following script:
```

  cat("file content is:")
  print(source_file$content)
  lintr::assignment_linter(source_file)
}

file <- "doublebackslash.R"
file_content <- "'\\\\'"

cat("\nMethod 1\n")
lintr::lint(file, linters=verbose_assignment_linter)

cat("\nMethod 2\n")
lintr:::expect_lint(content=NULL, checks=NULL, verbose_assignment_linter, file=file)

cat("\nMethod 3\n")
lintr:::expect_lint(content=file_content, checks=NULL, verbose_assignment_linter)
```

The result of running the script is:
```
Method 1
file content is:[1] "'\\\\\\\\'"
file content is:[1] "'\\\\\\\\'"

Method 2
file content is:[1] "'\\\\\\\\'"
file content is:[1] "'\\\\\\\\'" ""          

Method 3
file content is:[1] "'\\\\'"
file content is:[1] "'\\\\'"
```

I expected the same results for the three methods, but method 3 (`expect_lint` with string input) differed from the two others. I believe that `expect_lint` should be modified by escaping its string input.

title: Too many absolute_paths_linters false positives
description:
Hi Jim,

This issue is related to issue #58.

I get quite a few false positives from the absolute path linter. The strings that generated the lints look like: "/aS: 3\n/bS: Inf\n/cS: -2.2\n/dS: x" and to me, the offending character is "\n" which is highly unlikely to be included in a file path. I envison that the linter should:

1. Consider the string as a whole and estimate whether it is a valid path or not (i.e. if it contains forbidden characters).
2. Determine if the path is absolute.

The problem then boils down to which characters should be forbidden in Linux and Windows paths. These webpages (http://stackoverflow.com/questions/1976007/what-characters-are-forbidden-in-windows-and-linux-directory-names, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filename#Reserved_characters_and_words) make it clear that it is list them and on Linux, almost all characters are allowed. But a _pragmatic_ approach may be to blacklist:

- on Windows: `*` `?` `"` `<` `>` `|`
- on both Linux and Windows: all standard ASCII control codes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C0_and_C1_control_codes#C0_.28ASCII_and_derivatives.29), i.e. `\0` `\a` `\n` etc

Cheers,

Florent

title: Implemented an object_name_linter
description:
Hi,

I have written a new linter, called `object_name_linter`, which includes the features of the existing name
linters (camel_case_linter, snake_case_linter and mutiple_dots_linter) and adds new ones.

Features of `object_name_linter`:
* A single linter is needed to check for naming style (instead of several currently). Just specify the style to use and all others will be linted (including unrecognized styles, e.g. in a name like "my_inconsistentStyle").
* Possibility to enforce new styles: "alllowercase" and "UPPERCASE".
* The camelcase style is split into "UpperCamelCase" and "lowerCamelCase"
* The linters are digit-aware, i.e. digits count as both lowercase or uppercase and a name such as "html5Parser" is thus valid "lowerCamelCase" (in contrast with `camel_case_linter`).
* Style checking is turned off for names from functions that seem to extend known generics (even
  those that contain mutiple dots such as `as.data.frame.data.frame`), and this without having to load
  or require any packages.
* Private objects (with a name starting with one or multiple dots) are supported. Thus, ".my_var" is
  valid "snake_case".
* Quoted functions and operators are properly handled, i.e. backticks are removed and operators like `%in%` are not subjected to a style check.
* Only newly-defined object are submitted to style checking. This prevents imported functions (and other objects) to trigger lints.

This work partially derives from discussions at:
https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/issues/108
https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/issues/182
https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/issues/183
https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/issues/191

In my opinion, `object_name_linter` could effectively replace the existing name linters.

Best,

Florent

PS/ Not having the ability to contribute code directly through Github, I am attaching my code and unit tests here: [object_name_linter.zip](https://github.com/jimhester/lintr/files/711759/object_name_linter.zip)

title: Cache directory input not respected
description:
Hi Jim,

I found a small issue in the `lint()` function, when specifying a cache directory. In the root directory of a package, consider:
```R
setwd("tests/")
cacheDir <- file.path("..", ".lintr_cache")
lintr::expect_lint_free(cache=cacheDir)
```
This should create a directory ".lintr_cache", but it creates instead "~/.R/lintr_cache/".

After investigating, I found that in file "R/lint.R", function `lint()`, the line that reads:
```R
save_cache(lint_cache, filename)
```
should be replaced by:
```R
save_cache(lint_cache, filename, cache_dir)
```

Additionally, the documentation for the "cache" could be improved by stating that it is a directory (and not a simple file).

Cheers,
Florent

title: expectation_lint() message and marker bugs
description:
Hi,

I found a few issues with `expectation_lint()`:
```R
> lintr:::expect_lint("x <- 1", NULL)                # markers displayed!
> lintr:::expect_lint("x <- 1\n", NULL)              # markers displayed!
Error:  returned ...
> lintr:::expect_lint("x <- 1\n\n", NULL)            # markers displayed!
Error in stop(exp) : bad error message

> lintr:::expect_lint("x <- 1", "superfluous")
Error:  did not return 1 lints as expected from content:x <- 1
> lintr:::expect_lint("x <- 1\n", "superfluous")
As expected
> lintr:::expect_lint("x <- 1\n\n", "superfluous")
Error in stop(exp) : bad error message

```


1. **Markers displayed**:
When running tests, I expect no lint markers to be displayed in Rstudio (or other IDEs). Simply replacing `print(lints)` by ` lints` in `expectation_lint()` fixes this issue.

2. **Bad error message**:
This second problem is due to `expectation_lint()` passing a "msg" containing more than one element to `testthat::expect()`; the `lints` variable contains more than one lint. In addition, the name of the linters are supposed to be shown, but since I am using the default linters (using `...`), no linter name is shown. Personally, I would drop this information as long as the details of the lints (which contain the linter name) are shown.
In the case where `check=NULL`, "msg" could be:
```R
paste0("Got ", length(lints), " lints instead of none!\n", paste0(lints, collapse="\n"))
```
In the case where `check="superfluous"`, "msg" could be:
```R
paste0("Got ", length(lints), " lints instead of ", length(checks), "!\n", paste0(lints, collapse="\n"))
```

That's it! Cheers,
Florent


PS/ The sofware versions used are:
* R 3.2.5
* RStudio 1.0.136
* lintr development version (23/02/2017)

title: bookdown repositories are incorrectly scoped for linting
description:
When using [`bookdown`](http://bookdown.org) in RStudio (though I suspect this problem will exist elsewhere, too), it's customary *not* necessarily to call `library(foo)` in the same `*.Rmd` as some function `foo::bar()` therein.
Erroneously, RStudio (aka. `lintr`) will then lint `foo::bar()` as:

> no symbol named 'bar()' in scope

Though when run through `bookdown` (which the repository and RStudio "know") with the default "Merge-Then-Knit" strategy, there is, in fact no problem.

This is a bit annoying when editing a bookdown, and I'm wondering whether this could be fixed in `lintr` by somehow scoping all `*.Rmd`s inside a project.

@verenakasztantowicz had the same issue.

Hoping this is the right place, and it's not an RStudio or bookdown issue.

---

**MWE (sort of, not a fully-fledge bookdown, but I hope you get the idea)**

Let's have an `index.Rmd` like so:

    --- 
    title: "A not so minimal not so working example"
    author: "Calvin, Hobbes the Tiger"
    site: bookdown::bookdown_site
    ---
    
    ```{r preamble, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
    library(ggplot2)
    ```
    
    ```{r test-in-index}

    ```

This lints just fine:

![finelint](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/5372770/19947994/d14cd59c-a14a-11e6-9930-52dd50800044.png)

Try the same thing in `first-chapter.Rmd`, in the same repository and at root and no such luck:

    ```{r test-in-index}

    ```
